https://footballgroundguide.com/leagues/.text: News Stadiums England Northern Ireland Republic of Ireland Scotland Wales Non-League Europe Americas Other stadiums New stadiums Old Trafford redevelopment: Updates on new Man Utd stadium Everton new stadium – Bramley-Moore Dock Wrexham stadium expansion: Kop redevelopment Chelsea new stadium Elland Road expansion New Luton stadium – Power Court Stadium Reviews Gambling Free Bets Sports Betting Sites Casino Sites Bingo Sites Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Away days News Fans Game day info History West Bromwich Albion The Hawthorns - West Brom stadium See 39 reviews Submit a review Capacity: 26,688 (all seated) Club Nickname: The Baggies Year Opened: 1900 Pitch Size: 105m x 68m Address: Halfords Lane, West Bromwich, West Midlands, B71 4LF Phone: 0871 271 1100 Pitch Type: Grass Shirt Sponsors: Ideal Heating Fax: 0871 271 9861 Ticket Office: 0121 227 2227 Undersoil Heating: Yes Manufacturer: Puma Home Kit: White and Navy Away Kit: Lime with Black trim Third Kit: Navy and Red See more Last Update: July 26, 2026 What is the Hawthorns like for away fans? The Hawthorns has been the home of West Bromwich Albion since 1900 and remains one of the most recognisable stadiums in English football, making it a worthwhile away day for supporters visiting the Black Country. With a capacity of 26,804, the stadium strikes a good balance between hosting sizeable crowds and maintaining an intimate atmosphere, allowing fans to stay close to the action throughout the match. Visiting supporters are typically allocated around 2,500 tickets in the left-hand side of the Smethwick End. In league fixtures, the stand is shared with home supporters, although away allocations can be increased significantly for cup ties, with visiting fans occasionally occupying the entire stand. Getting to the stadium is relatively straightforward, with excellent transport links to Birmingham for those travelling by train, while motorists benefit from the ground’s location just off Junction 1 of the M5. There are also plenty of places to eat and drink in the surrounding area, with a range of pubs, bars and restaurants available nearby, while supporters looking for an even greater choice can head towards Birmingham city centre before kick-off. The Hawthorns in the news West Brom celebrate the 125th anniversary of The Hawthorns The 2025 calendar year marked 125 years since West Bromwich Albion moved into The Hawthorns, with the club celebrating the milestone by bringing the stadium’s historic roots back to life. As the name suggests, hawthorns are a type of thorny shrub, and the land on which the stadium now stands was once covered with them before Albion made the ground their permanent home in 1900. To commemorate the anniversary, the club planted 20 hawthorn trees along the stadium’s eastern boundary. The club’s Managing Director, Mark Miles, said: “We are excitedly preparing for the stadium’s 125th anniversary – and from our earliest conversations, it became clear it was time to bring hawthorns back to The Hawthorns. “The fact that the club’s crest features the leaves and berries of a hawthorn tree, with a throstle atop, will make it quite special for all visitors to be able to witness a similar view whenever they visit our home.” Those hawthorn trees already stand at around two metres tall and, provided there are no issues along the way, will continue to grow and mature for many more years to come. The Baggies played their 125th anniversary fixture on 13th September 2025. Unfortunately for Ryan Mason’s side, they were unable to mark the occasion with a win, as they fell to a narrow 1-0 loss against Derby County. On the day, the West Brom players wore shirts with a ‘125 years at The Hawthorns’ logo. The players then signed their shirts to be auctioned off, with the proceeds going to The Albion Foundation. Supporters were also given commemorative flags, a brass band played before kick-off and the match ball was presented by West Brom legend Tony ‘Bomber’ Brown. Safe standing areas to be installed at the Hawthorns West Bromwich Albion have installed 3,864 safe standing positions throughout the summer. Although the Baggies ultimately fell short of promotion during the 2024/25 season, the club will be hoping that the new standing areas inside the stadium could provide fans with the boost they need to continue turning out in large numbers to cheer the club on in the Championship next season. The safe standing ‘seats’ have been split across the Smethwick End and the Millennium Corner. The decision to follow the ongoing trend of safe standing areas in English football came following a consultation period with supporters’ groups, the Sports Ground Safety Authority and the club’s Safety Advisory Group. West Brom’s managing director, Mark Miles, said: “The club have long been an advocate of safe standing. A lot has changed since The Hawthorns became an all-seater stadium almost 30 years ago, and we’re confident now is the right time to bring standing back in a safe and controlled way.” West Brom chants West Brom fans singing “The Lord’s my Shepherd” ? What a sight! pic.twitter.com/kW0gaU5gTm — SAMUEL (@SamOgun_) September 26, 2020 Best views and seating plan The Hawthorns is a compact, all-seater ground that is enclosed with corners full of seats. However, unlike most modern ‘bowl’ stadiums, the Hawthorns certainly has more character with a mixture of different-looking stands. For example, the impressive-looking East Stand, which was opened in 2001, is a large single-tiered stand with a row of executive boxes running along the back. The lower part of the seating area extends around the corners, and the space above the previous open corners has been filled with corrugated sheeting. There is a thin supporting pillar on each side of the stand to support the corner structures. On the other side is the smaller Halfords Lane Stand. This stand, which was opened in 1982, stretches around two corners of the ground. The home end, the Birmingham Road Stand, is large, covered, and quite steep. At the other end, away fans are housed in the Smethwick End. Both these ends were built in 1994/95. There are two huge ‘widescreen’ video screens installed on the ground, one on either side of the East Stand. An interesting feature of the ground is that in one corner of the ground (between the East Stand & Birmingham Road End), you will notice perched up on a wall, a large Throstle standing on a football. This has been kept over from the previous stand (it used to sit above the clock on the half-time scoreboard) and maintains a link to the past. Outside the ground on the same corner are the ‘Jeff Astle Memorial Gates’ erected in tribute to the legendary striker. Just beyond the East Stand Car Park is a Memorial Garden. One interesting fact about The Hawthorns is that it is the highest ground in England (in terms of feet above sea level). They can be reached from Birmingham New Street, either by first taking a train to Smethwick Galton Bridge and changing there for The Hawthorns, or by taking a Metro Tram (which runs every eight minutes on Saturday afternoons) from directly outside New Street Station. Travel by train takes around 20-25 minutes, while the Metro is around 13 minutes. Alternatively, the Hawthorns Station is also served by direct trains from Birmingham Moor Street and Birmingham Snow Hill. The Metro Line also runs via Birmingham Snow Hill. Please note, though, that rail tickets to the Hawthorns are not valid on the Metro line. A separate Metro journey ticket will need to be purchased. A one-day saver ticket can be purchased for £5 (per Adult ticket), which covers the journey to the Hawthorns and back from either New Street or Snow Hill. Travelling Down From The North West? Matt Wharton informs me, ‘If you are travelling down from the North West and your train calls at Wolverhampton, then it is a lot easier to get to Hawthorns using the Midland Metro from Wolverhampton. The tram leaves from Bilston Street . You can either get off at the Kenrick Park stop for the Vine pub or The Hawthorns for the stadium. Continuing by train from Wolverhampton into Birmingham New Street and then taking either a train or Metro back out to The Hawthorns will add 45 minutes to one hour to your journey time.’ By car The Hawthorns is located on the A41 (Birmingham-West Bromwich Road). If approaching from outside the area, the ground is about half-a-mile from Junction 1 of the M5. On leaving the M5, take the A41 towards Birmingham, the ground is on your right. Beware, though, of speed cameras on this stretch of the A41. They played at Cooper’s Hill for a year, spent two years at Dartmouth Park, whilst Bunn’s Field also hosted home games for a solitary season. Next up was a three-year stay at Four Acres, a ground owned by the local Cricket Club, before 15 years at Stoney Lane. When the tenancy agreement on Stoney Lane expired, the Baggies moved to the Hawthorns. The capacity during the early days stood at an impressive 35,000, and the club opted to buy the stadium 13 years after moving in; that was 1913. Within a decade of purchasing the ground, West Brom broke the 50k mark for attendance figures; it was largely underpinned by large terraces being built after World War One. The next noteworthy changes to the stadium, apart from gradual increases in capacity, came in the late forties as the club became the first to install turnstiles that could automatically tot up the attendance figures. From then on, changes to West Brom’s stadium were to reduce capacity. These alterations ticked two boxes; they saw additional seating, which was a growing trend and, more importantly, helped to control spiralling hooliganism. By the 1990s, the Hawthorns was fully seated, whilst the 2000s saw stand redevelopment to bring a more modern feel to the place. The Hawthorns record and average attendance Record Attendance 64,815 v Arsenal FA Cup 6th Round, March 6th, 1937. Modern all-attended attendance record 27,751 v Portsmouth Premier League, May 15th, 2005. Average Attendance 2025-2026: 23,605 (Championship) 2024-2025: 24,942 (Championship) 2023-2024: 18,603 (Championship) 2022-2023: 23,038 (Championship) 2021-2022: 21,875 (Championship) 2020-2021: 283 (Covid) (Premier League) 2019-2020: 24,053 (Championship) Local rivals West Brom vs Wolves rivalry West Brom vs Wolves is dubbed the Black Country derby, and, somewhat surprisingly to most, it is one of the fiercest rivalries England has. There are just 11 miles between the two clubs, with clashes dating back some 140 years. The only reason it is not a better-known clash is that the vast majority of the time, the game has not graced the top flight; even so, head down to the West Brom ground on the day of a Black Country derby and sparks will fly. The two sides have not played in the same division since the 2020-21 Premier League season but that will change in 2026-27, as West Brom were able to survive in the Championship while Wolves suffered Premier League relegation, meaning they will meet again in the second tier. The two sides last faced off in the FA Cup fourth round in January 2024 when West Brom fell to a 2-0 home defeat against their bitter rivals. While they may have experienced disappointment in that cup tie, the Baggies have managed to avoid defeat in each of their previous four league encounters (W3, D1). Impressively, they have not lost a league game at home to Wolves since September 1996. West Brom vs Birmingham City rivalry The derby with Birmingham City is another based on location, location, location. These two are more tightly located than many other more recognised derbies at just 15 miles, but because both have bigger rivals to worry about, it doesn’t get the attention it deserves. Animosity does exist, though. The rivalry has intensified in recent times with the two sides both plying their trade in the Championship, with the clubs meeting in the second tier for the first time in the 2025-26 campaign in the autumn, when the points were shared. Alex Mowatt scored via a deflected strike to put the Baggies ahead at The Hawthorns, before former Germany international Marvin Ducksch equalised for Blues to force a share of the spoils at the Black Country venue. There is certainly no love between the two West Midlands side, however the teams will clash on Valentine’s Day in 2026, with West Brom suffering a heavy 4-1 defeat the last time they visited St Andrew’s for a league clash during the 2023-24 season. Both clubs are set for a new rival match next season, with Wolves officially relegated to the Championship after eight seasons in the Premier League. West Brom vs Aston Villa rivalry You can rinse and repeat the above here. West Brom and Aston Villa are not the best of friends; that’s clear on match days, but because Villa have Birmingham and the Baggies have Wolves to hate, this fixture doesn’t get much focus until it lands on the calendar; that doesn’t make it friendly, though. Future Stadium Developments The club are believed to be drawing up plans to expand the capacity of The Hawthorns to over 40,000 by either redeveloping or adding a tier to the Halfords Lane Stand. The expansion plans were benchmarked for £20m; the latest word from the club, however, is that any work is firmly on hold at present with the demand for extra capacity simply not there right now. The atmosphere was good throughout and is certainly helped in the away end by the fact that West Brom's loudest singing section seemed to be in the same stand right next to us! Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Getting back to the station was fairly easy and we didn't queue for too long at the Hawthorns before we were able to get down to the platform. They seemed to have a well-organised system in place for fans using the station. Getting into Birmingham turned out to be less straightforward as West Midlands Police wouldn't let Charlton fans off to go to the City Centre, and instead ended up putting lots of fans straight onto any train heading back to London, even if they weren't booked on it. It was very over the top policing and came without any explanation. Thankfully we managed to push past the Police at Snow Hill and escaped, but many others weren't as fortunate! Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: A good away day, and we were happy to take a point against a team expected to be up there at the end of the season. The heavy-handedness of the stewards beforehand, and then the Police when getting away from the ground was a shame, and was unnecessary. But all in all a good ground to visit and a worthwhile trip to the Midlands. See more 22nd September 2019 Paul Evans (Huddersfield Town) West Bromwich Albion v Huddersfield Town EFL Championship Saturday 22nd September 2019, 12 noon Paul Evans (Huddersfield Town) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Hawthorns Ground? I've developed the mindset 'Town have GOT to win sooner or later!' The Hawthorns is less than 20 miles from my home in Tamworth, so it was a good opportunity to see my team. I've made half a dozen visits over the last few decades; on the first occasion, I saw a very young Kevin Keegan play for Scunthorpe in an F.A. Cup tie. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? I use my bus pass as often as possible, but the early kickoff on a Sunday reduced the public transport options a lot. I parked in Water Orton, got a bus to Birmingham and another, No.74, to the stadium. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? I didn't fancy the local pubs as I was in my Town shirt. Didn't meet any home fans. Took my lunch and a drink with me – I've never understood why so many supporters fork out extortionate sums for food and drink within grounds. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hawthorns Stadium? The Hawthorns is surprisingly small for what purports to be a major club. It means, though, that it's nearly full for most games which produces a cracking atmosphere at the away end. This is shared with the most vocal home support, which causes a lot of not always friendly banter. At least segregation is rigorously maintained, notably after the match (see 'getting away from the ground' below). This makes the extremely zealous searching of away fans even more annoying – it's by far the most intrusive I've encountered. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. We went mental when we took the lead (TWICE!!), but as the game went on it became increasingly obvious that as usual, we'd chuck it away. West Brom are a far better team than when I last saw them, at the John Smith's in November 2017, and should make the playoffs at least. I was quite surprised at the silence in the opposite stand (the fabled Brummie Road end). We all stood up for the whole match; the stewards wisely left us to it. Toilets were clean and tidy. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Remember when Sunday was the quietest day of the week? Just a distant memory now. Birmingham Road, West Bromwich was but a few steps from Hell after the match – football traffic mixed with shoppers causes total gridlock. My relief at not going by car was soon replaced by frustration at not knowing if the bus would ever get there. But it did eventually! Due to segregation, getting out of the ground for away fans is by a footpath which leads you well away from the main entrance into Middlemore Road where visiting coaches park. It almost doubles the distance you have to walk to get to the bus stops on Birmingham Road. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: Quite enjoyable despite the result and the Stasi-like security check, but I can't see myself going there again. If I ever do, I'll try getting there by Metro – The Hawthorns Station is only a couple of furlongs away. The way Huddersfield are playing, though, I shall quite possibly be submitting a review of a League One stadium this time next year. See more 12th February 2019 Liam Smith (Neutral) West Bromwich Albion v Nottingham Forest Championship League Tuesday 12th February 2019, 8pm Liam Smith (Neutral) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Hawthorns Ground? Two of the people that I live with at my university accommodation are West Brom and Forest fans respectively so this fixture would be heavily debated. Quite a few of us planned on going since we finish at on Tuesdays and no lectures on Wednesdays. I was excited to see The Hawthorns as it would probably be a long while before I see my Stevenage team play there. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? The journey from Bristol to The Hawthorns was pretty straightforward, probably not enjoyable for the driver being the only person with a car with the West Brom and Forest fans bickering in the back. The journey took just over two hours and we parked at the WBA fans parents house just by Smethwick Galton Bridge Station. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? We made a sort of a day out of it, arriving at the house at around 3pm. We then headed off into Birmingham at around 5ish and ate and drank at The Dragon Wetherspoons, not far from New Street Station. We then took the train from Moor Street to the Hawthorns which took no time at all. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hawthorns Stadium? From the outside the ground was unspectacular however from the inside the view was very good. We were sat in the Millennium Corner which was right by the away fans and although the ground is modernised, it still has something about it and not like the new soulless bowl builds you see appearing in the Premier and Championship Leagues. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The atmosphere was shocking, the attendance was low and it was on a Tuesday night. It was also being shown live on Sky Sports so that probably made all the difference. The Forest fans were loud and took a full following. I would like to hear The Hawthorns when it's full and rocking like I've saw it on the TV with my WBA fan flatmate. The game wasn't the best despite it being a 2-2 draw, Forest's first goal was shocking defending and West Brom's late equalising penalty was controversial. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: We walked back from The Hawthorns into Smethwick which took around half an hour and then drove away easily, the car ride on the way back home was too fun, not. Our West Brom and Forest friends can't stand each other now! Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: It was quite eventful. I would like to see the Hawthorns it full one day and would definitely come back. Let us hope Stevenage get a cup draw there next season! See more 2nd February 2019 Con (Middlesbrough) West Bromwich Albion v Middlesbrough Championship League Saturday 2nd February 2019, 3pm Con (Middlesbrough) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Hawthorns? We thought would be a good test for Boro – a mark whether we have genuine promotion credentials. Also, I have never been before and was looking forward to see where the great Cyril Regis did his stuff. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Good. We drove up from London and parked off Beeches Road for a fiver. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? Went to the Vine pub as mentioned on this website and it is terrific. The facade doesn't do it justice. There is loads of room, grilled chicken cooked in front of you and a good selection of beers. The home fans were great. We had my young nephew and his friend with us. No problems. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hawthorns? We thought the Hawthorns was a terrific ground. All enclosed and reasonably close to the pitch so made for a good atmosphere. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. I would have taken a point so to get all three was a bonus – not sure we deserved it. The home fans created a good atmosphere – all sides seemed to be singing. The queue for refreshments was long and slow. And then to be charged £4.50 for what was effectively a can of John Smiths was naughty. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: The only way out is down a fenced off path heading south east – presumably to avoid trouble. So you end up on the Middlemore Road. No big deal but if you park on the West side of the M5 it just adds to the walk back. You need to be careful crossing above Junction 1 of the M5 on foot! Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: A very good day out. See more 12th January 2019 John Holland (Norwich City) West Bromwich Albion v Norwich City Championship League Saturday 12th January 2019, 3pm John Holland (Norwich City) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Hawthorns? I went with my two sons and my oldest was very keen to go to this ground as it was new for him and I hadn't been since 1979. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? We decided to drive and apart from various roadworks it was very straightforward. We parked at the Park Inn. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? We arrived at 1pm and aimed for the Vine pub but this already had a queue outside, so instead we ended up in the fanzone near to the ground where we had a choice of food, beer and could watch a match on a big screen or a band on stage. The fans of both clubs mingled without any issues. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hawthorns Stadium? The first impression was that the Hawthorns has changed a lot in the last 40 years. It felt both modern and traditional at the same time. The view and legroom were fine even though two of us are over six foot tall. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. Fans of my age would remember the great Albion side of the late 70s and early 80s and with the match being close to the anniversary of the sad passing of Cyrille Regis's sad passing, the club used this match to honour that team before kick off. When play started Albion looked the stronger team and took the lead, Norwich managed to keep it to one goal and came into the game later on and equalised in the last 10 minutes. A point at West Brom was very welcome. The atmosphere was okay and I had no problem with the stewards etc. My son tried one of the pies and was not impressed, however, the service was very efficient. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: It was a pain to have to walk around the stadium to get back to the car and the roads were very congested. We decided to leave the car for a bit and walk into the town centre for a bite to eat, this is not a short walk! Driving back at 7pm was fine. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: It was a good day out and a good game to watch. Norwich took 2,700 fans and with a home sell out it turned the match into an event. See more 29th December 2018 Luke Smith (Neutral) West Brom Albion v Sheffield Wednesday Championship League Saturday 29th December 2018, 3pm Luke Smith (Neutral) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Hawthorns Ground? This was the last stadium I had left to do in the West Midlands and with my team, Bristol Rovers selling out at Oxford, and unlikely to play West Brom any time soon I felt it right to go and see a sell-out at The Hawthorns. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Coming from Bristol my journey was mainly the M5, and as the ground is situated about 100 metres from M5 Junction 1. It's one of the best grounds on that front. Parking was a bit tricky, £5 everywhere to park and took nearly 45 minutes to leave the car park after the match had ended. That being said though, there is enough to do nearby to allow the car parks to empty and you can just drive straight out. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? Wandered along Birmingham Road, looked at the famous Jeff Astle Gates and grabbed a quick bite to eat from a local shop. The fans were friendly enough. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hawthorns Stadium? The ground is fairly unremarkable from the outside, though when you do get into the stadium it's quite impressive. I like that each of the stands has their own character, with the home end behind the goal being packed it was a sight to behold. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game was dreadful. Sheffield Wednesday took an early lead and I'm not sure the football left five metres either side of the halfway line until the 94th minute when West Brom equalised. Having seen Wednesday away (and been in among them a few times) on several occasions, I could make a very strong argument that they have the best fans in England. Certainly, they're the best in The Championship. They make loads of noise, have lots of original chants and turn up in numbers. That being said, once the Albion supporters got going it was very loud. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Other than the 45 minutes to empty a local car park, it was fairly easy to get out. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: The Hawthorns is not the best ground in the West Midlands but certainly not the worst. One of the worst games of football at that level I've seen for a long time. I can imagine that on derby days the atmosphere is absolutely phenomenal. I would definitely go again. See more 26th December 2018 John and Jason Southgate-Riley (Neutrals) West Bromwich Albion vs Wigan Athletic Championship League Wednesday 26th December 2018, 3pm John and Jason Southgate-Riley (Neutrals) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Hawthorns Ground? Driving back home from visiting my parents for the Christmas period, me and my son wanted to find a stadium that I have not attended yet. The perfect chance arose after finding out that there were going to be more seating being sold for this fixture as a result of the Wigan Atheltic supporters not filling their section, this also meant that my wife and three girls could do some boxing day shopping in Birmingham too. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? No trains on Boxing Day is always difficult so it was going on the bus from Birmingham to West Bromwich which took just over an hour. We found out that a Metro Light Rail system is by the stadium as well in which we got back on, which was easier. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? We arrived late so that meant that we could not get any refreshments before the kick off. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hawthorns Stadium? The view of the pitch was very good, directly behind the goal which would have been for away followers if was sold. The other sides of the ground were quite good as well, a modernised ground but still with character, in comparison to other stadiums. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. We just sat down as West Brom scored the first goal of a 2-0 win. A scrappy affair, with tackles flying in left right and centre. The atmosphere wasn't the best but it can never be with Boxing Day football. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Getting away on the Metro was a breeze in comparison to the bus. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: It was an okay day. Boxing Day football is never the best but it's another stadium ticked off of my list. See more 10th November 2018 Shaun (Leeds United) West Bromwich Albion v Leeds United Championship League Saturday 10th November 2018, 5.30pm Shaun ( Leeds United) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Hawthorns? Another new ground and interested to see how the players would adjust to the altitude. The answer: not very well! How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Pretty straightforward, just off J1 of the M5. You can see it on your right before you leave the motorway. We were staying in the nearby Premier Inn so parked there. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? I h ad something to eat then walked to the ground. Home fans tended to keep themselves to themselves. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hawthorns? Good view even though we were in a corner. The noisy home fans sharing the stand behind the goal helped to create some atmosphere. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The stewards were poor, to be honest. You enter the stand in the middle and we tried to go to the upper tier. Our allocated seats were for the lower tier but it was already full. However, the steward insisted we went down there and so we ended up standing on the stairs with 30-40 other fans. Another steward insisted we moved into a row and wanted us to stand directly in front of another supporter blocking his view. We refused. In the end, I asked a policeman to get us into the upper tier where there was space and he managed to persuade the stewards to do that. Rant over there was a great atmosphere and even when we were 4-0 down many of our fans sang in defiance (to be fair over the years we’ve got plenty of practice in that!) Photo : Hammersfan Everything you need to know ahead of our next trip to The London stadium, home of West Ham United FC. GETTING TO THE LONDON STADIUM BY CAR Exit the M11 : At the end of the M11 motorway, stay in the left-hand lane and follow signs for the North Circular A406 (S) towards the A12 and A13. Merge onto the A12 . As the roads merge, move into the left-hand lane for the A12. Exit onto the A106 , take the exit onto the A106, signposted for Stratford and Westfield. At the bottom of the slip road, at the traffic lights, use the left-hand filter lane towards Stratford and Westfield. Continue along this road; the stadium will be on your right. BY TRAIN The three closest train stations to the London Stadium are Stratford, Stratford International and Hackney Wick, which are all around 10 to 15 minutes walk from the stadium itself. Stratford station (Jubilee, Central Lines and DLR) is located next to Westfield and has overground connections to London Liverpool Street and Clapham Junction. Supporters are advised that after the match, fans heading back to Stratford station are diverted on a route that avoids the shopping centre and there the queues are managed to regulate the flow of supporters into the station. There are also likely to be lengthy queues on the platforms as well. Stratford International Railway station is on the other side of Westfield to Stratford and is served by local services from London St Pancras, which is about seven minutes away. It is also located on the Docklands Light Railway. Hackney Wick is on the west side of the stadium when to compared to the two Stratford stations and Westfield. It is served by trains from Clapham Junction, Richmond and Stratford. It also stops at Highbury and Islington, which is also situated on the Victoria Tube line. Supporters are being discouraged from using Hackney Wick on matchdays due to its small size, but it is open on matchdays and you are advised to arrive in good time. After the game, services from this station are likely to be packed with fans who have already got on at Stratford. BY TUBE Take any of the Elizabeth Line, Central Line, Jubilee Line, Overground or Docklands Light Railway to Stratford. Overground to Hackney Wick. You can take the Docklands Light Railway to Pudding Mill Lane. PARKING CAR PARKING There is car parking available at Westfield Stratford (£10 for 3 – 6 hours) and Stratford International Station (£19/event day). It can take an hour to get out of car parks after a match. BIKE PARKING There is a London Cycle Superhighway from central London (Aldgate) to Stratford City. Westfield has 780 secure bicycle parking spaces. The Olympic Park is bicycle friendly with several bicycle parking locations in close proximity to the Stadium. The Olympic Park has 310 docking points for London’s cycle hire scheme (Santander Bikes) spread across eight docking stations in and around the Park. ENJOYING THE AREA AWAY PUBS There are very few pubs that will welcome away supporters in the vicinity of the London Stadium, so Fulham supporters may prefer to drink in central London before heading to the ground. The Hamilton Hall Wetherspoon’s outlet at Liverpool Street station has been a popular meeting point for fans travelling to West Ham since they moved to the London Stadium. Some of the bars in Westfield may tolerate away supporters in colours, except during high-risk matches, which rarely would a fixture against Fulham be deemed so, although this will be decided by those running the bars on the day. PLACES TO EAT Westfield Stratford has various fast food outlets and many restaurants. Hackney Wick has over 30 places to eat and drink, plus street food vendors. OTHER RECOMMENDED STOPS The Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park has a number of attractions, such as the ArcelorMittal Orbit, Abba Voyage and opening in 2025 – Sadler’s Wells East, BBC Studios and the V&A Museum. GUIDES FOR YOUR DAY Official West Ham accessibility guide Level Playing Field Access Guide USEFUL TO KNOW Cashless – please bring a credit or debit card to make payments within the stadium. WiFi – wifi is available throughout the stadium. Children policy – Under 5s are allowed into the stadium on matchdays, as long as they have a ticket allocated for them. Under 16s are not allowed in the stadium unless accompanied by an adult. Walking to the stadium – It is a 10-minute walk from nearest stations. There are stop/go boards that hold supporters back on the walk back to Stratford station. https://www.brentfordfc.com/en/make-the-.text: Brentford FC Conference & Events Community Sports Trust Safeguarding Sign In Register Latest Video Fixtures & Results Teams Tickets Fans Shop Change language English Search burger menu More Next Match Hull City (A) Men's First Team Match Centre Make the most of your matchday Wolves v Brentford, Saturday 20 December, 3pm Make the Most of your Matchday - Wolves Ticket information Away fans are situated in the lower tier of the Steve Bull Stand, which will be stated on your ticket. The ticket office opens for collections from . Please remember to bring photo ID if you need to collect your tickets at the ground. Travelling by train Fans have the option to either travel directly to Wolverhampton or go via Birmingham. Direct trains to Wolverhampton Station depart London Euston hourly at 20 minutes to the hour (e.g. 11:40am) and take approximately 1 hour and 49 minutes. Alternatively, you can take any train from Euston to Birmingham New Street and change there, where frequent services to Wolverhampton take just 16 minutes. Supporters can also travel to Birmingham Moor Street from London Marylebone on a slower but often cheaper service. As well as trains from Birmingham New Street , there are also trams to Wolverhampton St George’s , which take just 25 minutes, or plenty of local taxis. Supporters are advised to carefully check the validity of their ticket and permitted route. Wolverhampton Train Station is less than a 15-minute walk to the ground. The last direct train to make kick-off is the , and the last direct train home is at . Travelling by car For those travelling from London, take the M25 and then the M40. After leaving the M40, supporters should join the M6 and exit at Junction 10. From there, follow the A454 via Willenhall to the Wolverhampton Ring Road. Once you reach the Ring Road, take the fourth exit towards Stafford and follow signs for Molineux Stadium. There are many parking options, such as Birch Street, Camp Street, and other city centre car parks. The postcode for Molineux is WV1 4QR . Travelling by coach We will be running away coaches for this match. Coaches will depart from Ealing Road , adjacent to the Novotel Hotel, at 9am . They are priced at £39 for adults and £29 for concessions . All coach information can be found here. Tickets can be purchased here. Before the match Most pubs in the city are strictly for home supporters; however, TWELVE on Broad Street has been recommended by the hosts as the new designated away pub. For away fans wanting a more relaxed atmosphere, The Combermere Arms is also welcoming visitors. This is a 15-minute walk to the ground. In previous years, supporters have headed to the Blue Brick by the Premier Inn or The Prince Albert near the station, but both are now closed. Alternatively, fans travelling via Birmingham can try any pub in the city centre there but should allow plenty of time before kick-off when travelling on to Wolverhampton. Near the ground, supporters from past seasons have recommended food at The Staveley Chippy and Shawarma . For families staying for the weekend, Wolves recommend several attractions such as Air Space , The Grand Theatre , and Wolverhampton Art Gallery . Before the match, the city centre also has plenty of restaurants to choose from. Getting back after the match The last direct train from Wolverhampton to London is at . For those travelling via Birmingham, the last train from Birmingham New Street Station to London Euston Station is at . After the game, traffic can build up on the roads. We advise supporters to follow the crowds back to Wolverhampton Station before taking a train either to London or Birmingham. Accessibility Wolves have 14 wheelchair places available for matches, plus assistant tickets if required. These are located in the Steve Bull Lower, Block J2. Buses or other vehicles carrying disabled supporters can arrange a drop-off by contacting the club in advance. There are accessible toilets in the away end. The home side’s Disability Access Team can be contacted on 01902 810485 . For any other accessibility queries in advance, please contact Brentford’s Disability Access Officer at [email protected] . Guide dogs can be accommodated anywhere in the stadium. Staying the night There is a range of hotels for visiting fans to choose from, suitable for every budget, including Novotel, Premier Inn, Redwings, and Britannia. Wolverhampton has a variety of bars in the city centre to suit all preferences. For those heading up the night before the game, options include The Bohemian , The Parisian , and the nightclub The Planet . Alternatively, fans can go out in nearby Birmingham, which offers a wider range of options. Safety Safety information and banned items can be found on Wolves’ website here We hope you enjoy the match. Come on you Bees! https://wrexham.com/visit/matchday/the-t.text: News Council Columns Senedd Contact News Council Columns Senedd Contact Home / Visit Wrexham / Matchday / The Turf Matchday ▾ Matchday — Overview The Ground Tickets The Turf Songs & Chants What to Expect Matchday The Ground Tickets The Turf Songs & Chants What to Expect ← All sections The Turf If the Racecourse is the body of Wrexham AFC, The Turf is its soul. This small, famous pub on the corner of the Racecourse Ground is where the football club was born in 1864, and it has been the centre of matchday life ever since. It is the oldest public house at any sports stadium in the world. A pub older than the football club The original Turf Tavern was built sometime between 1795 and 1819 on the edge of what was then a racecourse used for horse racing and cricket. The upper section of the building is believed to have been constructed specifically as a grandstand for racegoers after the first meeting took place at the ground in 1807. On , the Turf Tavern hosted the end-of-season dinner of the Denbighshire County Cricket Club. During the evening, chairman Edward Manners lamented the lack of winter sports and proposed forming a football team. The members present agreed, and Wrexham Association Football Club was founded on the spot. The pub where you are drinking your pre-match pint is the exact place where one of the oldest football clubs in the world came into existence. The club has played at the Racecourse almost continuously since that night. The Turf has been there for all of it – the European nights of the 1970s and 1980s, the financial crises, the dodgy owners, the meeting in the back yard when fans looked to raise cash to save the club recently, the years in non-league, and the Hollywood takeover that changed everything. When the Mold Road Stand was constructed in 1999, it obscured the Turf from external view, but the pub remained, tucked into the corner of the ground where it has always been. Before that, you used to be able to watch matches from the balcony – with some speculation that redevelopment could see that open up again. In 2007, the pub was threatened with demolition as part of stadium redevelopment plans. Wales First Minister Rhodri Morgan stepped in to support its survival. It also also served as a point of note on the Olympic Torch Relay when it visited Wrexham on . The Turf on matchday On a home matchday, The Turf is the place to be. It fills up early, two to three hours before a Saturday 3pm kick-off is not unusual, and the atmosphere builds steadily as the crowd grows. The pub spills out into the car park area, where a special ‘fan zone’ area has been created. Wayne, the long term landlord (he has been in place well before the takeover and knows all about where we have come from and the journey since!), and his team are well known for making everyone feel welcome, whether you are a season ticket holder of 40 years or a first-time visitor from the other side of the world. There is a warmth to The Turf that is difficult to replicate. Conversations start easily, strangers buy each other pints, old songs get sung. If you have come to Wrexham for the football and want to understand what the club means to this town, spend an hour in The Turf even if not on a matchday. The pub shows live sport on screens throughout and hosts live music from local bands. The walls are covered in Wrexham AFC memorabilia, storied shirts, scarves, photographs and mementos from across the decades. It is part pub, part museum, part living room. It is genuinely everything you would want it to be and more. Famous visitors Since Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac took over the club, The Turf has become something of a pilgrimage site. The owners themselves have been regular visitors, Reynolds was famously filmed pulling pints behind the bar, and he and Mac have been known to down shots with fans and pose for selfies on matchday visits. Reynolds has spoken publicly about how much The Turf means to him. If you have seen the TV series you will recall one section where the shots shots shots were clearly being felt the day after ! The pub’s guest book reads like a Hollywood call sheet. Among the famous faces who have stopped in: Prince William, Paul Rudd (who was in the ground for the 2023 National League title win), Will Ferrell, Channing Tatum, Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige, director Joe Russo, and food presenter Adam Richman. Many of these visits were captured in the Welcome to Wrexham documentary. Practical information The Turf is on Mold Road, directly on the corner of the Racecourse Ground at the Kop end. If you are walking from the town centre along Mold Road, you will see it on your right as you approach the stadium. It is primarily a home fans’ pub. Away supporters are admitted in small discreet numbers on occasional matchdays, but capacity is limited and the pub can operate a one-in-one-out door policy when full. The Turf gets extremely busy. If you want a drink inside, arrive at least two hours before kick-off for a 3pm Saturday game. After the match, it fills up again quickly. There is no table service it is a traditional bar. Check if there are any specific tickets or fanzone tickets required. Other matchday pubs If The Turf is too full or if you want a different vibe – there are other options nearby: Wrexham Lager Sports & Social Club – on Regent Street, a short walk past the ground towards town. A good alternative if The Turf, and has a small fanzone outside area at the back perfect for warmer weather. Maesgwyn Hall Club further along Mold Road past the Shell garage, on the left, usually has a range of offers on and some interesting food offerings! Town centre pubs the pubs on and around the High Street, Hope Street and Yorke Street fill up well before kick-off. These are a 10 to 15 minute walk from the ground. See our pubs guide for more on the town centre options. For the full picture of matchday eating and drinking, including where to eat before and after, see our matchday eating guide . Whilst this has not always been the case, the Cherry Red Records Stadium is now a fairly good destination for away fans for a number of reasons. Firstly, the ground generates an excellent atmosphere, helping to create an electric matchday experience. Secondly, the stadium is well located. It is not too far from the centre of Wimbledon, while the town itself boasts excellent transport links, particularly for supporters travelling to and from central London. The away end at Plough Lane is situated in the North Stand, with visiting supporters entering the stadium via Gate 7. Entrance to the North Stand at Plough Lane. Photo by Imago Away fans can expect an allocation of around 1,500 tickets for a trip to the Cherry Red Records Stadium, which represents a fairly decent number given the size of the ground. The home supporters regularly generate an excellent atmosphere inside the stadium, making for an enjoyable matchday experience on most occasions. While the food offering is far from revolutionary, it is more than adequate, with supporters usually able to choose from a range of matchday staples, including burgers, hotdogs and pies. Cherry Red Records Stadium in the news AFC Wimbledon 2026-27 fixtures confirmed The first League One clash at the Cherry Red Record Stadium in 2026-27 will see AFC Wimbledon host Reading on Saturday, August 22. The Dons will also welcome Peterborough United to their home ground on New Year’s Day 2027, and close out the campaign on their own turf against Notts County on May 8. Stadium revenue on the up In June 2025, The Cherry Red Stadium generated a record £7.2 million in revenue for the financial year, marking a 10.6% increase compared to the previous 12 months. Various factors contributed to the rise, with a record number of season tickets sold being a key one. Further income from hosting rugby league side London Broncos, along with a strong year for commercial partnerships, also played a big role in the club’s improved financial performance. Although the progress has been good, AFC Wimbledon acknowledged that competing in the English Football League, while operating at Plough Lane under the current structure, is not financially sustainable. Consequently, the club has since announced it will be actively looking for new investment partners and are hoping to return to a 50.01 ownership over the next year. AFC Wimbledon promoted to League One At the end of the 2024-25 campaign, Johnnie Jackson and his AFC Wimbledon team secured promotion to League One. The Dons have not appeared in the third tier since their relegation in the 2021-22 season, with a play-off victory over Walsall marking their return and representing a significant achievement. Despite winning only one of their last five regular league matches, the Dons were able to confirm their League One status and are currently three points adrift of the relegation zone with just four games remaining. Yet another flood at Plough Lane Historically, AFC Wimbledon’s Plough Lane ground – now called the Cherry Red Records Stadium following a sponsorship deal – has always been prone to flooding due to its high-risk location. However, when the club demolished its old stadium and constructed a brand-new one on the same site, that was supposed to change. That appeared to be the case until , when the venue flooded once more, leading to a sinkhole appearing on the pitch. It resulted in two home fixtures being relocated – one of which was a massive Carabao Cup tie against Premier League outfit, Newcastle United. Speaking on the matter, a Merton Council spokesperson said: “The stadium is built on previously developed land with a historic risk of flooding, a risk common across many developed areas of London. “Given this risk, and the increase in flash flooding caused by our changing climate, the planning proposal was, like all proposals, examined rigorously. “The council’s planning committee and the Environment Agency sought to ensure the stadium would remain safe, that the building would not increase the risk of flooding nearby, including to homes, and that damage mitigation and recovery plans were thorough and robust. “We are working closely with the Environment Agency and AFC Wimbledon to manage the risk of flooding, and to support in the review of the club’s flooding processes.” Famous people seen at Plough Lane AFC Wimbledon is a particularly unique club with a complex and controversial history. This has naturally attracted the attention of several local(ish) celebrities. John Green Plough Lane never. Gets. Old. #afcw Heaven on Earth. pic.twitter.com/qzeo1S4Jwx — John Green (@sportswithjohn) August 12, 2023 For supporters who are into their books, or have perhaps seen the film version of the novel, you will know that John Green is the author of ‘The Fault In Our Stars’. However, what you may not know is that Green is also a massive fan of AFC Wimbledon and is even a part-owner of the club. While he does not get to attend the Cherry Red Records Stadium in person as much as he would like, he is incredibly vocal about his love for the team and regularly uses his huge platform on X, formerly Twitter, to showcase it. AFC Wimbledon chants Here is a video posted in September 2023, showing all the best AFC Wimbledon chants: Cherry Red Records Stadium tifos In truth, tifos are not as common in English football as they are in the rest of Europe and across the world, however, that doesn’t mean they are never used at all – usually in the form of a banner rather than an artistic display. Banner aimed at Milton Keynes Dons AFC Wimbledon fans have made a banner to accompany their “Where were you when you were us?” chant ahead of their EFL Cup tie with Milton Keynes tonight. pic.twitter.com/U0ocvlzhcy — Natter Football (@NATTERFOOTBALL) August 13, 2019 The vast majority of football fans in England are aware of the controversial relationship between Milton Keynes Dons and AFC Wimbledon. First, there was Wimbledon FC, which relocated to Milton Keynes and rebranded itself into Milton Keynes Dons. Some of Wimbledon FC’s supporters therefore became MK Dons fans. Those that didn’t, created AFC Wimbledon in 2002. This banner is a reminder of the tension that exists between the two fanbases. Best views and seating plan As is often the case, the best views at the Cherry Red Records Stadium are found in the two stands that run along the length of the pitch. At AFC Wimbledon, these are the West Stand, also known as the Cappagh Stand, and the East Stand, referred to as the Ry Stand. These stands offer the clearest view of the entire pitch, unlike the stands behind the goals, where parts of the action can feel more restricted depending on where you are seated. For the best views available at the Cherry Red Records Stadium, many supporters recommend sitting towards the back of the Cappagh Stand. Seating Plan Photo by AFC Wimbledon Entrances The postcode for AFC Wimbledon’s home stadium is SW17 ONR. If you are coming from the southern end, Plough Lane can be accessed using the A24. Given the scarcity of parking in London, it is advisable to access the ground via public transport if possible. Nearly 1,500 away fans are located in the North Stand. The entrance for this stand is Gate 7, which you can find via Maskell Road and St Martin’s Way. Home fans with tickets in the South and East Stands can enter the stadium via Greyhound Parade. Pubs for away fans near the Cherry Red Records Stadium While the offering of pubs at most clubs is fairly dire for away fans, it is perhaps more so at AFC Wimbledon than any other. The vast majority of the pubs in the local area, including those in the town centre, will be full to the brim with home fans on matchday. The Earlsfield , which is located beneath Earsfield Railway Station, is widely considered to be the closest pub to the ground for away fans and is about a 20-minute walk away from the stadium. Other than that, our suggestion would be to drink elsewhere in London and then use the Underground service to get to Wimbledon. Home fan pubs As outlined above, home fans will have the choice of virtually every pub in the local area so there will be an option for everyone. Our top three suggestions are as follows: By the Horns – Plough Lane, London, SW17 0NR The Corner Pin – 10 Summerstown, London SW17 0AY Leather Bottle – 538 Garratt Lane, London SW17 0NY Food and drink Plough Lane pale ale AFC Wimbledon have confirmed a new partnership with Wimbledon Brewery, who will now serve as the club’s official craft beer partner. As part of the deal, a specially brewed Plough Lane Pale Ale will be available alongside Wimbledon Lager across the Cherry Red Records Stadium. Supporters can enjoy both in the Phoenix Pub, Speedway Bar, and the brand-new East Stand venue, Trap 6, with Wimbledon Brewery also becoming the latest partner of The Phoenix Pub. Food Whether you are an away fan or AFC Wimbledon supporter, there are plenty of restaurants and hotels a round Plough Lane. Below, we have sampled some of the best foods you can eat at the venue on matchdays. Roast duck Yorkshire puddings at AFC Wimbledon ( @AFCWimbledon ) 💷 £6 pic.twitter.com/hHL5gOnGi4 — Footy Scran (@FootyScran) December 4, 2022 Pie and mash with gravy at AFC Wimbledon ( @AFCWimbledon ) 💷 £9 pic.twitter.com/e0vIhiXGBK — Footy Scran (@FootyScran) November 27, 2022 Pie, mash, peas and gravy at AFC Wimbledon ( @AFCWimbledon @MYPIE_LDN ) 💷 £9 pic.twitter.com/HvESxO7rvy — Footy Scran (@FootyScran) April 27, 2022 Beef brisket and pulled pork in a roll at AFC Wimbledon ( @AFCWimbledon ) 💷 £7 pic.twitter.com/voQcCBLabz — Footy Scran (@FootyScran) March 26, 2022 Pepperoni pizza at AFC Wimbledon ( @AFCWimbledon ) 💷 £11 pic.twitter.com/1A83nmjCD7 — Footy Scran (@FootyScran) August 28, 2023 Chicken tenders at AFC Wimbledon ( @AFCWimbledon ) 💷 £6 pic.twitter.com/XVE0MIZqTf — Footy Scran (@FootyScran) November 11, 2021 Getting to the stadium By train and metro Wimbledon is a very well-located town, particularly to the rest of London. Several trains run between major stations, such as Waterloo and Wimbledon, and the journey takes less than 30 minutes. Once you arrive at Wimbledon Station, the Cherry Red Records Stadium is approximately a 25-minute walk away. The tube ride to Plough Lane takes an average of 50 minutes from different regions. One has to look for the District and Northern lines. Tooting Broadway Station is the best option when using the Northern line, while Wimbledon Park is the best pick when using the District line. By bus While using buses for your entire journey may be pretty time-consuming, they are an excellent way to get from the town centre to the stadium. If you do not fancy the 25-minute walk from the station, regular bus services run between the two locations on matchdays. By car The stadium can be reached using the A24 if you are heading up from the southern end. The M3 or M4 would be a better pick for those coming from the west of London. Where is the best place to park for the AFC Wimbledon game? In general, though, driving to the stadium is not advised due to the tight parking regulations in the areas surrounding the ground. The club does not guarantee parking spaces for fans, so we highly recommend travelling by public transport when possible. If driving is a must, our suggestion is to park further afield and finish the rest of your journey either on foot or by public transport. Accessibility and disabled facilities at Cherry Red Records Stadium Having been opened in 2020, the Cherry Red Records Stadium boasts relatively good facilities for supporters with disabilities. These include: 92 wheelchair-user spaces 450 easy-access seats 11 accessible toilets 1 Changing places facility Audio commentary service Hearing loops at key locations 28 accessible parking spaces However, as always, we strongly recommend contacting the club ahead of your arrival if you have any specific needs on matchday. Cherry Red Records Stadium ticket prices Wimbledon avoided relegation in 2025-26 and will once again be playing in the third tier for 2026-27. Season tickets are currently available via the club website, with the following price ranges: Adult: £484 – 694 Concession: £339 – 486 18-21: £290 – 416 Under-17: £121 – 208 Individual match tickets will typically go on sale four weeks before a game, and are set to be priced as follows for 2026-27: Adult: £27 – 40 66+: £20 – 30 18-21: £18 – 26 Under-17: £9 – 22 Please note that ticket prices vary depending on the location of your seat and the age of the supporters. Also, the prices may vary from one stand to another. Securing season tickets at the club is subject to purchasing membership priced as follows: Adult: £60 Concession: £45 Junior Dons Membership: £25 Cherry Red Records Stadium programme and fanzines The current price of the AFC Wimbledon match programme is £3. Cherry Red Records Stadium capacity In its current form, the Cherry Red Records Stadium has a capacity of approximately 9,300, with the capacity of each stand as follows: Cappagh West Stand – 4,267 South Stand – 1,092 Ry Stand – 2,391 North Stand – 1,465 However, those figures could one day change with the club already having permission from Merton Council to one day expand the ground to a capacity of 20,000. Map showing the location of the Cherry Red Records Stadium, railway stations, tube stations and pubs ﻿ Cherry Red Records Stadium tours For supporters that are interested, AFC Wimbledon does in fact offer stadium tours of their Plough Lane stadium. Understandably, these are not held as frequently as is seen by the clubs in the Premier League, however, there are usually at least a couple of dates available in each month through the year. This can change throughout the season so always consult the club’s website for exact dates available. A stadium tour of the Cherry Red Records Stadium is priced as follows: Adults – £15 Over 65s & Students – £12 Under 18s – £5 Some of the facilities you will receive behind-the-scenes access to on the Cherry Red Records Stadium tour are: Changing rooms Pitchside area Referee’s room Executive Box Padded Seats Museum Nearby attractions As well as being very well-connected to the rest of London, Wimbledon is also a town with plenty to offer fans who plan on making a day, or perhaps a weekend, of their trip to Plough Lane. Wimbledon Lawn Tennis Museum For supporters who are also into their tennis, visiting Wimbledon is already likely to be high on your bucket list. However, the Wimbledon Lawn Tennis Museum is an equally entertaining attraction too. At this venue, visitors can see a large collection of memorabilia, including various rackets, balls and trophies that have been made over the years. While you will likely want to use a bus to travel between the museum and Plough Lane, a 40-minute walk means that you could potentially visit the attraction directly after the game. Wimbledon Common Wimbledon Common may be for you if you are keen to enjoy the laid-back nature of a large public green space. Wimbledon Common is an area abundant with a variety of woodland and wildlife, making it an excellent place for a relaxing stroll or perhaps even a bike ride. A golf club is also located within the common, which will likely appeal to a large number of supporters. New Wimbledon Theatre An altogether different option is to visit the New Wimbledon Theatre and watch one of the many plays or musicals being shown there. The theatre has several exclusive shows on offer, including: Snow White and Rose Red Here You Come Again – The New Dolly Parton Musical Cruel Intentions Blood Brothers AFC Wimbledon ground history When AFC Wimbledon were formed in 2002 they didn’t have the luxury of picking and choosing a stadium. Instead, they had to settle for using the Kingsmeadow Stadium; it was the former ground of semi-pro side Kingstonian. It wasn’t until 2014 that the return to their true home – Plough Lane – looked like it could one day become a reality. That was only when planning was sought though; it wasn’t until three years later that building works got underway. The club eventually returned to action at Plough Lane in 2020, making it one of the newest football stadiums in the UK . Record and average attendance Record Attendance The record attendance at the Cherry Red Records Stadium is 8,623, which was set in 2024 during a match against Walsall. Average Attendance AFC Wimbledon’s League Two average attendance during the 2024-25 season was one of the best in the division. A promotion to the third division means we could see more fans turn up at Plough Lane during the 2024-25 season. Meanwhile, here is a breakdown of Plough Lane’s average attendance in recent seasons. 2025-2026: 8,396 2024-2025: 8,008 2023-2024: 7,893 2022-2023: 7,604 2021-2022: 7,704 2020-2021: 0 (Covid-19) 2019-2020: 4,383 2018-2019: 4,297 2017-2018: 4,325 2016-2017: 4,477 AFC Wimbledon local rival AFC Wimbledon vs Milton Keynes Dons rivalry Although not a traditional local derby, Milton Keynes Dons are the only side that can really be considered rivals to AFC Wimbledon. The hostility stems from the controversial decision to allow Wimbledon FC to relocate to Milton Keynes and rebrand as MK Dons. In reply, angry supporters formed AFC Wimbledon and began again further down the football pyramid. It is not a fierce rivalry in the usual sense, with many AFC Wimbledon fans choosing not to recognise MK Dons at all. For them, the issue is more about principle than competition on the pitch. The first meeting between the two sides took place in December 2012, when Wimbledon fell to a narrow 2-1 defeat in the FA Cup second round. In recent times, the Wombles have put together a five-game unbeaten run against MK Dons, starting with a run of three consecutive victories without conceding before playing out a goalless draw in January 2025. The two sides were involved in another goalless affair in their most recent encounter at Stadium MK in September 2026, meaning Wimbledon have now recorded five consecutive clean sheets against MK Dons since suffering a 3-1 defeat in January 2024. South London rivalries As mentioned, the Dons’ main rival is Milton Keynes Dons, however, there is always a little extra needle in games against other teams based in South London. They aren’t what fans would typically refer to as derbies, but there is a sense that some South London bragging rights are up for grabs in these matches. There are three other major teams in the South London area, those being Millwall, Crystal Palace and Charlton, and one match is not particularly more intense than any other. As AFC Wimbledon continue to rise through the ranks though, that could potentially change. Retro football pictures at Plough Lane Plough Lane as we know it today only opened its doors to supporters in 2020 so there is nothing retro about any of the pictures taken at the ground. But Plough Lane is a stadium with a long and winding history… A sad day for all AFC Wimbledon fans Remembering the sad remains of Wimbledon’s iconic former home Plough Lane, opened in 1912, closed in 1998, demolished in 2002. pic.twitter.com/3haglvy0mi — Football Back Then ⚽️🏐⚽️ (@FootballThen) September 6, 2019 While Plough Lane only opened in 2020, the land upon which it is built was the previous home of Wimbledon FC and was beloved by the entire fanbase. The pictures above showcase the ground just before its demolition in 2002, looking a far cry from its once impressive former self. I have a great respect for AFC Wimbledon and how the club has reformed and returned to the Football League. Also, I was delighted when they moved to their new stadium in 2020 so near to the old Plough Lane. Therefore this was easily one of the grounds I was most looking forward to visiting. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? I travelled up on the supporters’ bus with Newport County. We left South Wales at 8-00 am and got to Wimbledon around 12-30 pm. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? Before the game I went to the Against the Grain cask ale pub. Beers were obviously at London prices’ but of exceptional quality. Well worth the cost. Afterwards I made my way to the ground. The ground is impressive on the outside (see pics) and respect is given to the history of its former incarnation with a statue to Lawrie Sanchez and Dave Beasant, two of the heroes in their 1988 FA Cup win over Liverpool. All the home fans I met were friendly and inquisitive over my quest to ‘do the 92.’ What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the stadium? An impressive modern stadium ideal for this level of football. Neat compact stands on all sides and I’ve heard that the club has options to extend stands if and when the need arises. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game was an exciting affair and Newport took the lead early in the first half. There afterwards they defended well and even extended their lead 10 minutes into the second half. Regarding the stewards, they were friendly and helpful at all times. The atmosphere in the away end was as it always is with Newport excellent especially has they won 2-0. And finally, the ‘pie question.’ Prior to the game I asked if they had vegetarian pies. They did and even had the curtesy to set one aside for me at half time. Needless to say I was not disappointed, especially with the quality. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game Considering that a section of the M25 was closed on this weekend the journey back to south Wales was relatively straight forward and we got back to Newport at 8-30pm. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out A really good day out especially as Newport won. As always after visiting a new ground I ask myself ‘if I lived there would go and support the team’? In this case it is an emphatic yes! I can only wish AFC Wimbledon my best regards in their dream to one day return to the Premier League. If there’s higher demand, the allocation can expand, offering up to 4,700 tickets (the stand has a total capacity of 6,000, but it’s reduced to maintain a significant buffer between away and home fans in the East Stand). The stand’s acoustics are quite good, allowing visiting fans to create an impressive amount of noise. The concourse facilities are adequate, and there’s access to a nearby open-air area for fans who wish to smoke. A row of support pillars is positioned toward the rear of the stand, so if your team brings a large crowd and you’re seated above Row NN, a pillar might partially block your view. Best view The West Stand has the best view of the pitch, either the upper or lower section, depending on your personal preference. Away entrance Visiting supporters enter the stadium through the dedicated away turnstiles next to the Barry Murphy Stand. Away fans should note that the entrance does not offer level access into the stadium. The Pontefract Road End (now the Norman Rimmington Stand) is a covered, all-seated stand for home supporters. It opened in 1995 and has a capacity of 4,500. The opposite end, the Barry Murphy Stand, is a large, single-tier, covered stand that houses around 6,000 fans. Replacing a former open terrace, it was opened in 1999. Oakwell Stadium capacity Oakwell Stadium has a total capacity of 23,287, distributed among four main stands and one corner stand. However, the capacity has currently fallen to 18,515 due to safety issues with the West Stand. The Barry Murphy North Stand, which is the most recent addition to the stadium, accommodates 6,257 fans. It is primarily designated for away supporters, and as a result, it often operates below its full capacity. On the south side of the stadium is the Norman Rimmington South stand, traditionally known to fans simply as the ‘South Stand’ or the ‘Pontefract Road End’, which can hold 4,508 fans. This large single-tier stand features the club’s superstore integrated within it and is located behind one goal. The East Stand, the largest section of the stadium, is a two-tier structure completed in 1993 with assistance from the football trust. Due to its impressive size, accessing the upper seating area involves climbing numerous steps. Another two-tier structure, the West Stand, has only the upper area covered by a roof. Originally designed for 4,752 spectators, it is currently closed for safety reasons. Plans for improvements to this stand are under consideration, but no concrete proposals have been developed yet. Lastly, the Car Seekers Corner Stand connects the East and South Stands, providing seating for 202 fans. Visitors can explore a wide array of outdoor installations from well-known international artists, with sculptures positioned throughout woodland, lakeside areas and open fields, making it an engaging visit even for those who would not tend to go to a museum. For more attractions near Oakwell, check out: Worsbrough Mill Experience Barnsley Museum Barnsley Market Ground history Barnsley Football Club has been hosting its home matches at Oakwell since 1888. The ground takes its name from an oak tree and a well that stood on the site. The two symbols have remained central to the town’s footballing identity for well over a century. During its early years, Oakwell grew rapidly alongside the club, with stands gradually added over following years. The West Stand, parts of which still survive today, dates back to around 1904 – this makes it one of the oldest surviving structures in English football. However, Oakwell isn’t entirely traditional. The other three stands have been rebuilt or enhanced since the 1990s. Plans were in place for the West Stand to undergo similar renovations, but mismanagement and financial struggles led to the club’s debt and eventual administration. This ultimately resulted in the sale of the stadium, a situation that continues to affect the club today. Latest developments For many years, Oakwell has faced neglect because neither Barnsley nor Barnsley Council held ownership of the stadium. In 2023, however, the council acquired sole ownership of the stadium and the surrounding land following successful negotiations with the Cryne family, who had owned it since 2003. In early 2024, Barnsley Football Club and Barnsley Council announced a new partnership, solidifying Oakwell’s status as Barnsley’s home for the next three decades. This partnership is expected to bring essential investment to the stadium. Barnsley's local rivals Given their location in South Yorkshire, a hotbed of EFL clubs, Barnsley are not short of local rivalries, with Sheffield Wednesday, Rotherham United and Doncaster Rovers considered amongst their fiercest. Their closest and most historic rivalry is with Sheffield Wednesday, who they last met in the League One playoff final at Wembley in 2023, which they lost to see Sheffield Wednesday snatch the final promotion spot to the Championship after completing a double over the Sheffield side in the regular season. They will reignite their rivalry with the Owls in the 2026-27 season after the Steel City side suffered relegation from the Championship back down to England’s third tier, with the Reds set to welcome Sheffield Wednesday to Oakwell in November 2026 and make the trip across South Yorkshire to Hillsborough in 2027. Like the Tykes, Doncaster Rovers and Rotherham United have spent much of the last 20 years between the Championship and League Two, giving rise to plenty of derbies. Heading into 2026-27, they are set for Yorkshire derbies in League One with Sheffield Wednesday, Huddersfield Town and Doncaster Rovers, while Rotherham’s relegation to League Two means they are not set to meet in the coming campaign unless they are drawn against one another in a cup competition. The Reds will take on Huddersfield Town twice in quick succession around the turn of the year, with the Terriers visiting Oakwell in December before Barnsley head to the Accu Stadium for the reverse fixture in early January 2027. Their first derby of the season came away at Doncaster in August and ended in a goalless stalemate, while their first home derby will be that November fixture against Sheffield Wednesday.
