See more 27th December 2019 Henryk Piotrowski (West Bromwich Albion) Barnsley v West Bromwich Albion Championship Friday 27th December 2019, 3pm Henryk Piotrowski (West Bromwich Albion) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Oakwell Stadium? I had never visited Oakwell before so this was an opportunity to tick off another ground. Also with Albion in such great form at the top of the league I thought we had a chance of finally ending our Oakwell hoodoo where we hadn't won since the late 1940's! How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? A really simple journey up the M1, then J37 and A628 into Barnsley. All told less than 2 hours door to door. Arrived well before kick-off at about and managed to park a stone's throw from the ground. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? I had a pint in a local pub (the Mount- all home fans from what I could see/hear) and got chatting to a few Barnsley supporters. A very friendly bunch with a great sense of humour. Very relaxed atmosphere. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Oakwell Stadium? Oakwell is located slap bang in the middle of the town centre and the stadium encompasses a mix of old (West Stand) and new stands, which is a welcome relief from some of the sometimes soulless and uninspiring modern-day stadia around the country. It also has old-style corner floodlights too. The North Stand, where the Albion fans were located, was absolutely fine. Great views. Fantastic atmosphere (over 3500 made the trip). Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. Albion took the lead in the opening 10 minutes when their keeper miscued a rushed clearance straight to Krovinovic who lobbed it back over him. However Barnsley had a lot of the ball and had a number of chances to equalise but our keeper Johnstone was in exceptional form, making some great saves. A similar picture in the second half. All square until the last minute when Barnsley deservedly equalised. Frustrating from an Albion point of view, but no qualms about the result. I bought a coffee and a pie in the ground. Reasonable prices/decent quality. Stewards were helpful, kind and unobtrusive. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Absolutely no problems at all. Away by , very little traffic to contend with, straight back onto the M1, Home by . Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: A fantastic day out. Oakwell is a lovely ground to visit. fans are welcoming. Easy to get to. Pity we couldn't secure the victory but that would have been hard on Barnsley. I would definitely go again! See more 11th December 2019 Kevin Nash (Reading) Barnsley v Reading Championship Wednesday 11th December 2019, 7.45pm Kevin Nash (Reading) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Oakwell Stadium? I had not been to Oakwell, since 1998 – A Coca Cola cup game and I think Barnsley were in the Premier League then. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? I followed the sat nav and didn't see any signs for the ground until you see the imposing ground lit up on the hillside. I parked opposite the ground at a Horse Riding Club, only £3 but it was pitch black. The path up to the main road was steepish full of deep puddles & mud but did me. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Oakwell Stadium? It is imposing when lit up with the mist/fog blowing around the stadium. I didn't find the home fans that I spoke to, to be particularly friendly. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game was good, Reading were expected to thrash this bottom of the league team, but I know Reading! Barnsley looked in control for most of the game, going 1-0 up. If they had a set of decent strikers then they could have scored 4 easily! Reading had their moments and needed it to equalise, Barnsley looked like a team that could get out of the relegation scrap – I think they were unlucky not to beat us. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: The traffic was solid around the ground, but I took a punt up a back street and the sat nav took me back to the hotel, so not too bad. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: It was a better game than the score 1-1 draw suggests, but I was thankful for the point. Barnsley battled hard and were slightly unlucky not to win. See more 9th November 2019 Steve (Stoke City) Barnsley v Stoke City Championship Saturday 9th November 2019, 3pm Steve (Stoke City) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Oakwell Ground? Bottom of the table clash! Also, a first visit to Oakwell and Barnsley in general and I wanted to see what it was like. Was staying in Sheffield for the weekend so it was a short trip over to Barnsley. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Went by train. A simple walk from the station to the ground through rows of terraced houses, helpful stewards and police pointing the way. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? Had a pint in Annie Murray's before the game (an Irish pub in the town centre), and popped into the Dove for a local ale afterwards. The Dove was mostly home fans with a smattering of away supporters, loads of Barnsley memorabilia so obviously a home fan favourite. All very friendly and a decent pint in both pubs. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Oakwell Stadium? Great to see a ground near the town centre, unlike so many new stadiums (ours included, unfortunately). In fact, the location reminded me of our sadly departed Victoria Ground. The stadium was more modern than I expected and was quite neat apart from the one older stand down the side (although it had a nice classic feel in my opinion!). The away stand had great views and an excellent atmosphere. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. Great atmosphere, great game and a great 4-2 result (for us)! Stewards and police very friendly, as were fans. Most away fans were standing and the stewards didn't insist on forcing us to sit as we have probably all experienced at other grounds (looking at you West Ham). Very crowded in the concourse and not selling beer (not missed though, go to the pub after, save yourself a few pounds and not be forced to drink Carling from a plastic glass!). It probably would be more comfortable with fewer fans. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Easy walk from the ground to the pub/station/bus/car park. Police guided us. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: I would definitely go to Barnsley again. Recommended for any fans. See more 19th October 2019 Andrew (Swansea City) Barnsley v Swansea City Championship Saturday 19th October 2019, 3pm Andrew (Swansea City) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Oakwell Ground? It was the first game of the season for me due to work commitments and I had never been to Oakwell before. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? I drove from North Wales along the M62, M60, M67 and A628. An easy straight drive, no turning off, straight across at any roundabouts. I parked near the ground in a factory car park on Langdale Road for £5. There was on-street parking nearby but you'd have to get there early for this. We arrived about 1.30pm for a 3pm kick off. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? Langdales chippy just around the corner from the ground. Very good fish and chips with mushy peas for under £6. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Oakwell Stadium? The ground looked fine, turn around a corner and there it is among the houses. Three newer stands and an old stand along one length of the pitch. A great view from the away end. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. I had already eaten but it was £3.30 for a pie against £2 in the local chippy. Only cans and bottles of lager, bitter and cider in the away end which weren't cheap so I abstained. Police and stewards were friendly. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Took nearly an hour to get out of the car park. I had to wait for cars that were parked in front of us and then the traffic was chaotic as the roads are closed for an hour afterwards. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: Not the best game from two sides lacking confidence but I'm glad I went. I'd probably park a bit further away next time. See more 2nd October 2019 Andrew Davidson (Doing the 92) Barnsley v Derby County Championship Wednesday 2nd October 2019, 7.45pm Andrew Davidson (Doing the 92) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Oakwell Stadium? I had a couple of days off work and I love Yorkshire so Barnsley seemed a good opportunity to visit a new ground. Especially as I could buy a ticket very easily on the night. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Getting from London to Barnsley by train is not as easy as other Yorkshire destinations. Having to travel from St Pancras to Sheffield and change for a local train to Barnsley. We arrived at 2.45pm and checked into the Premier Inn. Later on, in the evening, the ground was an easy 15 minute walk from the hotel. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? We had a meal at the hotel and walked via the Barnsley interchange to Oakwell. The home fans were friendly, even having some friendly banter with the Derby support. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Oakwell Stadium? The ground emerges as you approach it between terraced streets, the impressive East Stand being visible first. I liked the brightly painted red walls around Oakwell and the contrast between the old and new, the very old West Stand and the rest of the ground. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game itself was a pretty entertaining affair, with both sides having many chances. Barnsley were let down by comical defending and were lucky to scrape a very late draw. The stewards were helpful and I had a couple of diet cokes. The Derby fans were very noisy! Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: The walk back to the hotel was an easy 15 minute stroll. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: I liked Oakwell, the best part being its location to town/station. I feel BFC made the right choice, to redevelop their ground rather than build a hard to reach out of town venue. See more 30th March 2019 James (Coventry City) Barnsley v Coventry City League 1 Saturday 30th March 2019, 3pm James (Coventry City) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Oakwell Ground? Another ground I'd never been to. An upturn in our recent form meant we still had an outside chance of making the playoffs and with Barnsley being a decent team, It should probably make for a good game of football. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? After driving over the peaks from Manchester where I live, I arrived near the Dove Inn around 1.30pm and the traffic was already quite heavy. After a few U-turns, I managed to find some street parking near to the pub. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? I met my mate who had the tickets and went for a quick pint in the Dove Inn which had inside a mixture of both sets of fans with no problems. After that we headed straight to the ground. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Oakwell Stadium? We walked towards the stadium and cut through a gate onto the club car park behind the South Stand. We then walked around the ground to the right towards the away end…. which was a mistake as this side of the ground is fenced off and we had to walk back around almost the entire stadium. Eventually, we made it inside and headed up to our seats. The away end is fairly large and modern as are the other stands with the exception of the stand to our right which looked ancient in comparison and the bottom half of which was exposed to the elements. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. I grabbed a quick pie before kick off, (overpriced and nothing special) one of the stewards enquired with myself about a potential protest with regards to our own ground at the end of the game. I informed him that there may be a few fans have a bit of a sit-in after the game for 15 minutes or so but should be nothing to worry about. The game itself was a very entertaining one and but for a couple of defensive errors we'd have sneaked a win and nearly snatched it at the end but for a great save by their keeper. But 2-2 in the end was probably a fair result and the Sky Blue army were in fine voice throughout. As a side note if the weather's decent as it was for this game take a pair of sunglasses as the sun dropped below roof level just after kick off. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Exited the ground fairly quickly and headed back up the hill to the Dove Inn and had a glass of coke and chatted to a few Barnsley fans and tried to explain our horrendously complicated stadium situation to them. After the traffic had died down headed straight back over the peaks. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: A decent day out but a draw probably all but ends our already slim playoff chances. I just hope that we can sort out where we'll be playing next season. I parked in the away car park at £10 but was told by home steward it was a £5 then direct elsewhere by another steward! Very unhelpful. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? Just went straight into the away end and didn't really see any home fans. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Oakwell Stadium? As I had previously been to Oakwell in the past before the away end was redeveloped. The stewards were unhelpful Seem if you complained you were going to be thrown out for no reason. The facilities were poor with only two refreshment kiosks. Our Supporter Liaison Officer, Kristine Green, gives a run down of all the key information for supporters making the trip to the Hayes Lane Stadium. What colour kit will the team be wearing? We’ll be in our yellow away kit it for this game. What’s the ticket information? All tickets have completely sold out with no further tickets available. Those with standing tickets should enter via Exit 2. Anybody in the seating area should also enter via Exit 2 – they will then be escorted to their seats in the Glyn Beverly Stand. What time will turnstiles open? Turnstiles open at 1.30pm How do I get to the ground? Leave the M25 at Junction 4 and take the A21 towards Bromley and London. After five miles turn left at the traffic lights onto the A232 towards Croydon/Sutton. At the 2nd set of traffic lights turn right into Baston Road (B265). Continue straight on this road through Hayes. The road becomes Hayes Lane and after the mini roundabout, the entrance to the ground is down on the right. Where is the best place to park? Hayes Lane has a small car park that costs £2. This is on a first come, first served basis. Once full, it’s street parking. Is there disabled parking available? Disabled parking is now sold out – fans are advised to use the above or street parking, being mindful of any restrictions that blue badges won’t override. What is the nearest train station to the stadium and what is the approximate distance and walking time? Bromley South Railway Station, served by trains from London Victoria, is around a mile from the ground (15-20 minute walk) so factor this in if you’ll be elsewhere in London before travelling in for kick off. Recommended pubs for away fans? The Ravens Bar at the ground is home fans only. The Bricklayers Arms in the closest pub to the ground welcoming both home and away fans. Located on Masons Hill, around a 15 minute walk away from the ground. Slightly further up Masons Hill is The Crown of Bromley which will also be welcoming away fans. If you’re coming into Bromley South there’s a Wetherspoons called the Richmal Crompton that will also welcome away fans. Food available in the area? There’s a Domino’s on Mason’s Hill and a Toby Carvery on Bromley Common as well as other takeaways along Bromley High Street. Where is the nearest cash machine to the Stadium? The nearest cashpoint is at the Southern Co-Operative on Homesdale Road, about half a mile away. What food and drink is available at the stadium? The Exit 2 outlet will have alcohol and is covered, although space is at a premium. Exit 5 (closest for those transferred to the seating) will not have alcohol. Usual football food will be available including burgers and pies. Both cash and card will be accepted at Exit 2 outlet (standing) and Exit 5 outlet (seating). Card payments are preferred to speed up service. Is a programme available? Programmes are available for £3.00 – payment by cash or card, with card preferred. What the flag policy? Flags are permitted but must not be placed in front of advertising boards. All games are now segregated at Hayes Lane. Visiting supporters use turnstiles located on the far side of the North Terrace (on the other side of the ground to the main entrance). The away section stretches from the corner flag to just past the halfway line. As the home team dugout is located in front of the visiting fans, this can lead to a number of ‘suggestions’ being aimed in their direction. Although this Side Terrace is of a reasonable height, being only 12 steps high, it does have a row of floodlight pylons running across the front of it, which could hinder your view. The terrace is also open to the elements, so hope it does not rain. Most fans enjoy their visits to Bromley as it is a proper old-fashioned ground with plenty of character. Hayes Lane in the news Norman Park redevelopment The Club have redeveloped the Norman Park (South) End of Hayes Lane. This involved the construction of a large multi-purpose office type building, which saw 1,450 seats installed out front. The project was completed in the summer of 2019. Thanks to Paul Willott for the photo below showing the progress works. It was taken in January 2019: Photo by Imago Upcoming projects According to latest information in late 2025, there is a new proposal from Berkeley Homes to build approximately 2,000–2,200 new homes on “Hayes Farm” area that partially surrounds Norman Park and Bromley FC. As of December 2025, this proposal is in the early stages with the developer hoping to submit a formal application in 2026. Bromley chants Bromley fans are some of the most passionate in English football. With that, here are some popular Bromley F.C. chants. Famous Black and Whites Raven mad I’m Bromley Till I die Walking Down the Masons Hill Best views and seating plan at Hayes Lane Hayes Lane has seen a number of improvements in recent years, most notably at the Norman Park End where a new stand and club offices were completed in 2019. The Glyn Beverly Stand, named after the club’s former president, is a modern single-tier seated stand split into five sections and accommodates around 1,450 supporters. Club offices sit behind the stand, creating a high rear wall, while the roof provides cover for much of the seating area. Running along the west side of the ground is the John Fiorini Stand, which serves as the stadium’s main stand. Opened in 1993, the covered seated stand offers unobstructed views thanks to the absence of supporting pillars and houses 285 spectators. Its seats are believed to have been relocated from Wimbledon’s former Plough Lane stadium. On the opposite side is the open Cricket Club Terrace, named after the cricket ground situated behind it. The terrace stretches the full length of the pitch and features two rows of traditional crush barriers, while a black timber fence has been added at the rear in more recent years. The team dugouts are also located on this side, with the dressing rooms positioned behind the Main Stand. Behind the opposite goal is the North Terrace, a partly covered standing area where the roof is supported by a number of pillars across the front. Hayes Lane also switched to a modern artificial 3G playing surface in 2017, allowing the stadium to host football throughout the year. The ground is shared with London City Lionesses, who play in the Women’s Super League. In 2018, Hayes Lane was renamed the Westminster Waste Stadium in a corporate sponsorship deal, but is now simply known as Hayes Lane. Hayes Lane entrance To get to the ground, you need to leave the M25 at Junction 4 before going on the A21 towards Bromley and London. Travel on this road for five miles and then turn left onto the A232 towards Croydon/Sutton. At the second set of traffic lights turn right onto Baston Road (B265). From here continue straight through Hayes and after the mini-roundabout, you will find the entrance to the ground on the right. There are two main entry points at Hayes Lane. Away fans are located in the East Terrace, with turnstiles at the far end of the stand. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Very easy on all counts. A train up from the South Coast to London and then an easy connection from London to Bromley. The ground is a fairly straightforward 15 minute walk from the train station, although it would benefit from being signposted from the town centre for first-time visitors. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? As I didn't arrive in Bromley until an hour before kick-off, it was pretty much straight to the ground. For anyone visiting for the first time, Bromley is a good town for shopping, with the large precinct only five minutes away from the train station. If you fancy a drink or a bite to eat, there is an excellent 'Wetherspoons' pub called 'The Richmal Crompton' which is large and spacious, and unusually for a Wetherspoons never seems too full (in my experience at least). What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hayes Lane Ground? The uncovered terrace behind one of the goals is no more, as apparently, a new stand is to be built in its place. This meant there was less room than usual. I initially stood on the uncovered side terrace, but a floodlight pole obscured my view, so I ended up behind the part covered home terrace. There is a nice seated area along one side of the pitch, but this fills up really quickly, so getting a seat may not be an option at present unless you arrive early. Away fans had part of the covered terrace, but although segregated by a fence, anyone wishing to access this area from the home end only had to walk down the terrace and then back up into this area, as the dividing fence seems only to reach three-quarters of the way down the terrace? Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game was brilliant! Fylde took an early lead and looked a class act, but you got the impression Bromley were up for it and scored twice in a five minute spell via a scrappy finish and a confident penalty to lead 2-1 at half time. Fylde made three early substitutions and deservedly levelled early in the second half. Unfortunately, the game was then held up for 13 minutes due to a serious injury to a Fylde player who landed badly and broke his arm. When play resumed, Fylde had no more substitutes to use, so Bromley made the extra man tell and scored a brilliant winner through JJ Hooper 10 minutes from time. All in all, the best match I've seen this season. The stewards were friendly. I had my bag checked prior to being admitted to the ground, which is slightly odd when you can buy cans of drink inside the ground, so had I wished to take out the officials/players or fans, suitable ammo was on sale inside! It was slightly disappointing was that Bromley charge a whopping three quid extra for admission on the day, which is somewhat unfair on the likes of me who couldn't know in advance where they were going on any given day. There's an excellent bar in the ground called 'Ravens', which is spacious, and has a good range of beers, and has a sensible queuing system ensuring it's 'First come, first served'. Unfortunately, every time I've been here, the heating has been up full blast making it somewhat uncomfortable. There's a decent selection of food from (at least) two outlets (I think if there's a large away following, a third outlet opens up toward one end of the covered terrace). The steak and ale pie was nice, but they gave me a spoon to eat it with (!) which was little use when trying to get through the pastry. When I did make the breakthrough, the pie was so hot, the amount of steam that escaped from it must have come close to setting off the smoke alarm in the clubhouse! You could also get pasties, burgers, pizzas, hot dogs and bacon rolls, so fair play to Bromley for providing decent snap, always important for football foodies such as myself! The loos were inadequate, sad to say. A choice of a rundown temporary unit with no hot water, or the clubhouse loo which only had a couple of urinals. I wouldn't want to get caught short here in the event of a big crowd, although, again, I think there may be a further loo at the other end of the covered terrace. You could also (I think) possibly use a further bar area above the seating area, but this was guarded by a steward and it wasn't too clear whether you were allowed to use this area without him admitting you. Probably worth asking, as I'm sure he wouldn't bite, just seemed a bit confusing. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game : A d ead easy walk straight back to train station and home. The main road is a bit of a nightmare to cross, I might add! Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: A g reat game of football, although slightly annoying that I was forced to pay three quid extra on the day. The ground still has some of it's old charm, but progress will shortly prevail. All in all, though, Bromley is a nice club, and well worth a visit. Plenty of people wanted to chat with us and the atmosphere was very friendly indeed. Once the match was due to get underway, we drifted out and took a spot on the long terrace that runs opposite the main John Fiorini Stand. This really was a lovely old terrace with a few primitive crush barriers on it. We commented on how the two ends of the ground contrasted; although both were partly covered, they had enough supporting pillars to resemble the wing structure of a Sopwith Camel but were all the more attractive for it. One however was a pure terrace, the other had an eclectic mix of wooden benches and white plastic seats. Terraced End Worthy of comment is the “Playzone” that sits the other side of the John Fiorini Stand to the bar and social club; this consists of a marquee emblazoned with the title of “playzone” so we mused whether the club in some way runs a crèche style play area for youngsters whilst their Dads are watching footy! If the facility is nothing to do with the club, one can only comment that it really is situated almost on top of the pitch! We guesstimated the crowd to be 1,500+ which was a little less than I might have expected given that there were not many games in the professional leagues on the Saturday, and given the profile of the fixture itself (I having previously witnessed a 4,500+ crowd at what was then Gravesend & Northfleet when they entertained Canvey Island for a similar 1st v 2nd fixture). The lyrics for Burton’s adaptation of the famous song are as follows: “Take me home, Derby Road, “To the place that I belong, “To Pirelli, to see the Brewers, “Take me home, Derby Road!” Manchester United sing their version of ‘Country Roads’ before every match at Old Trafford, with Derby Road being replaced by United Road in the chorus. Ground history Burton started out at the Lloyds Foundry Ground, but the stadium soon proved insufficient for the strong crowds that turned up to regularly watch the Brewers. As a result, the club built and then moved into Eton Park, which opened in 1958 and remained Burton’s home stadium until the club made the switch to the newly-built Pirelli Stadium in 2005. Pirelli donated the former site of their sports and social club to Burton Albion; in exchange, Burton Albion would have to name their new stadium after the company. They include Port Vale , Notts County , Walsall and Chesterfield . There have been a total of 20 head-to-head encounters between Burton and Port Vale since 2010. Albion have only managed six victories in this fixture and are winless in their last five meetings. Neither side was able to come out on top in their two clashes in the 2025-26 League One campaign, which produced a goalless draw at the Pirelli Stadium and a 2-2 scoreline in the return fixture at Vale Park. It is unclear when the two sides will next face off following Port Vale’s relegation to the fourth tier. Elsewhere, the Brewers seem to dominate the rivalry versus Chesterfield. A total of 12 matches were played over the years, as Burton Albion have won 50% of them. The remaining six matches resulted in four Chesterfield wins and two draws. Derby County are equally regarded as Burton Albion’s rivals due to shared fan bases. Others include Crewe Alexandra, Nottingham Forest and Wolverhampton Wanderers. During their brief stay in the Championship, the Brewers also faced Aston Villa and Birmingham City in relatively local fixtures. However, before promotion to the Football League, Burton Albion’s biggest rivals were Stafford Rangers, Nuneaton Borough, Tamworth and Gresley Rovers. Away supporters are accommodated in the Mead Grab & Plant Stand, more commonly known as the South Stand, where around 1,600 fans can be seated. In most league fixtures, however, only the section nearest the Habbin terrace is usually opened. The covered all-seater stand is one of the newer parts of the stadium and offers good facilities throughout. Although it sits slightly further back from the pitch than some away ends, sightlines are generally excellent and the raised seating position provides a clear view of the action. For larger fixtures, the southern end of the Habbin terrace can also be made available, allowing the club to accommodate close to 1,000 additional away supporters. Accessing the away end is a little unusual, requiring supporters to walk along a path through Coldham Common. While the route is memorable, it can feel isolated, particularly for evening kick offs. Food options inside the ground include burgers, hot dogs, chips and pies, while Street Eat vendors provide rotating options throughout the season. Supporters can also purchase alcoholic drinks, including lager, pale ale, cider, wine and gin and tonic. Abbey Stadium in the news In 2022, Cambridge United finalized the purchase of the Abbey Stadium from Grosvenor Estates for an impressive £3.5 million. However, when additional costs and expenses related to the acquisition are taken into account, the total rises to £4.5 million. The club had to sell Abbey Stadium due to financial issues, but successfully bought it back in 2022. In January 2024, the club reached a five-year partnership with the software management company Cledara, leading to the renaming of the venue to Cledara Abbey Stadium . Abbey Stadium redevelopment Cambridge United Stadium is not falling behind in the redevelopment projects across the UK football landscape. The club aims to increase the capacity of Abbey Stadium to accommodate its growing fanbase. Plans are underway to redevelop the venue, focusing particularly on the Newmarket Road End and the Habbin Stand. The goal is to raise the seating capacity to just below 12,000, up from the current 8,000. The Habbin Stand is projected to have at least 3,300 seats, primarily for home supporters, along with improved family and hospitality facilities. The Newmarket Road End Stand will undergo a complete overhaul, being replaced with a 3,500-capacity terrace that will include safe standing zones. Other elements of the Abbey Stadium redevelopment include a museum, a club shop, and office facilities. As reported in October 2024, Bluerock Sports is currently conducting feasibility studies to ensure that the redevelopment plans meet the needs of the local community and supporter groups. Furthermore, Cambridge United has indicated its intention to submit a proposal for the stadium redevelopment project to the council by the summer of 2025. In a recent update, Cambridge United announced that the Mead South Stand will officially become a home family stand starting in the 2024/25 season. This decision aims to create additional space for the expanding home supporter base and to enhance the matchday experience at Abbey Stadium. The statement also noted that family seating locations in Blocks A and G within the Main Stand are still available. The Mead South Stand will undergo improvements in the summer of 2025 to ensure fans enjoy the best catering services, more social spaces, and additional retail areas. Additionally, there will be 15 new wheelchair spaces along with seats for accompanying assistants. Block H1 of the main stand will replace Block A as the designated calm area for fans. To make attending matches more appealing, Cambridge United will offer free season tickets to children under 14, or a discounted Under-18 season ticket at half price for supporters who purchase a concession or adult ticket in the main stand. Cambridge United fans are undoubtedly on the edge of their seats, as they have been expecting concrete designs for the new redeveloped Cledara Abbey Stadium for a while now. Back in October 2024, CEO Alex Tunbridge promised the fans that good news would come sooner rather than later, as a huge number of meetings have been held in connection with the stadium’s redevelopment. Tunbridge himself expressed his delight at the fact that talks are going so smoothly and said that he expects the fans to be very happy with what the men in charge of the project have cooked up in the lab. Cambridge United ground history The Cledara Abbey Stadium, which is Cambridge’s current ground, is 102 years old, having been built in 1923. However, Cambridge United has only played their games there for 93 years, having first occupied the stadium in 1932. At that time, the ‘stadium’ consisted of a single stand with changing rooms, but it provided Cambridge with a home. Before moving to The Cledara Abbey Stadium, the club was somewhat nomadic, using various pitches around the city. Formerly known as Abbey United, the U’s played at Parker’s Piece, where they stayed for one year. The club’s fortunes changed when Henry Piece, a former president of Cambridge United, donated land to the club. On this land, he constructed a grandstand along with changing rooms. This grandstand did not open until 1934, two years after an inaugural match. The first game played at the venue was a friendly match between a team from Cambridge University Press and Cambridge United on August 31, 1932. On May 1, 1970, a record 14,000 spectators attended a match between Chelsea and Cambridge United following the installation of the first floodlights. The ground was officially renamed Abbey Stadium in 1961, following the construction of additional stands, with the last one, the Habbin Stand, being erected in 1954. Since then, a lot of redevelopment has taken place, including roof installations and extra seating. However, due to financial challenges, the land of Abbey Stadium was sold in 2004, but the club managed to buy it back fully in 2022 for a staggering £3.5 million. In 2017, the stadium was named Cambs Glass Stadium due to sponsorship reasons. It has also been known as Costings Abbey Stadium and Trade Recruitment Stadium in recent years for the same reasons. With Cambridge returning to League One for the 2026-27 season, the two rivals are set to meet each other in the league. Other rivalries Aside from Peterborough and Stevenage, Cambridge United has other notable rivals, including Northampton and Luton , although these rivalries are not as intense. The home fans I spoke to were all very friendly and welcoming, which is more than can be said for certain other clubs in this division. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the stadium? The approach to the ground is far from glamorous, and felt more akin to a hike through a rural field. We were housed in the standing terrace to the left of the goal, which didn't give the best view of the action but did allow us to create a decent amount of noise. There was quite a big gap between the away fans and home fans, which meant that the atmosphere lacked some of the usual intensity you find at most Sunderland away games in League One. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game itself was full of commitment from both sides, but generally lacking in quality. We took the lead when a corner flew in directly off the post, but were quickly pegged back when our defence parted like the Red Sea to allow Cambridge to equalise. Fortunately, Nathan Broadhead then made it 2-1 to Sunderland with a screamer from outside the box, and despite Cambridge having about thirty corners in the second half, that's how it stayed. The facilities were very basic; at half time the lights briefly went out in the men's toilets, which was both a hilarious and slightly grim experience. https://footballgroundguide.com/leagues/.text: News Stadiums England Northern Ireland Republic of Ireland Scotland Wales Non-League Europe Americas Other stadiums New stadiums Old Trafford redevelopment: Updates on new Man Utd stadium Everton new stadium – Bramley-Moore Dock Wrexham stadium expansion: Kop redevelopment Chelsea new stadium Elland Road expansion New Luton stadium – Power Court Stadium Reviews Gambling Free Bets Sports Betting Sites Casino Sites Bingo Sites Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Away days News Fans Match day info Events History Huddersfield Town Accu Stadium - Huddersfield Town See 33 reviews Submit a review Capacity: 24,121 (all seated) Club Nickname: The Terriers Year Opened: 1994 Pitch Size: 115 x 76 yards Address: Huddersfield, HD1 6PX Phone: 01484 960 600 Pitch Type: Grass Shirt Sponsors: Hey Dude Fax: 01484 484 101 Ticket Office: 01484 960 606 Undersoil Heating: Yes Manufacturer: Castore Home Kit: Blue and White Stripes Away Kit: Ecru with Blue trim Third Kit: Dark Green with Gold Trim See more Last Update: July 20, 2026 What is the Accu Stadium like for away fans? An away day in Huddersfield is generally a good one for away fans both in terms of pubs and eateries in the local area and the stadium itself. The Accu Stadium – previously known as the John Smith’s Stadium – is relatively modern having been built in 1994 and it still stands up today. The away end at the Accu Stadium is in the South Stand where an allocation of up to 4,000 can be given to travelling supporters. Typically, though, an allocation of around 2,500 is given with the rest of the stand being given to home supporters. The atmosphere in the away end can be excellent, with home fans and away typically going back and forth with each other. The acoustics are brilliant with the roof hanging over the entire away end which also adds to the appeal of Huddersfield away. The view from the away section is good, particularly when the action is down at that end of the stadium. However, the facilities are a little dated and the concourse is uncovered which is far from ideal when the weather isn’t playing ball. Away fans enter through turnstiles 17-20 at the Accu Stadium and are advised to get in early to avoid the late surge in the minutes leading up to kick-off. Accu Stadium in the news Huddersfield get full ownership of the stadium In October 2024 it was announced that Huddersfield Town were being given Kirklees Council’s 40% share of the Accu Stadium. Since the stadium opened in the 1990s, the ownership of it was shared by the council, Huddersfield Town and Huddersfield Giants Rugby League Club, however, as of October, Huddersfield Town have been the majority owners. Furthermore, on , it was confirmed that the club had acquired 100% control and ownership in the stadium and the 53-acre surrounding site. The acquisition secured the Terriers’ home in the heart of Huddersfield for the future having signed a long-term leasehold for the next 300 years, working alongside Kirklees Council and Huddersfield Giants in the process. Under the agreement, Kirklees Council wrote off £4.3 million in previously provided loans, while Huddersfield Giants signed a new tenancy agreement for the 2026 Rugby League season, with their future beyond that point currently unclear. The decision means Huddersfield Town will be able to press on with redevelopment work in the coming years to help with their long-term plan to get back into the Premier League, with owner Kevin Nagle advising that the Terriers will seek to bring the Accu Stadium up to its full potential in the coming years as their long-term home and potential destination venue. New screen installed Huddersfield installed an all-new big screen, replacing the previous screen in the Cowshed South Stand. The new addition extended the size of the screen to over three times as large as its predecessor. Famous people seen at the Accu Stadium Huddersfield Town may not be the most glamorous football club in the world but they do have a couple of famous fans. Some that have turned up at the Accu Stadium in recent years include: Sir Patrick Stewart Sir Patrick Stewart is undoubtedly the most famous Huddersfield Town fan in the world and was even once the Chancellor of Huddersfield University. The Star Trek actor is seen here with the club mascot, Terry the Terrier, back in 2018. Photo by Imago Jodie Whittaker Jodie Whittaker is another famous actor who supports Huddersfield Town. Born in the local area, Whittaker has been spotted at the Accu Stadium on a couple of occasions. The club dedicated a social media post and a special shirt to her when she was unveiled as the first female Doctor Who in 2018. 👏 Congratulations to #htafc fan #JodieWhittaker on the launch of @bbcdoctorwho on @BBCOne this evening. (AT) pic.twitter.com/mNIEIfGrBW — Huddersfield Town (@htafc) October 7, 2018 Huddersfield Town chants When the Accu Stadium is packed to the rafters, the Huddersfield Town supporters can make quite a racket. Some of their most popular chants include: Ooh to be a Terrier Falling in love Smile a while And it’s Huddersfield Town We love you Huddersfield A video compilation of some of the most well-known Huddersfield chants can be watched below. Huddersfield Town tifos Huddersfield Town aren’t known for putting on colourful, grand tifos before matches but on a few occasions, their supporters have pulled out an inspirational banner or two. A few that stick in the memory books are as follows: Huddersfield tifo against Man Utd Photo by Ultras-Tifo.net Once a Terrier, always a Terrier Photo by Getty David Wagner tifo Photo by Yorkshire Live Best views and seating plan The Accu Stadium was built to ensure that no supporters have a ‘bad’ or ‘restricted’ view when they visit. In terms of the seats with the ‘best’ view, though, fans should consider the two stands that run along the side of the pitch – the Riverside Stand and the Kilner Bank Stand. The Riverside stand is one of two stands at the stadium to have two tiers and the best views of the pitch can be found towards the front of the upper tier. For these seats, fans should target blocks four and five while blocks five and six in the lower tier also provide an excellent view of the action. The Kilner Bank Stand is just a single-tiered stand so fans will need to try and get quite high up it to get a good view from the action. However, blocks 5-7 in this stand are the most central in the stadium (that aren’t taken up by sponsors and hospitality) so are worth considering. If you are more concerned about buying tickets in an area of the stadium where the atmosphere will be good, then you should look for seats in the lower tier of the Terriers Together Stand. This stand is located at the opposite end of the pitch to away fans but is where the most local Huddersfield fans are situated. Seating plan Photo by Huddersfield Town Pubs for away fans at the Accu Stadium The following pubs in the local area all welcome away fans on a matchday: The Yorkshire Rose – 217 Leeds Rd, Huddersfield HD1 6NW Turnbrige Working Men’s Club – 9 St Andrew’s Rd, Aspley, Huddersfield HD1 6SB Head of Steam – St George’s Square, Huddersfield HD1 1JB Food and drink at the Accu Stadium Huddersfield Town put on decent food for their fans on the concourses at the Accu Stadium with their roast potatoes and gravy boxes particularly popular. In addition to these boxes, they also offer fans hot dogs, pies and loaded sweet potato bhajis so there is something for everyone. In terms of drinks, fans can purchase lager, soft drinks, and hot drinks at all food kiosks on the concourses before kick-off and at half-time. Huddersfield is one of the few clubs in the world to offer a special kids’ menu to younger supporters. Their Terrier Kidz Box includes a sandwich, fruit, biscuit, cherry tomatoes, cucumber sticks, and a bottle of water. Roast potatoes with beef brisket gravy at Huddersfield town ( @htafc ) ? £3.90 pic.twitter.com/m8rH4DXbYX — Footy Scran (@FootyScran) May 8, 2023 Best places to eat near the Accu Stadium If you’d rather take your chances with a sit-down meal as opposed to a box of roast potatoes and gravy then there are plenty of restaurants in the local area. The stadium is less than a mile away from the train station and the town centre where the following establishments can be found: Vudu – 1 Firth St, Huddersfield HD1 3BB Apadana – 9 Viaduct St, Huddersfield HD1 5DL Med-One – 10-12 Westgate, Huddersfield HD1 1NN Getting to the stadium By car The Accu Stadium is located just off the A62 Leeds Road. It can be easiest reached from Junction 25 of the M62. Simply follow the signs for Huddersfield (A62) and you will reach the stadium over on your left. The Accu Stadium is generally well signposted around Huddersfield town centre If approaching from the South, then leave the M1 at Junction 38 and take the A637 towards and then the A642 into Huddersfield. As you approach the town centre try to keep to the right-hand lane as you will turn right at the roundabout and onto the A62 Leeds Road. The stadium is a short distance down this road on the right. Alternatively if coming up from the South and looking for somewhere to park then along St Andrews Road several small businesses offer parking for around £5. There is no parking available for away supporters at the stadium itself. Post Code for SAT NAV: HD1 6PX By public transport The Accu Stadium is walkable from Huddersfield Railway Station, it should take no more than 15 minutes at a comfortable pace. After coming out of the Railway Station, turn down past the front of The George Hotel. Go straight over the crossroads into Northumberland Street and walk down across the Ring Road straight on into Leeds Road. Turn right down Gasworks Street. Straight over the crossroads to the ground. Disabled facilities and accessibility at Accu Stadium As alluded to above, the facilities at this ground are far better than you may expect, and as such, it possesses plenty of features designed to help accommodate supporters who need extra assistance upon their visit. These include: 38 dedicated disabled parking spaces 399 accessible seats 13 accessible toilets Designated accessible stadium tours for disabled supporters The club advise that fans with disabilities seeking to purchase tickets should call the Ticket Office on 01484 960 606 and select option 5 , or get in contact with the Disability Liaison Officer at [email protected] . Likewise, people that wish to make use of disabled parking spaces are advised to contact the club a week in advance of their trip to Accu Stadium via [email protected] or by calling 01484 960 606 and selecting option 5 . Supporters with disabilities may also benefit from the detailed guide offered by Huddersfield Town specifically for people with accessibility requirements, here . This document also features helpful pictures of the facilities at Accu Stadium, as well as additional information for visitors. Contact Details: Huddersfield Town Disability Liaison Officer Email: [email protected] Huddersfield Town Disabled Supporters Club Email: [email protected] Email – Dave Heatherill: [email protected] Webpage: www.htafc.com/terriers-together/disabled-supporters-club Accu Stadium ticket prices Huddersfield Town supporters can book tickets online or visit the Accu Stadium ticketing office. You can also make inquiries via email or the telephone number provided on the club website . The ticket office is open from Monday to Friday, starting at and closing at . On Saturdays, when The Terriers have a home game, you can buy tickets from the physical office from until kick-off. When there are no matchdays on Saturdays, the ticket office closes at noon. However, the office is closed on Sundays. Most importantly, Huddersfield have a dedicated ticket news platform on their website that lets you know, in advance, prices for upcoming home fixtures. Like most UK football clubs, booking Huddersfield tickets will take you to an e-ticket platform. Ticket at Accu Stadium are priced in the following ranges for different age groups: Adult : £15-£25 Over 65 : £10-£20 U18 : £10-£15 U11 : £10 Accu Stadium by capacity The Accu Stadium currently has a capacity of 24,500 and this has been the case since the North Stand was completed in 1998. The stadium initially opened in 1994 with just two of the four stands built (the Riverside Stand and Kilner Bank Stand). At this point, the capacity of the stadium was just shy of 14,000 but this increased when the South Stand was completed at the end of that year and then again when the North Stand (Terriers Together Stand) was built four years later. The attendance at the club’s first match at the stadium in August 1994 was 13,334. Stand by stand capacity at the Accu Stadium Terrier Together Stand – 2,750 Kilner Bank Stand – 7,000 South Stand – 4,054 Riverside Stand – 10,365 Huddersfield Stadium tours Huddersfield Town provide stadium tours of the Accu Stadium every Wednesday where fans have the opportunity to get a behind-the-scenes look at the place they call home. The fully guided tour gives fans a look at the dressing rooms, the tunnel and the dugout area to get a feel of what a matchday is like for the players before visiting the boardroom and hospitality areas to see how the other half live. Tours should be pre-booked on the stadium website and cost £5 for adults and £3.50 for juniors and seniors. Nearby attractions Huddersfield is not a city overflowing with tourist attractions, but for supporters planning some extra time around a trip to the Accu Stadium, there are still some worthwhile options to explore, some of these include: Greenhead Park Greenhead Park is located around a mile away from the Accu Stadium and one of the area’s most popular green spaces. With open lawns, scenic paths and a Victorian bandstand, the park offers a great chance for a relaxed time away from the matchday buzz, with a cafe also available. Tolson Museum and Ravensknowle Park Also around a mile from Huddersfield Town’s stadium, Tolson Museum is located within Ravensknowle Park. Here, visitors can immerse themselves into the town’s history, covering its industrial heritage as well as natural history. Another quieter option for those hoping for a change from the matchday experience, the surrounding park also offers pleasant views of the Colne Valley. Castle Hill Overlooking the town of Huddersfield from around two miles away, Castle Hill is one of Huddersfield’s most recognisable landmarks. The hill is topped by Victoria Tower, offering amazing panoramic views of the town and its surrounding countryside. For those with time to spare around a matchday at the Accu Stadium, Castle Hill is a popular spot for a walk and pre-match viewpoint. Given its relatively steep climb compared to other hills nearby, the reward at the top is worthwhile with amazing views, particularly on a clear day when much of the West Yorkshire landscape is visible. Huddersfield Narrow Canal Running through parts of Huddersfield and accessible within a short distance of the Accu Stadium, the Huddersfield Narrow Canal offers a quiet and scenic spot away from the matchday buzz and crowds. Originally built during the Industrial Revolution, the canal provides peaceful waterside walking routes, traditional stone bridges and great views of the surrounding Pennine landscapes. Supporters with time before or after a matchday, or those making a weekend of a trip to the Accu Stadium, can enjoy a relaxed stroll along the paths with several pubs and cafes located nearby as convenient rest stops. The area, particularly on clear afternoons, allows visitors another perspective into Huddersfield’s industrial heritage as well as its natural scenery. Other things to do around Huddersfield include: Enjoy a few drinks on the Huddersfield Real Ale Trail Take a boat ride underneath Standedge tunnel If you want to check out another big football stadium while you’re in the area then Elland Road , the home of Leeds United, is only around a 20-minute drive away. You will also find a lot more to do in Leeds, with a wider array of restaurants, bars and attractions. Concerts at the Accu Stadium Like most modern stadiums, the Accu Stadium was built with more than just sport in mind. Concerts have regularly been held at the stadium over the years with some of the biggest artists playing here in recent times. Some notable names include: Elton John Elton John played at the Accu Stadium back in 2005 when the idea of retirement wasn’t even on the horizon for the British icon. The gig was part of his Peachtree Road Tour which took John all over the world for over a year. Little Mix Little Mix played to a sold-out Accu Stadium back in 2018. The concert was part of their Summer Hits Tour and was their first-ever stadium tour in the UK. The girl band wowed fans with famous hits such as ‘Shout Out to My Ex’ and ‘Wings’. Remember when little mix performed to 28k fans “Tonight was EPIC!! Thank you Huddersfield, thank you to all our fans for supporting us and getting us to a stage in our careers where we can sell out stadiums like this. We are so grateful and it’s all thanks to you, the girls xx” pic.twitter.com/wOctN5XWVb — Josh (@cloudleigh) June 16, 2021 Take That Take That played to a sold-out Accu Stadium in 2019 as part of their Greatest Hits Tour. By this point, the band were just a trio but they still put on a brilliant show in Huddersfield for all of their fanatical supporters. Others Stereophonics performed at the stadium in June 2025 as part of their “Stadium Anthems Summer ’25” tour. Muse played the stadium in June 2023, while Green Day (along with Fall Out Boy and Weezer) took part in the “Hella Mega Tour” in June 2022. Huddersfield Town ground history Huddersfield Town started playing at Leeds Road in September 1908, just a month after the club was founded. They remained there for almost 90 years. This changed after the Hillsborough disaster in 1989, in which 95 Liverpool fans were killed at the time. Off the back of this, all teams in the first two divisions of the Football League were required to have an all-seater stadium by the 1994-95 season. Due to this, the Terriers started making plans for a new stadium in 1992. The Kirklees Stadium was completed just in time for the 1994/95 season and the Terriers moved in after spending 86 years at Leeds Road. Changes to the new Huddersfield stadium have been minimal but the ground has gone through a few name changes over the past three decades. It was named the Alfred McAlpine Stadium up until 2004, the Galpharm Stadium up until 2012, and Accu Stadium until this very day. In September 2025, Huddersfield Town became the sole owners of the Accu Stadium for the first-ever time, as well as the 53-acre surrounding site, after reaching an agreement with Kirklees Council and Huddersfield Giants. The latter will continue their Rugby League operations at the stadium until at least 2026. Latest developments at the Accu Stadium Huddersfield Town made a whole host of improvements to the Accu Stadium throughout 2024 and 2025, including: Refurbishing the stands, fan bars, concourses and hospitality areas Renovating the players’ changing rooms Rebranding the club shop That is believed to be just the start of a multi-million-pound redevelopment of the ground, with more improvements expected over the next few years given the club recently became sole owners of the stadium for the first time in their history, incentivising the Terriers to make improvements to their home.. Accu Stadium average and record attendances Record attendance At the Accu Stadium: 24,169 vs Tottenham Hotspur Premier League, At Leeds Road: 67,037 vs Arsenal FA Cup 6th Round, 27 February, 1932. Average attendance 2024-2025: 21,325 (League One) 2023-2024: 19,181 (Championship) 2022-2023: 19,151 (Championship) 2021-2022: 17,274 (Championship) 2020-2021: 0 (Covid) (Championship) 2019-2020: 21,748 (Championship) Huddersfield Town's local rivals Leeds United rivalry – Although Leeds have much bigger rivalries with other clubs, there isn’t a bigger game for Huddersfield than a match against the Whites. Both clubs are based in West Yorkshire which makes matches between them quite heated. The sides last met in the 2023-24 Championship campaign, when Huddersfield suffered a 4-1 away defeat and drew 1-1 on home turf. It is unclear when the rivals will meet next, with Leeds now two divisions above in the Premier League, unless they are drawn against one another in a cup competition. Bradford City rivalry – Bradford City are another club in West Yorkshire that Huddersfield Town fans aren’t particularly fond of. The two teams reignited their rivalry in the 2025-26 League One season, with Huddersfield losing 3-1 away from home in September and returning the favour with a 1-0 home victory at the Accu Stadium in January, and they will again square off in England’s third tier in 2026-27, with the away game coming in October and the Terriers’ home fixture against the Bantams taking place in January 2027. Barnsley rivalry – While the games may not receive the same attention as those with Leeds and Bradford, Huddersfield also share a rivalry with Barnsley having met regularly through the Yorkshire sides’ histories. They have played one another in the last two League One campaigns, with the Terriers most recently winning 2-1 at home in February, and they will again do battle in the 2026-27 term. Huddersfield will travel to Oakwell in December before welcoming the Reds to the Accu Stadium for the reverse fixture in January 2027. Sheffield Wednesday rivalry – Huddersfield also have a Yorkshire rivalry with Sheffield Wednesday, with the two clubs having regularly crossed paths across the Championship and League One in recent years. While it is not generally considered among either club’s fiercest rivalries, meetings can still carry plenty of local pride with Sheffield and Huddersfield separated by around 25 miles. The teams have met in both league and cup competition over the years, including Huddersfield Town’s memorable penalty shootout victory over Wednesday at Hillsborough in the 2017 Championship playoff semi-finals on their way to promotion to the Premier League. With both clubs having spent significant periods outside the top flight in recent decades, it is a fixture that has become relatively familiar to supporters. The two clubs reignited their rivalry in 2026-27, after the Owls suffered relegation back to League One to join the Terriers, with the clash at the Accu Stadium taking place in mid-October 2026. Huddersfield led 2-0 heading into injury time but were eventually held to a 2-2 draw and will travel to Hillsborough for the reverse fixture on New Year’s Day. Retro football pictures at the Accu Stadium The Accu Stadium is barely 30 years old so there aren’t too many photos that would qualify as retro, particularly as the stadium hasn’t really changed since 1998. Check out a picture of what the stadium looked like when it first opened below when just two stands were finished. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly?
