Away fans are located in the Magic Rock Brewing Stand, behind the goal to the south west of the ground. The stand is shared between roughly 2/3 away and 1/3 home fans, with a thin transparent cordon between them. The main (Core) stand is quite an impressive two tier structure, as is the Big Red Stand behind the other goal. Strangely, the lower tier of this stand is covered in banners over the seats which are retractable for concerts etc, so there are no fans pitchside behind one goal. The final stand (the Chadwick Lawrence Stand) is a one-tier structure along the entire touchline. Overall, it's very tidy. Biggest complaint, however, is that the concourse area behind the Magic Rock Brewing Stand is all outdoors with the toilets (pitifully inadequate) and one food outlet in a separate building. It was just about bearable in the heat, but would completely put me off queueing for any food or drinks if the weather was poor. (As it happens, the queues were so long that there was no point in queueing up anyway!) I can't understand how they got this so hopelessly wrong when they designed the stadium. The area is simply inadequate for the number of people congregating there, and this was not even a sell-out crowd. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game kicked off in the stifling heat and both sides played a high line, which meant that most of the action seemed to be centred around the middle third of the pitch, with the odd breakthrough for a shot on goal. Stoke were awarded a penalty in the 20th minute, which was saved and then the rebound hit the post. The Terriers went ahead 20 minutes later with a free header from a corner (painful to watch as we were in Row E right behind the goal!) Stoke looked energised after the break and equalised roughly ten minutes after the restart with a beautifully drilled shot from Baker. There's nothing like being sat behind the goal knowing that it's going in before most other people in the stadium realise it. Stoke thought they'd got a second 20 minutes later but it was (wrongly) ruled offside. Town went ahead with a fast break a couple of minutes after that, and sealed the three points with a similar goal in the last five minutes. The score certainly didn't reflect the balance of play between the teams - a draw would have probably been a fair result. We chose to stay in the shade during half time, rather than queue for refreshments, but I did notice that the two-pint glasses of lager were selling particularly well! As mentioned, the facilities were woefully inadequate, but due to the layout of the ground, it's difficult to see how they could be improved. There was a cracking atmosphere in the ground - it's clear that the noisy Terriers fans choose to sit adjacent to the away fans as they were making far more noise than the rest of the stadium put together. Sometimes this spilled over into some nasty confrontation between the two sets of fans, but there was a very heavy presence of stewards and police to deal with any issues. In fact, I found the police presence to be quite heavy-handed and wonder whether this contributed to the tension both inside and out of the ground. (That's not to excuse some appalling behaviour from both sets of fans and I appreciate it's a delicate balance to get right.) Comment on getting away from the ground after the game Despite being right near the front and all the exits at the back, it was very quick to get out of the stadium. As mentioned by another reviewer, pies for a pound were in abundance as we left. Surprisingly, given the earlier tension, there was no separation between home and away fans until reaching the away supporters' coaches. We walked the ten minutes back to the car and were on the open road ten minutes after this - a very easy departure. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out This was a great day out, despite the result. It's a great stadium and to be too hot when watching football is a rare problem indeed for a Stoke fan! See more 16th April 2022 Gary Jarvis Game Attended Qpr Competition Championship Date 15/04/2022 Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the ground itself? It was a special offer for Good Friday of only £10 per person and Huddersfield isn't too far from my home its only £8.30 on the train and a ground I've never visited before so couldn't turn it down How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Easy train ride from Keighley taking just under the hour with a change at Leeds , ground is less then 15 mins walk from station and very easy to find What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? Had a look round the town centre and had something to eat before making my way to the ground, both sets of fans sermed friendly enough ,apart from the usual banter their was was no animosity What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the stadium? It's an unusualground with all stands semi circular the, I was in the home stand which is shared with the away fans with a small bit of no man's land in between, the opposite end seemed the only stand with two tiers Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. Finished 2-2:which probally pleased QPR more having twice come from behind, either side could of nicked it at the end so a draw was probally a fair result though I felt QPR played the better football, good suport from both sets of fans with plenty of singing/ chanting etc, the concourse area was uncovered, fortunately it was a dry day but might not be much fun in bad weather, had a Bovril which was reasonably priced and alcohol is also available be warned though they don't accept cash at the catering outlets it's card only, programmes are also given out free on a first come first served basis and whilst smaller then usual they contain all the necessary info except I was surprised no league tables but then as they free I can't complain !! Comment on getting away from the ground after the game Easy walk back to the station via a quick pit stop at the burger van that was parked just outside the main entrance, train was slightly delayed but journey back to Keighley was pretty uneventful and got back at a reasonable time Summary of overall thoughts of the day out Was a good and enjoyable day out, can't complain when I only paid £18 in total for train journey and championship football and think Huddersfield ought to be praised for putting on offers like that See more 8th March 2022 Justin Bentley Game Attended Huddersfield Town V Peterborough United Competition Championship Game Date 04/03/2022 Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the ground itself? Not been since 1996 when it was 3 sided, I like this as a new build especial at night, not a bad journey from South Lincs and moved to a Friday night was advantageous for me. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Didn't leave Bourne until and did it in just over 2 hours. As it was a night game Council parking was free so parked on the Old Leeds Road council car park (also Covid test site at the time of writing), approx 10 mins from ground What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? My mate needed cash to get in so just went to Sainsburys, everyone friendly, though POSH and them have a history. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the stadium? Looks really impressive at night, and busy around the ground (too busy for the shop to get a badge), free programmes! Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. Posh were awful, no change there this season. £8 pie and pint deal (a Craft local lager), stewards friendly enough but saw a little ding dong with one of our youth. Unusual that no concourse but outside for the toilets and catering, not raining so not an issue. Good atmosphere from the home fans, they went second and were 2 nil up after 10 minutes. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game Quite a lot of traffic but got back on the Leeds Road ok and back on the M62, Standard roadworks on way home Summary of overall thoughts of the day out I like this ground, interesting and unique, See more 23rd February 2022 Steve Bolland Game Attended Huddersfield Town v Coventry City Competition Championship Date 11/12/2021 Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the ground itself? I don't often go to away matches this far away (I live in Somerset) but my wife was meant to be in New York for the week so I thought I'd make the most of it. In the end though, her trip was cancelled last minute. It was probably just as well the game wasn't at Rotherham, that would really have rubbed salt in the wound. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? I drove up from London, having picked my son up, so it was an early start for the 4 hour drive. We just followed the directions above. The last bit of the journey, after leaving the M1, is a lovely drive through the Yorkshire countryside. We paid a few quid to park on a site on St. Andrew's Road. There are quite a few to choose from and they're only a few minutes walk from the ground. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? There are no obvious pubs close to the ground and we were going to head to the Rope Walk but found the Legends' Cafe Bar tucked under the Revell Ward/Core Stand where there was a mix of home and away fans. We got there about 1.30pm but they were turning people away later; I'm not sure whether this was due to Covid restrictions or not. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the stadium? This is the best new stadium I've been too. Some attention has been paid to the architectural aspects so it's not simply a boring bowl. It's also tucked nicely away under a wooded hill so it kind of fits into its surroundings. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. Coventry came into this game in a rich vein of form and we outplayed the home team for large periods of the match. Rotherham, however, were 1-0 up until we scored an equalizer in stoppage time which certainly made the long drive home more palatable. I have to commend the stewarding. We were talking to one of the stewards throughout the second half and he was basically telling us to remain calm as the way we were playing, a goal was sure to come. He was right too! If only being a supporter was always so simple. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game It looks like it could take some time to get out of St. Andrew's Road if you are parked near the ground end. We were at the other end though and some kind person let us into the queue and we were out onto the A629 in no time. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out A great day out despite the long journey. A nice looking stadium and the injury time goal helped. See more 18th September 2020 John Hague (Leicester City) Huddersfield Town v Leicester City Premier League Saturday 6th April 2019, 3pm John Hague (Leicester City) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the John Smith's Stadium? I had been to the John Smith's Stadium when it had been called the McAlpine/Galpharm Stadium many times for Rugby League but never football. My girlfriend's daughter and her friend secured me a £30 ticket for the Leicester City section. About the only thing, I can like the Premier League for. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Two family Metro Day Rovers ensured we only paid £6.50 for all our travel during the day. We had stayed in Leeds the night before and were staying Saturday night too to make a good weekend of gigs and football. A 17 minute journey from Leeds and we were soon having a few beers first in the Kings Head and then Head Of Steam, both on Huddersfield Station. There were plenty of Leicester City fans and the atmosphere was very good-natured. We tried to Northern Quarter Bar but found it closed and instead I had to suffer a Wetherspoons. At least I didn't pay but I had to think on my feet when asked where I was from (even though I was with three women) and said proudly 'Barnsley!' From here it's a pleasant 20 minute walk to the ground. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? The King's Head, Head Of Steam and sadly Wetherspoons. Some great beers though and a good laugh. Home fans were sanguine but friendly. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the John Smith's Stadium? I remember being impressed when I first for a Great Britain Rugby League International years ago but now the stadium seems a bit unloved. I guess the fact it was daylight and no floodlights blazing disappointed me. The away end is pretty badly designed and the area for food and toilets far too small. A trip to the loo at halftime was a major logistical operation. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc. . The stewards were good and friendly, the pies were tasty but I have to be honest… overcooked! The game itself was a very end of the season. Huddersfield had been put out of their misery last weekend so I expected them to cut loose a bit but if anything they were even more rubbish than for most of the season. 4-1 flattered a Leicester City side who strolled through the game. In terms of atmosphere, the few Terriers fans who could be bothered soon gave up singing. I guess they've had a long season and the team just hasn't given them anything to sing about. The Leicester fans kept up the noise throughout the game and the 'ole's' at the end were sticking the knife in a bit. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: A twenty minute walk back to the station to meet my girlfriend was pretty simple. A couple more beers and we hoped on a train back to Leeds. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: Another ground ticked and five more goals for the year but I've seen more exciting games even at Step 11 of the pyramid. Not one to live long in the memory. See more 1st January 2020 Tony Mills (Stoke City) Huddersfield Town v Stoke City Championship Wednesday 1st January 2020, 3pm Tony Mills (Stoke City) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the John Smith's Stadium? A chance to attend the game with my two sons doesn't occur very often as one is based overseas with the British Army. Huddersfield is not too far from our family home in Nottinghamshire, and Huddersfield was for me another ground to add to my list of those visited. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? The journey was very easy the motorway was quite quiet and we parked up about 10 minutes walk from the stadium on a nearby street. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? We went for a couple of drinks in the bar right outside the stadium which had a good mix of Huddersfield and Stoke fans. The pub was busy but getting drinks was quick and efficient and there were no problems with any fans. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the John Smith's Stadium? I thought the stadium looked superb from the outside, great design, and still looked very neat and tidy, the away end was again fine, with a great view. The overall look of the ground from inside was even more impressive, it is quite simply a wonderful stadium. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. For Stoke, it was a cracking game ending in a 5-2 away win. Stoke also had a great following of around 2,200, who made a great atmosphere. The Huddersfield fans, also made good noise when they felt they had something to cheer, the stewards seemed very friendly wishing us a Happy New Year on entry to the stadium. The police on the other hand were cold and unapproachable without any hint of trouble, the general facilities seemed pretty standard. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: A 10 minute walk uphill back to the car and we were away, again no problems at all. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: A cracking day out. A great journey there, couple of pints close to the stadium, friendly home fans and a great result for Stoke and then an easy journey back home, away days don't get much better than that. See more 7th December 2019 Shaun (Leeds) Huddersfield Town v Leeds United Championship Saturday 7th December 2019, 12:30pm Shaun (Leeds) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the John Smith's Stadium? My first trip to the ground and a local derby is always a bit more special. We don’t have a great record at Huddersfield so I was hoping to see a rare win! How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Pretty good. There’s plenty of private parking a short walk from the ground. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? The guy I was driving over with is a bit of a petrol head and so took me to Shaks which if you have a spare £150k has a great range of sports cars! I was surprised we were let in wearing 2 Leeds scarves! What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the John Smith's Stadium? Usual new ground although this has 4 definite stands rather than one continuous one. Views are uninterrupted and hard to think of a criticism really. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The atmosphere was good, not least because Huddersfield are one of those teams who’ve created a noisy section in the same stand as the away fans and to be fair they made plenty of noise and it was quite hard for us to get our own chants going. Huddersfield also started the game well which helped that, however as it wore on so we became stronger and eventually ran out deserved 2-0 winners. Stewards were fine and handled any issues well. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Not too bad. The M62 is to the west of the centre and the ground is to the east so a bit slow on the ring road but after that okay. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: A great day out, 3 more points to keep our promotion hopes alive just not quite enough spare change in my pocket for that Ferrari. See more 27th October 2019 David Crossfield (Barnsley) Huddersfield Town v Barnsley Championship Saturday 26th October, 3pm David Crossfield (Barnsley) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the John Smith's Stadium? Under caretaker manager Adam Murray Barnsley had changed system to 3-5-2 and, having had commendable draws against Swansea at home and West Brom away, there was hope that things were improving. I had arrange to meet my ex-cricket playing friend, who is a Town fan and have a few beers. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Barnsley to Huddesfield is only 17 miles but public transport is limited. No buses. One direct train an hour or change trains at Wakefield. West Yorkshire Police have a habit of meeting Barnsley fans at the station and escorting them to the ground so I decided to travel by changing trains at Wakefield. Some Reds fans had the same idea and left the train to going drinking in Mirfield. After a few pints in Huddersfield we walked to the ground. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? I went with my friend and his brother to the Sportsman. We were in early and got seats. Three pints of real ale and pie and peas as pre-match preparation. There were a few other Barnsley fans in the pub and they mingled without any problems. There isn't much history of problems between the two sets of supporters, but there was a huge Police presence outside the railway station and on the walk to the ground, including horses. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the John Smith's Stadium? I've been several times so I knew what to expect. What I didn't expect was a long queue to get through the turnstiles. I joined the queue at 2.45 and got in the ground at 3.05. Three turnstiles were open for 2200 fans, but it seems it was the parting down by stewards that was apparently causing delays. I missed the minutes silence etc for remembrance day. My seat was in a section of the Abzorb stand reserved for families and older people (like me!) and holds about 600. It's good for families not to have to sit amongst some of our fans! My seat was in row S near the corner flag and I had a good view of the game. The Abzorb stand in now shared with the noisy home section, with away fans allocated 2300 seats. My Town friend said this was a David Wagner initiative to negate the noisy away fans presence. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. Another defeat for Barnsley. A record fourteen games without a win now. The first half-hour was a dull contest with little quality. Barnsley perhaps having slightly the better of it with three corners. Huddersfield scored with their first attempt on target in the 30th minute. The Barnsley defence were asleep when a quick free kick was played out wide and the cross evaded everyone to reach Schindler who tapped in from a few yards out. McGeehan missed a great chance to equalise. He couldn't hit a barn door with a banjo this season, having missed two easy chances against Swansea. 1-0 at half time. Huddersfield went 2-0 up early in the second half with a great curling shot. Barnsley huffed and puffed but lacked any creativity to trouble Huddersfield, who looked comfortable. A smart turn and cross shot from Jacob Brown, Barnsley's first shot on target, made it 2-1. Huddersfield looked rattled but hung on for the win without any major problems. A really disappointing performance from a jaded looking Reds after a great midweek performance at WBA, which gave us some hope of some improvement. It wasn't a pretty game. Credit to Cowley for his tactics in negating any Barnsley creativity. As usual, I didn't have any refreshments inside the ground. The toilet facilities were inadequate for the number of fans. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: No problem. I met my friend outside the famous Gas Club and we walked back up to Town. Lots of police presence as there doesn't seem to be any way to segregate fans leaving the ground. More ale in the Courtyard, Mallinsons brewery tap. Not really my kind of bar/pub. A final pint in the Kings Head on the railway station, which is a great real ale pub, before our trains home. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: Great to catch up with my friend. Good ale and good company. Pity about the football. Huddersfield is a good away day. See more 15th September 2019 Adrian Hurst (Sheffield Wednesday) Huddersfield Town v Sheffield Wednesday Championship Sunday 15th September 2019, 12 noon Adrian Hurst (Sheffield Wednesday) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the John Smith's Stadium? Not been to a game at Huddersfield since the days of them playing at their old Leeds Road ground, so I looked forward to visiting a new ground. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Thanks to Sky Television changing the fixture time to noon on a Sunday and living over 250 miles away it was a crack of dawn (05.30) start for this game. Thankfully the roads were very quiet and we found free parking on Thistle Street by 09.30. The ground was easy to find and well signposted from the outskirts of the town. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? After parking up we walked around to Subway for breakfast, which was next door to a Greggs. No pub this time as it was a 12 noon kick off and no problems at all with the home fans. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the John Smith's Stadium? The ground looked quite impressive, but I couldn't help thinking how much they could have increased the capacity if they had levelled off the tops of the stands and filled in the corners! Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. We saw this as a potential 'banana skin' game as they hadn't won since March. I was impressed with the vocals from the locals – at least until we opened the scoring! A bit disappointed that in the John Smith Stadium they only had John Smiths in a can despite having lager and cider on draft! Could have done with larger toilets, one smallish block for a full away following was simply not enough. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: Only had a 5 minute walk back to the car but quite a wait to get out of the town – probably because most of the Owls fans were travelling in the same direction as us. As it was a Sunday it probably helped as the roads were generally quiet except for the football traffic. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: A long but very enjoyable away day and a 2-0 win were very nice. At least we could get virtually home during daylight hours thanks to the early start! See more 16th August 2019 Pete Woodhead (Doing the 92) Huddersfield Town v Fulham Championship Friday 16th August 2019, 7.45pm Pete Woodhead (Doing the 92) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the John Smiths' Stadium? My first trip sitting in the away end and I was looking forward to the experience. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? I managed to park on a side street around ten minutes walk away. It seemed that everyone was parking in a similar industrial area which meant that to find the ground it was a simple case of following the others. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? The away tickets did not turn up until 10 minutes before Kick off meaning that a lot of fans barely made it to their seat for the start of the game. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the John Smiths' Stadium? A lovely ground. I really enjoyed the modern curved stadium, however, the away end food and toilet area were not undercover, luckily it was not a rainy night. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game ended with a Fulham 2-1 win thanks to a late goal. There were a limited number of away fans but were louder than the home support. The facilities as stated were poor, not undercover and with slow service. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: A nice 10 mins walk back to the car following the crowd. Leaving the town was quite congested as lots of traffic lights being occupied by the fans. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: An enjoyable game. A nice looking stadium, however with poor facilities. I would expect better from a League 1 club let alone a team who were in the Premier League in recent years. It was the first game of the new season, and after another summer of upheaval at Derby I was looking forward to seeing new players, a new manager, etc. On top of that, Huddersfield were newly relegated, so I was interested to see how they would cope as newcomers to the division. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? Getting to Huddersfield was simple enough – parking not quite as much, as even though we arrived a good hour and a half before the game, the various car parks operated by local companies near to the ground were already full up. We followed signs to a nearby outdoor car park about 15 minutes walk from the ground, and after that, it was a simple matter of following the trail of shirts to the stadium. Photo : Pink Spider Everything you need to know ahead of our next trip to The King Power stadium, home of Leicester City FC. GETTING TO THE KING POWER STADIUM BY CAR The M1 and M69 Motorways interchange at Junction 21 (M1), where you should exit and follow the signs for the City Centre via the A5460. After three miles, turn right onto Upperton Road, follow the road down until you get to the Liberty Statue Island and take the fifth exit down Western Boulevard. You will then see King Power Stadium on your right-hand side. BY TRAIN Leicester Station which is around a 15 minute walk – the quickest route is out of the station, straight across the road onto Waterloo way, which leads onto Tigers way, you will see the Rugby stadium, take a left along Welford Road. You can then walk along Almond road or through Freeman’s common, this will lead to Aylestone Road where you should be able to see the stadium and follow along Raw Dykes Road. OTHER FORMS OF TRAVEL Buses run along Aylestone Road regularly and these go straight to the City Centre. Several bus services run from Leicester city centre to King Power Stadium, stopping on Aylestone Road, which is a five-minute walk from King Power Stadium. Most buses in Leicester are low floor vehicles, meaning they can be lowered to pavement level once the bus has stopped. Buses all include wheelchair spaces. Birmingham and East Midlands airport are the closest airports to the stadium both are around a 45 minute drive. TAXI’S Uber and Bolt are the quickest way of getting a taxi from the stadium. Leicester station is around a 15 minute walk and black cabs are normally waiting just to the side of the station. PARKING CAR PARKING The ground has multiple official car parks, all need to be booked in advance. There is parking available at Freeman’s Common, procing varies on the length of time you are there and is limited. There is some street parking availbe on Aylestone Road and Saffron Lane but is probably around a 15/20 minute walk. BIKE PARKING Supporters travelling to King Power Stadium on bike can use the cycle park, free of charge. The facility offers 20 spaces on a first come, first served basis. Cyclists should enter via Car Park B and show their match ticket on arrival. ENJOYING THE AREA AWAY PUBS The Counting house used to be a designated away pub a few minutes’ walk from the ground at the far side of Freeman’s Common, but it has now closed down (updated in January 2025). The Holiday Inn and the Fox & Soar are located right next to the ground and also allow away supporters in. Bars and restaurants in the city centre do allow away supporters; this is around a 15-20 minute walk. PLACES TO EAT There is a Nando’s and McDonald’s situated about a 5 minute walk from the ground on Freeman’s common. There are cafe’s located on Aylestone Road, Narborough Road and Braunstone Gate, all of which are a 10-15 minute walk. OTHER RECOMMENDED STOPS The ground is situated 15-20 minutes from the City Centre which has a good range of bars and restaurants. For those driving, Fosse Park is situated just off Junction 21 and has shops as well as a limited amount of restaurants available (this includes parking). GUIDES FOR YOUR DAY LCFC Accessibility Guide Level Playing Field Disabled Access Guide USEFUL TO KNOW Cashless – please bring a credit or debit card to make payments within the stadium. WiFi – wifi is not available throughout the stadium. Children policy – Under 2s are not allowed into the stadium on matchdays. Under 16s are not allowed in the stadium unless accompanied by an adult. Drop-off point – Away coaches drop off and pick up right outside the away end so works well for accessibility. https://www.brentfordfc.com/en/news/stad.text: Brentford FC Conference & Events Community Sports Trust Safeguarding Sign In Register Latest Video Fixtures & Results Teams Tickets Fans Shop Change language English Search burger menu More Next Match Hull City (A) Men's First Team Match Centre Supporter information 19 Feb 25 Things to know if travelling to the King Power Stadium Travel advice, ideas for family activities and essential matchday information ahead of Brentford’s away Premier League fixture against Leicester City Written By Brentford Football Club Brentford take on the Foxes at the King Power Stadium in our next Premier League fixture on Friday 21 February, 8pm kick-off. The match will be broadcast live in the UK on Sky Sports. If you are heading to the match, here’s some useful information on getting to the ground and tips to make the most of your trip to Leicester. Travelling by train Direct trains to Leicester station run every 30 minutes from London St Pancras International and take approximately one hour and 10 minutes. On arrival at Leicester station, bus services 80 and 20 will take you from Leicester city centre to within five minutes’ walk from King Power Stadium. Alternatively, the ground is around a 25-minute walk from the station. The last direct train back to London from Leicester station is at 10.52pm. Return tickets to London are liable to sell out. We recommend you use Trainline to book your ticket as soon as possible. Travelling by car Parking at King Power Stadium can be booked in advance of the match. The club car park is on Filbert Street and costs £19 per car. Parking cannot be booked on the day of the match. Find booking information on Leicester’s website . There are several independent car parks in the surrounding areas that are up to 10 minutes’ walk to the stadium, such as Freemans Common and Leicester Tigers Rugby Club. These car parks typically cost £5 and are first come, first served. Leciester City FC King Power Stadium Filbert Way Leciester LE2 7FL Ticketing information and ticket collections Ticket collection for this fixture is available at the Brentford FC box office at the Gtech Community Stadium until 7pm on Thursday 20 February. After this time, including on matchday, tickets must be collected from the matchday ticket collection point at the King Power Stadium, located to the left of the Foxes Fan Store. Collection opens 90 minutes before kick-off. Any duplicate ticket requests must be sent to Leicester City by the Brentford box office. Please contact Brentford's box office with any inquiries ahead of the matchday. If you’re collecting your ticket at the King Power, please remember to bring ID. We would also like to remind fans travelling to the King Power to observe and respect the family friendly seating. Anyone who holds a ticket in the family friendly area is reminded that they should be seated for the duration of the match. Meet, eat and drink before the match The Barley Mow pub, near to Leicester station, welcomes away supporters and will be a place to meet other Bees fans before kick-off. Please note that there are no designated away pubs in the vicinity of the King Power Stadium. The previously popular location The Counting House is permanently closed. Entering the ground Entrance to the away section will be in the corner of the north and east stands at turnstiles 40-49, open 90 minutes before kick-off. The accessible entrance is at turnstiles 42 and 43. Fans will be searched on entry and bags larger than A4 size will not be permitted. There is no bag storage at the ground. The stadium has a multi-faith prayer room. Please speak to a steward if you would like to use the room. If you experience or see any form of harassment or discrimination while at the stadium, please speak to the nearest steward. You can report a hate crime by texting ‘FOXES’, followed by your message, seat details and the nature of your concern to 60066. Accessibility The King Power Stadium includes wheelchair access for away fans and accessible toilets, with designated accessibility stewards on hand for any support or to provide RADAR keys. Stewards can also help with ordering food and refreshments. Visually impaired fans can request audio-descriptive headsets and access for guide dogs in advance of the game. For any requests and questions, and to enquire about accessible parking, contact Leicester’s Disability Liaison Officer by email at [email protected] . A longer stay Staying the night in Leicester? The city is renowned for its nightlife with many restaurants, bars and pubs. For budget hotels, Novotel, Premier Inn and Travelodge have sites in the city centre. Activities for families Make the most of the February half-term and enjoy some family fun before the game. Leicester is home to the National Space Centre with interactive galleries and the UK’s largest planetarium. Discover how archaeologists uncovered a lost king at the King Richard III Visitor Centre . Immerse yourself in art at the Van Gogh Immersive Experience . Theme park Drayton Manor is also a short car journey west of the city. Have a safe trip and enjoy the match! We will be wearing our Blue kit for our trip to Leyton Orient. What’s the ticket information? The Club have received 1250 tickets, all of which will be likely sold before matchday. No further tickets will be available. It is unallocated seating – fans are advised to arrive in time to avoid delays in finding a seat. How do I get to the ground? Post Code is E10 5NF Leave the M25 at junction 27 and onto the M11 towards London. As the motorway comes to an end, follow the signs for North Circular A406 W. As you come over the flyover, move into the left-hand land to take the A104, then turn left at the roundabout. At the next roundabout continue on the A104 towards Walthamstow and Leyton. Turn left at the traffic lights signposted Leyton Leisure Lagoon. As you reach a block of flats turn left onto Leyton High Road. After passing the Jet garage, bare right. The stadium will be on the right-hand side. What stand are we in? Town fans are located in The Green Inc. East Stand (top right on the map below). Entry is via turnstiles C + D. When do turnstiles open? Turnstiles open at 1:30pm. Where is the best place to park? The stadium has no parking and street parking around the ground is largely permit/residential only. If you are looking to drive to the stadium the nearest pay and display car parks are around a 20-minute walk away. Church Lane – E11 4QN – 24-hour car park – £6 for over 4 hours – only a small car park Leytonstone Station – E11 1HW – 24-hour car park – £3 for the day – only a small car park Stanley Road – E10 7FF – 24-hour car park – £5 over 4 hours Alternatively look at northern stations on the Central Line, such as Epping which has a large car park, and use the underground to avoid traffic. Stratford is also an option (1 stop down from Leyton on the Central Line), it is likely to be very busy with Saturday shoppers. Is there any disabled parking? 3 spaces at the ground that are pre-booked Leytonstone Station has 2 disabled bays Please be mindful of street restrictions in London that mean usual Blue Badge parking is not applicable. What is the nearest train station to the stadium and what is the approximate distance and walking time? The nearest underground station is Leyton on the central line, it’s about a 10-minute walk away. Turn right out of the station down Leyton High Road until Coronation Gardens is on your left. Turn down Buckingham Road and the ground is right in front of you. Leyton Midland Road is the nearest overground station and is around a 15-minute walk away. Turn left towards Leyton and down the High Street past Leyton County Cricket Club. Turn right down Osborne Road and the away stand is right in front of you. Strike action means, at the time of writing, that no trains will be running from Grimsby down to London Recommended pubs for away fans? The Coach and Horses on the High Road is now home fans only (fans may have used it on previous visits) as is the Leyton Star near the tube station. Pubs welcoming away fans: The supporter’s bar at the ground on Oliver Road. £1 entry, smallish capacity and will refuse entry once this is met. Leyton Technical on the High Road, E10 5QN – decent size Birkbeck Tavern – Langthorne Road, E11 4HL – Near to Leyton tube station. Northcote Arms – Grove Green Road, E11 4EL NO ALCOHOL is served to any away fans in the ground. Is food available in the area? Plenty of different outlets are available on the High Street and in Stratford. Where is the nearest cash machine to the Stadium? Tesco Metro and Sainsbury’s Local on the High Street both have free ATM’s. What food and drink is available on the concourse at the stadium? Both hot and cold food and drink items are available inside the ground. Please note inside the stadium is now CASHLESS. The purchase of food and drink is via card only. The away end DOES NOT serve alcohol. Is a programme available? A programme is available at a cost of £3.50. What is the drum and flag policy? No flags on poles. It is possible that large flags won’t be accommodated as the away section is pretty much sold out so no space to place them. INFORMATION Reckless Guide | Leyton Orient LEYTON ORIENT Vanarama National League Saturday 15th September 2018 Kick Off: 3.00 pm Stadium: The Breyer Group Stadium, Brisbane Road, Leyton, E10 5NF Telephone: 0871 310 1881 Club Colours: Red, White and Black Nickname: The O’s Key Personnel: Basildon born Justin Edinburgh is the current Gaffer at The Breyer Group Stadium. He spent 10 seasons with Tottenham and also represented Southend Utd and Portsmouth. He joined Orient in November 2017 but has a wealth of managerial experience notably at Rushden & Diamonds, Gillingham, Newport County and Northampton. Brief Directions by Road: The ground is situated off the Leyton High Road and the journey is very stop and start from whichever direction you travel. Yet from the North Circular Road (A406) by turning right at what is traditionally known as the Crooked Billet Roundabout it is pretty straightforward. From the A406, having passed under and over the Great Cambridge roundabout and Silver Street, turn south onto the A112 Chingford Road signposted Walthamstow and Leyton. Go straight over at the A503 junction where the road becomes Hoe Street. Pass Walthamstow Central Station and carry straight on into Leyton High Road passing Leyton Midland Road Station. After another mile (still A112) the ground is accessible from side roads on your right. Please note all these access roads are all very “British”, Balmoral, Windsor, Buckingham etc. Buses 58, 69, 97 and 158 run along Leyton High Road. Car Parking: Representatives of the club have asked me to point out that parking is severely restricted by residents permits around the stadium on matchdays. Directions by Train: The nearest tube station is Leyton (about a 1/2 of a mile away) which is on the Central Line (Red). Out of the station and turn right down Leyton High Road. On the other side of the road, you will eventually find Coronation Gardens on your left and the floodlights of the ground can be clearly seen behind them. Take the next left into Buckingham Road for the ground. Eating and Drinking Locally: The rather snug supporters bar at the ground does allow away fans and the cost on the door is £1.00. It can be found under the new West Stand and is actually listed in the CAMRA Good Beer Guide. The Coach and Horses on Leyton High Road is now, I’m told, “home fans only” but the Leyton Technical pub on the corner of Adelaide Road is a beaut. It is built into the old Town Hall building. Lots of choice and serves food too. Something more quirky and “old school” is the Birbeck Tavern on Langthorne Road behind the Underground station. It will take you back to what a pub used to be like when the world was black and white! Ground Description: The ground has had a major facelift in the last decade and since our first visit in the League in September 1993 the only part still basically unaltered is the main East Stand although it has some new smart exterior cladding. It was allegedly purchased from Mitcham Greyhound Stadium, was erected in 1956 and holds around 3,500. Notice the splendid centre roof gable (now nudged along a little) which allegedly once held the dog track photo finish equipment. We will be allocated a section in this stand for the afternoon. To its left is the Tommy Johnson South Stand which seats around 1,400 and this replaced the original open away terrace. Opposite the Main Stand is the West Stand. It replaced the original stand which started life was a popular covered terrace which was made all-seated in the 1990’s. The new structure was built in September 2006. It is as it appears, an office block flanked by residential apartments with a skirt of seating for 2,800. It offers fantastic corporate facilities but is a perfect example of us saying goodbye to football ground character and welcome efficiency with commerce. The North Stand which resembles the Tommy Johnson Stand completes the picture. Admission Prices: Advance ticket prices- Adults: £18.00 Seniors 65 & Over: £16.00 18-24 Years (advance only): £10.00 Under 18’s: £5.00 Matchday ticket prices- Adults: £20.00 Seniors: £18.00 Under 18’s: £5.00 Our Last Meeting & Memories: Our last visit was in January 2017 when two Ricardo Santos goals and another from Curtis Weston won it 3-1. On other bright sides of life, two Division 3 away games stand out – firstly a fantastic 3-3 draw in 1996, the Bees goals coming from Sean Devine x2 and Lee Hodges and secondly the following year when a very rare Linvoy Primus goal won it for Barnet in front of over 4,000 spectators. However, the best is left to last as is customary. A majestic two-goal Dougie Freedman performance and two quality finishes by Mark Cooper doesn’t even get close to telling the whole story of the 1994 1st Round 1st Leg Coca-Cola Cup tie at Underhill, it ranks as one of the greatest ever performances by a Barnet team in my opinion. Overnight Stay Factor: Leave it aat! Celebrity Watch: A luverly jubberly cockney cavalcade for your autograph books! Jonathan Woss, Graham Gooch, Fanny Cwaddock, Alfred Hitchcock, David Bailey and Angela Landsbury all are associated with the area. Comedian Bob Mills and musician Andrew Lloyd Webber are regular visitors to the ground as is one my best and nicest customers – I must mention him – Nick Sonenfeld and his family. While the actual away end is fairly standard, it is the entrance that often catches peoples attention. Getting inside has caused widespread fascination as it appears that away fans have to enter the stand via someone’s front room, while this isn’t exactly the case, it does add plenty of character to the stadium. Now in League One, Luton did experience a brief one-season spell in the Premier League in the 2023-24 season. Hosting bigger teams on a regular basis and with a small allocation, away tickets were like gold dust for travelling teams. With a general good view from the away end, visiting fans are situated on the left-hand side of the stadium. A small and compact ground, travelling supporters are close to the action no matter if they are standing low down or high up. A brilliant atmosphere can be generated in the Oak Stand due to the combination of the excellent acoustics, the stand being shared with home fans and the installation of safe standing rails to promote persistent standing. On the downside, there are some supporting pillars in the Oak Stand which can obstruct the view for some fans, and the general facilities inside the stand aren’t the best. If you are after a home ticket rather than an away allocation, our guide to how to buy Luton Town tickets covers general sale, membership and the official ticket exchange. The Kenilworth Road away entrance One of the most unique aspects of visiting Kenilworth Road as an away supporter is getting into the stadium itself. Unlike most modern grounds, with fans entering through large concourses and open spaces, the route to the away end feels more like walking through a tightly packed residential neighbourhood. Away fans approach the turnstiles through a narrow terraced street, with houses sitting alongside the stadium’s outer walls. The famous entrance, tightly tucked between homes on Oak Road, has become iconic across English football, particularly since the Hatters’ spell in the Premier League, due to the unusual sight of football supporters climbing tight staircases wedged between rows of residential buildings. Once through the narrow turnstiles, fans are directed up steep stairways and narrow passageways, overlooking the back gardens of Oak Road homes, before emerging into the stand itself. The compact nature adds to the character of the old-fashioned ground, providing a major contrast for those used to newer and larger stadiums, making it clear why many visitors love the experience. With noise from both sets of fans echoing around the tight ground, adding to the unique entry, going into Kenilworth Road feels more like stepping back into another era of English football. New Luton Town stadium - Power Court construction update Construction work progressing well at Power Court site Luton Town fans are naturally nervous about the move from their traditional Kenilworth Road home, but they will also be excited by the progress at Power Court . The Hatters’ new 25,000-seater stadium is beginning to take shape, as all four stands are being worked on concurrently, though each is at a different stage of construction. Attention is currently being paid to the West Stand’s second floor, where hospitality areas will eventually be installed, as well as the corner sections’ utilities, access and ticket kiosks. Progress is also being made on the South Stand, which will feature retail spaces, as well as general supporter access to the ground. The East Stand – the future home of a police room and broadcasting area – is set for further concrete pours and is having shutters placed in preparation, while the North Stand could be closest to completion, with its notable continuous design. Luton Town 2026/27 League One fixtures released Luton Town will kick off their latest push for promotion back to the second tier with an away trip against Reading on August 15, before their first home game of the season, when they welcome newly-promoted Notts County to Kenilworth Road on Saturday, August 22. The Hatters will also be playing in front of their own crowd on Boxing Day, when Bromley are set to visit, and on Good Friday, with Plymouth Argyle currently pencilled in for a trip to Kenilworth Road on Friday, March 26. Luton will end their 2026/27 campaign at home, too, hosting Blackpool at 12:30pm on May 8. New stadium plans Back in 2019, Luton confirmed they were looking to move to a new stadium called the ‘Power Court Stadium’. At the time, the ground was slated to have a 17,500 capacity, but recent developments have upped this to 25,000 In May 2024, the stadium took a step closer to being green-lit for construction when the club submitted key plans to the local council on how to reroute the nearby River Lea . Then, in December 2024, the final plans were approved by the local council, meaning that groundwork is expected to begin imminently. In April 2025, the club announced that they had partnered with Limak International for the build. The international construction company have been working on the Nou Camp renovation for the past couple of years, so Luton should be in good hands. The club’s Chief Executive, Gary Sweet, said: “Partnering with a company of Limak’s international standing offers us a global perspective with local delivery.” Luton edge closer to leaving Kenilworth Road In December 2024, Luton Town’s final plans for a new 25,000-seater stadium were approved by Luton Borough Council. The news means that Luton are set to leave Kenilworth Road in the coming years to move to the new stadium at Power Court . The club’s board will now be hoping that they can beat the drop to avoid the dreaded back-to-back relegations. The Hatters spent very modestly during their one-year stay in the top flight recently, with CEO and Project Manager Gary Sweet very keen to stress that the majority of the money Luton would receive from being a Premier League club, and the subsequent parachute payments, would go to improving all of the club’s facilities. Development at Power Court is now underway, with Luton set to move in ahead of the 2027-28 season, while wider regeneration of the centre of the town is expected to come with the new venue, as a new hotel, housing and a music venue should accompany the stadium. The club have not owned Kenilworth Road since the local council took it over in 1989, leasing it back ever since, but instead of buying the ground back and redeveloping it, the Luton board took the decision in 2015 to pursue the opportunity of building a new venue on at a different site. Famous people seen at Kenilworth Road Harry Styles Harry Styles isn’t a Luton Town fan but the former One Direction star was in attendance for Luton’s clash with Manchester United in February. Styles, who grew up in a village on the outskirts of Manchester and is believed to be a Man Utd fan, was in attendance with Luton legend, Mick Harford. How those two became friends is anyone’s guess. Made in Luton by @silvertoadltd , made possible by every Luton Town fan 🧡 #LTFC #COYH | @LutonTown pic.twitter.com/i48OUsvsds — OK Football (@OKFootballShow) January 30, 2024 Best views and seating plan The Bobbers Stand opposite the Main Stand was redeveloped for Luton’s 2023-24 Premier League campaign. It was mainly rebuilt to meet the league’s requirements for broadcasters but has now provided home supporters on that side of the ground with one of the best views in the stadium. If you’re a first-time visitor to Kenilworth Road, a ticket in any part of the Bobbers Stand puts you in close proximity to the action with comfortable seating. The Main Stand has two tiers. If you’re looking for somewhere with passionate home supporters, you should try and get a seat on the far side of the Main Stand next to the Oak Road Stand. In fact, on Luton’s website, they note: “Kenilworth Road is famous throughout the country as an exciting and atmospheric ground. Although there aren’t designated ‘singing sections’ we’d recommend the main stand or in the Oak Road end, where you’re guaranteed plenty of atmosphere and noise.” It is worth noting that there is a large supporting pillar in the middle of the Main Stand, which can restrict the view of the pitch, depending on where you are sitting. At the other end of the Main Stand is the David Preece Stand, which can hold just over 700 supporters. Away fans are located on one side of the Oak Road Stand. This covered, all-seated stand is shared with home fans, making it one of the most atmospheric parts of the ground. It is worth noting that the view isn’t optimal with several supporting pillars. With not long left until Luton move into their new home, if you have the chance to go to Kenilworth Road as an away fan, you should take the opportunity to witness one of the most historic grounds in the country. On the opposite side of the stadium is the Kenilworth Road Stand, which is typically allocated for season ticket holders and academy players and families. Kenilworth Road seating plan Pubs for away fans at Kenilworth Road Just inside the away turnstiles is a small bar that serves both draught and bottled beers. Although fairly simple inside and with no seating, it serves its purpose. Nearby pubs that welcome away fans include: The Red Lion – 2 Castle St., Luton LU1 3AA Bricklayers Arms – 16-18 High Town Rd, Luton LU2 0DD Food and drink at Kenilworth Road In terms of inside the ground itself, there isn’t too much to write home about in terms of food. There is a bar area inside the away end where fans can buy snacks and confectionery but nothing in terms of anything substantial. Outside the stadium, however, there are plenty of vendors offering something different from the standard football fayre of burgers and hot dogs to more ‘exotic’ options such as honey bbq and chips (as see in the post below). When terraces were still common in English football, the ground could accommodate well over 20,000 supporters, with a record attendance of 30,069 recorded during an FA Cup match in 1959. The stadium was reduced in size in 1986 when it became all-seater, bringing the capacity down to 22,601. It was then scaled back further in the mid-2000s to 10,356 following the redevelopment of the Kenilworth Stand. That remained the case until Luton Town’s surprise promotion to the Premier League in 2023. During that summer, the Bobbers Stand was redeveloped, increasing capacity to 11,500, before the introduction of safe standing in the Oak Road Stand later in the season raised it to 12,056. To ensure the tours are intimate, the club place a ten-person limit on each tour which ensure everyone gets their moneys worth. Ground history Luton played their home games at Dallow Road immediately after their formation but within a couple of years they’d moved to a ground on Dunstable Road. Dunstable Road was the recognised Luton stadium for 18 years before moving to Kenilworth in 1905. The stadium’s first big renovation came in the 1920s after a fire. By the late thirties, attendances were on the up, and an expansion followed, taking the capacity of Kenilworth Road up to 30,000. Twenty years later, another rebuild followed, but then money became an issue, and the stadium deteriorated. The ’70s, ’80s, and ’90s all saw considerable changes as the club moved with the times to be in seating. The latest changes came in 2023 upon the club’s promotion to the Premier League. However, with rumours of a stadium move on the horizon, the Hatters may not be at Kenilworth Road for too much longer. The same cannot be said about their form in away meetings, given the fact they have lost their last three games at Vicarage Road without troubling the scorers. This forced a £10m upgrade; the majority of that spending was devoted to enhancing broadcasting facilities. Included in that media overhaul was a bigger press conference room, additional spots for cameras, a room for TV coverage, including the ability for the broadcasters to tap into data analytical software and a revamp of the WiFi situation. As for factors that impact the field of play, the main outlay was for the addition and upgrade of floodlights. In March 2024, Luton installed safe standing in the Oak Stand which increased the overall capacity by 800. Further installations are expected in the future. Fire breaks out at Kenilworth Road On Friday, , a fire broke out a Kenilworth Road just a day before Luton Town faced Coventry City at the stadium. Reports of the fire began to circulate on social media on the Friday evening, with images and videos showing a blaze coming from the laundry room at the stadium. Thankfully, the local fire service acted quickly enough to limit the damage and the game with Coventry went ahead as normal. Following the fire, Luton released this statement: “Smoke was found to be coming from a small appliance that had caught fire in the stadium’s laundry room, which was contained within that area and has been dealt with swiftly to prevent any substantial damage. “We would like to offer a huge thank you to Beds Fire & Rescue for their quick intervention, along with club partners and staff who are also on site to help resolve the issue and ensure that everything is now safe.” Those involved with the club were more than likely just glad that it wasn’t a repeat of the fire that engulfed the stadium back in the 1920s. The blaze resulted in significant refurbishment work at Kenilworth Road, but thankfully, this one was tackled before any structural damage could occur. Why are Luton called the Hatters? Luton are known as ‘The Hatters’ due to the town’s long-standing connection with the hat-making industry, which has been prominent in the area since the 1600s. The hat-making trade in Luton peaked in the 1930s – in between World Wars One and Two – but suffered a decline following the latter conflict. Nevertheless, Luton supporters continue to embrace the Hatters nickname with pride, and the club’s badge also features a straw-boater hat. Entrances Most stadiums at this level boast multiple turnstiles that are usually dotted around the ground – Mansfield Town is no different. While home fans can use the majority of entrances at the venue, away fans are often instructed to use the turnstiles behind the ground’s North Stand, located off St. Peters Way, as this is where they are usually accommodated. On the other hand, home supporters are encouraged to use the turnstiles situated behind the South and West Stands – both of which provide exclusive access to the ground for fans of Mansfield Town. Pubs for away fans near the Field Mill Stadium There is a bar at the ground called the Sandy Pate (underneath the Ian Greaves Stand). Except for high profile matches the bar welcomes away fans and shows Sky Sports. However, as you would expect it gets quite busy on matchdays. Therefore, enjoying your pre-match pints at a local pub, of which there are many, is an equally viable, and perhaps better for some supporters, choice. Our top suggestions are as follows: William IV , 208 Stockwell Gate, Mansfield NG18 5QE Sir John Cockle , Sutton Rd, Mansfield NG18 5EU Bold Forester , Botany Ave, Mansfield NG18 5NG Home fan pubs Naturally, many home fans choose to head straight to the on-site bar at Field Mill for their pre-match drinks. However, as mentioned above, this bar can get very busy, so if you are looking for nearby alternatives, our top recommendation is: Talbot Inn , 151 Nottingham Rd, Mansfield NG18 4AE Food and drink at the Field Mill Stadium While Mansfield do not reinvent the wheel when it comes to their food menu, they do keep it simple and classic, something which many football fans crave anyway. Often on offer at the Field Mill Stadium is a selection of burgers, sausages and pies. The food is simple and the prices often reflect that, so all-in-all it is okay value for what you get. Getting to the Stadium By train The Field Mill Stadium can be seen from Mansfield Railway Station, which is no more than a 10-minute walk away. The station is on a local line and is served by trains from Nottingham. To get to the ground from the station; Leave the station and turn left along the dual carriageway, (away from the town centre), you should see a retail park on the right. Go straight ahead at the first set of traffic lights, along Portland Street and then right at the next lights and into Quarry Lane. The ground is a short distance down this road on the right-hand side. By car From The North Leave the M1 at Junction 29, and take A617 to Mansfield. After six miles turn you will pass the Pheasant Inn on your left. At the next set of traffic lights, where there is a Tesco Store on one corner turn right into Rosemary Street (signposted Derby A38). Follow the road for around one mile and after passing a Burger King and Retail Park on your right, turn right at the next traffic light into Quarry Lane. The ground is up on the right-hand side. From The South Leave the M1 at Junction 28, and take A38 to Mansfield. After passing the Kings Mill Hospital on your left and then the Nell Gwyn pub on your right, turn right at the traffic lights after the pub into Sheepbridge Lane. After passing under a railway bridge (height restriction 10′ 9″) you will reach a set of traffic lights where you turn left into Quarry Lane. You will reach the stadium on the left. Where is the best place to park for the Mansfield game? There is some parking on the ground, which costs £5. There is also the station car park, which costs £4 for the day. This car park is located behind the adjacent Portland Retail Park (behind Burger King), which means it is handily placed for the away end. It is also signposted from the town centre ring road. Otherwise, it is a case of finding some street parking, especially on parts of Nottingham Road and the side streets off it. Please do not park in the retail park behind the away end. Parking is restricted to two hours and is camera-monitored, so you will end up with an expensive parking ticket if you do park for longer than two hours. Ticket prices: Adult – £20 Child (8-17 years) – £15 Family ticket (two adults and two 8-17 years – discount applied at checkout) – £50 Under-8 – FREE (with a full paying adult ticket) Mansfield Town ground history Despite being built before 1861, Mansfield Town did not play at Field Mill until 1919. Three years after Mansfield Town moved in, the Grandstand was built with the other three sides’ mound formed from ash from nearby Coal Mines, all of which was completed by 1926. In 1929, funds used from a cup run the year before were used to erect a covered stand on the Bishop Street side. The first terracing was built during the 1930s from railway sleepers and lasted 20 years. In 1961, floodlights were installed and turned on before their League Cup game against Cardiff City. Also, in the 1960s, a new grandstand was built on the west side of the ground after being purchased from Hurst Park Racecourse. The stand cost Mansfield Town £30,000. The stand was first used in 1966 but was not fully completed until 1971. Nowadays, the ground operates with just three stands open, however, work is currently ongoing to reopen the Bishop Street Stand. Field Mill History Field Mill, currently One Call Stadium, is the oldest ground in the English Football League, hosting sporting events since 1861 and football on a continuous basis since that era. Once a site of a textile mill, the land became used for various sports like greyhound racing and cricket before becoming a dedicated football venue by 1894. Although Mansfield Town were founded in 1897, the Stags have only played at the site since 1919. Over the many decades it has been the home of Mansfield Town, it has been through many developments and set various records. The record attendance was set in the 1950s when 24,447 fans watched the Stags take on Nottingham Forest. The ownership of the ground has changed hands many times, with current club owner John Radford purchasing the stadium in 2012, which led to significant renovations. Despite being the oldest stadium in the English Football League, it is not the oldest ground still in use in the country. Field Mill is still recognised as the second-oldest football ground that is still in use, behind Hallam FC’s Sandygate in Sheffield which predated it by just a few months. It now stands as a historic venue, having transitioned from a 19th-century recreational field to a modern League One stadium that still sees thousands of people through the doors every week. Stemming back to a conflicting approach to strikes in 1984 and 1985, the citizens of each town grew to hate each other, and that has spilt into football, too. Known as the Miner’s Strike Derby, the match between Mansfield and Chesterfield is incredibly fierce, with a deep-rooted hatred of the other present in each fanbase. Mansfield have avoided defeat in each of their last four head-to-head meetings, including a 2-0 victory in the EFL Cup in their most recent encounter in August 2025. Surprisingly, each of Mansfield’s last three wins in this fixture have taken place away from the One Call Stadium. As a result, they have not beaten Chesterfield on home turf since recording a 4-2 victory in December 1994. Competing in a league above Chesterfield, Mansfield may have to wait until at least next season for their next head-to-head clash. Mansfield Town vs Notts County rivalry: A far more traditional rivalry, albeit a far less intense one, is contested between the Stags and fellow Nottinghamshire-based outfit, Notts County. Neither side is their counterpart’s main rival; however, with both languishing in the bottom two divisions of the English Football League in recent years, tensions have been allowed to rise. They last faced off in the 2023-24 League Two season, when Mansfield followed a 4-1 away win with a 1-0 home victory. However, the rivalry will be rekindled in the 2026-27 season now that Notts County have been promoted to League One. Mansfield Town vs. Doncaster Rovers rivalry: To a lesser extent than Notts County and certainly Chesterfield, Mansfield share a bit of a rivalry with Yorkshire foes Doncaster Rovers, who are back in League One during the 2025-26 campaign after winning League Two last season. It did not take long for the two sides to clash in the third tier this season after over two years without a meeting, with the Stags and the Rovers pitted up against each other on matchday two of the League One campaign, with the One Call Stadium hosting the clash. Following a goalless first half, the Nottinghamshire contest burst to life with a goal from Mansfield substitute Stephen McLaughlin, with the hosts looking set to claim maximum points. However, Doncaster rallied late on to snatch all three points, with right-back Owen Bailey coming up with a match-winning brace, meaning that the Stags lost back-to-back games at the beginning of the 2025-26 League One season. Milton Keynes is a well-connected city, particularly from London, with a range of transport links making it an easy journey for away supporters. Stadium MK, which has a capacity of 30,000, is comfortably the largest ground in League Two, although the club rarely fills its full home allocation, which can at times impact the atmosphere. Away fans are usually found in the upper tier of the North East Corner, where around 3,000 supporters can be accommodated. When demand is high, the allocation can be expanded to include both tiers of the North Stand behind the goal, allowing for much larger travelling contingents. This flexibility has helped create some memorable away days in recent years, most notable when Coventry City brought around 8,000 supporters in January 2018. Visiting supporters generally enter through turnstiles 1, 2 and 3, which are located behind the North Stand. While seats close to the pitch are rarely available, the elevated position in the upper tier offers excellent views of the action, with the best vantage points found in the front rows of the away section. Stadium MK in the news No pre-season friendlies at Stadium MK MK Dons have revealed their pre-season schedule and the club will not be playing any friendlies at their home ground. They began with a visit to Maidenhead United on July 10, followed by a training camp in Croatia that included a friendly against NK Istra on July 17. MK Dons will then face Tottenham Hotspur behind closed doors on July 22 before playing two friendlies simultaneously on July 25 against Wealdstone and an unnamed Premier League club. Their final two friendlies are against Barnet on July 28 and Cheltenham Town on August 1. SMK reveal headliners for SMK Live Stadium MK is set to host one of the most significant musical events of the summer, with SMK Live set to take place across June 27th and 28th. The Saturday roster features headliners Basement Jaxx, Clean Bandit, Ella Henderson and Jax Jones, with Sunday featuring Black Eyed Peas, Cat Burns, Jalen Ngonda, Maverick Sabre and all hosted by Big Narstie. The stadium will fully transform itself to provide the festival experience, with the pitch to be transformed to include two stages of non-stop live music, street food villages and hospitality tiers ranging from luxury suites to premium viewing. Club legend plays final ever match at Stadium MK At the end of the 2024/25 season, Dean Lewington played his final ever match for MK Dons in front of 10,000 fans at the Stadium MK. The 40-year-old, who has played for the club since it was founded in 2004, was playing in his 916th appearance for the club and was greeted by a guard of honour by those on the pitch and a standing ovation from those in attendance. The defender played for an hour before being substituted, where he received another standing ovation from the crowd as he left the pitch at Stadium MK for the final time. Speaking after the match, Lewington said: “I’m not always one for emotions, but it got to me a bit today. It was the best atmosphere of the season in terms of the noise and the colour. It was a great effort from everyone. “It was weirdly emotional. I felt funny for a couple of days, I didn’t realise I’d get a guard of honour, I was walking out with the girls, it was a little emotional! But coming off I was ok, I had the game emotions. This will take a while to get over, I think, before I start something new.” Club takeover The most recent news to come out of Stadium MK involves the takeover of the club and the Stadium MK Group by a Kuwait-based consortium in August of 2024. While the deal naturally had a huge impact on the club in a multitude of ways, one of the biggest impacts was felt by the stadium itself, which is now completely debt-free as a result of the takeover. The consortium, which entrepreneurial figure Fahad Al Ghanim heads, appears to have big plans for the club. Speaking on the deal, Al Ghanium said: “My ambition is to build on the fantastic foundations already here in Milton Keynes and to take MK Dons to the next level, both on the pitch and off it.” It is an exciting time to be an MK Dons fan, and Stadium MK’s debt-free status is a huge boost for the club’s future. MK Dons Women to Play All Home Games at Stadium MK MK Dons Women are playing all their home fixtures at Stadium MK during the 2025/26 season, marking a significant step in the club’s commitment to women’s football. This move provides the team with a professional environment and enhances the matchday experience for supporters. The first home game at the stadium was scheduled for Sunday, 17th August, against QPR Women, which gave fans the chance to experience the women’s team at Stadium MK. MK Dons eye Championship return MK Dons CEO Neil Hart is looking to guide the club back to the Championship for the first time since 2016 following their promotion to League One. “We should be definitely (in the Championship) and that’s where we want to be,” he told BBC Three Counties Radio. “There’s a lot of work to get there, but we want to realise the ambition, not just the stadium, but the size of the city and the region, and we want to give people a club to be proud of and come and support to get involved in. “We want 20,000 to 25,000 people in that stadium week in, week out, but we’ve got to deliver the football and we’ve got to get it right, and that’s what we’re trying to do.” Milton Keynes Dons chants After their controversial formation, Milton Keynes Dons has been steadily growing both as a club and as a fanbase and nowadays, boasts a passionate core of incredibly vocal supporters. Since opening in 2007, seats inside Stadium MK have been praised for the leg room and comfort for fans in both the home and away sections. In the upper tier of the West Stand, there are executive and corporate hospitality areas with guest speakers for every home match. For the travelling supporters in the north end of Stadium MK, the view of the pitch is excellent, and there is plenty of legroom. The concourse at the ground is popular with away fans as it is inside the stadium, meaning supporters can still watch the action while they are grabbing some food or a drink. There is a ticketing office adjacent to the away entrance (Gates 1,2, and 3), where visiting fans can purchase their seats. Getting to the stadium By train The nearest railway station is Fenny Stratford, which is just over a mile away from Stadium MK; however, this is on the local Bletchley to Bedford line. Surprisingly, taxis are scarce outside Bletchley station, so best to pre-book one in advance (Skyline 01908 222111 are a local taxi firm). Otherwise, you can embark on the 35-40 minute walk to the stadium. The station is served by trains from London Euston & Birmingham New Street. Turn left immediately after leaving the station building and continue down the steps. At the bottom of the steps, turn left and go under the railway bridge. At the roundabout by the Park pub, turn left onto Saxon Street. Keep straight on this road, and you will eventually reach the stadium. Take the A509 towards and into Milton Keynes. It wasn’t their first ground under the MK Dons name, though; that honour went to the National Hockey Stadium. They played their games there until 2007. For those who are unaware, both sides were originally the same team and can be traced back to Wimbledon FC. However, when Wimbledon were granted permission to relocate to Milton Keynes and rebrand, it divided the fanbase. Some fans followed their beloved club across the M25, while others felt betrayed. The latter group then formed AFC Wimbledon as a result. While the rivalry isn’t quite as intense as it once was, many AFC Wimbledon fans refuse to acknowledge the existence of MK Dons; there is still an undeniable tension that will likely remain for many years to come. However, AFC Wimbledon’s fans can’t deny the fact that there is a big difference between their beloved club and Milton Keynes Dons right now. Priced at €6.75m, MK Dons’ market value is twice as high as AFC Wimbledon’s, although that significant difference has not been evident on the pitch in recent meetings. MK Dons have failed to win any of their last five meetings with Wimbledon since winning 3-1 in January 2024.
