Reading’s Select Car Leasing Stadium remains a solid away day destination for travelling supporters, with the ground offering a relatively straightforward journey despite its somewhat isolated location. The stadium benefits from strong transport connections, with regular train services operating from major cities including London and Birmingham. Away fans visiting the Select Car Leasing Stadium are housed in the South Stand, which can accommodate around 2,327 supporters. The stand is considered one of the more comfortable away sections in the country, offering plenty of space, good legroom and an excellent view of the action thanks to the lack of obstructing pillars. Despite the club’s recent off-field problems and declining attendances, Reading are still capable of generating a positive atmosphere on matchdays. The home end features a drummer who helps create noise throughout games and often sparks interaction between the Royals supporters and the travelling fans. Select Car Leasing Stadium in the news Council approves key step in major development plans Reading FC have seen decade-old plans to redevelop the area around the Select Car Leasing Stadium take one step closer to fruition this month (September 2026), as Reading Borough Council approved details regarding the use of the surrounding contaminated land. Under proposals originally submitted to the council in 2016 and approved in 2018, 600 apartments, a 246-room hotel, an ice rink and a convention centre are in the works, all with the goal of revitalising the local area as part of a development called Royal Elm Park in homage to Reading’s former ground. However, one aspect blocking the project from commencing was the need for the council to sign off on the details of the risk, and changing conditions of the gas and contaminated land nearby. That hurdle has now been removed for the time being after the planning committee agreed to approve on September 9. Speaking on the approval, Cllr Micky Leng (Labour, Whitley) joked: “I welcome this, I think the residents’ focus on this will be the ice skating rink, which they keep talking about.” Reading FC takeover In 2017, businessman Dai Yongge purchased Reading Football Club, and while that purchase promised a brighter future, nothing could have been further from the truth. Under Yongge’s ownership, the Royals have failed to adhere to EFL financial regulations on multiple occasions, which has resulted in a near-endless conveyor belt of points deductions for the club. A former Premier League side, Reading, are currently in League One, however, there is finally some good news for their supporters. In December 2024, it was reported that former player and chairman Roger Smee was behind a fresh takeover bid of the club. Despite Reading’s turmoil, Yongge has proved to be a stubborn seller, and multiple other deals have fallen through. So, while we are far from a final resolution, Reading supporters at least have a reason to believe this nightmare is nearing an end. Latest 2025 update: Final sale agreed In late April, Reading confirmed that the terms of sale had been agreed with a buyer, covering both the Select Car Leasing Stadium and the Bearwood Park training ground. By early May, the club announced a sale in principle to Redwood Holdings Limited, a subsidiary of Dogwood Football LLC, led by Rob Couhig—former Wycombe Wanderers owner. The sale was officially completed on 14 May, with the EFL granting clearance. Redwood Holdings Limited acquired the club, including stadium and training ground. Owners promise stadium upgrades in Q&A session with fans Reading owner Rob Couhig has promised a series of long-overdue improvements to the Select Car Leasing Stadium following a fan Q&A session held on Thursday evening. Speaking to around 100 supporters in the Lower West Stand, Couhig acknowledged delays in delivering on previous promises but assured attendees that work is underway to improve WiFi, bathroom facilities and the sound system. He also admitted it was “embarrassing” that the seats have not been repainted in such a long time. The American businessman added that the club is reviewing who should operate the stadium and exploring ways to make better use of it beyond matchdays. Discussions about introducing a safe-standing section are also taking place, with managing director Neil Peters said to be looking into the proposal. Couhig hinted at a “substantial” upcoming announcement regarding developments at the ground but stopped short of confirming a date, noting that his original plan was to reveal details by 12 October. He emphasised, however, that he hopes to make the announcement later this season. Owners announce £5m stadium investment Reading chairman and owner Rob Couhig has announced plans to spend around £5m improving the stadium during the summer. Among the projects currently planned are the installation of a new pitch and safer standing spaces. “We’re going to redo the field in the sense we’ll dig down two or three feet we’ll redo the entire base we’ll make it pristine and available to play, it’ll be the best surface in EFL next year,” Couhig said. “We’re going to change out the lighting system and put in better lights more syncopated lights which will be able to go with music and go with the times but they’ll also be cheaper in that they’ll less energy consuming. “We’re going to change out our LED boards around the side of the pitch they’ll be bright they’ll be crisp, one of the problems with the LED boards we have now they never go off even though they turn the lights off they continue to run so it costs us £10-20 thousand a month to run. “We’re going to change out our management of the stadium and get it out of house and bring in a full-time venue director so that we don’t just have 25-30 games but we’re using the stadium a 100 days a year or more.” Famous People seen at Select Car Leasing Stadium Reading do have several celebrity fans, including actors, comedians and musicians. Ricky Gervais The actor and comedian is a Reading native who has repeatedly referenced the town in his work and fans have even displayed a banner at games featuring his David Brent character. The Amazons The popular rock band was formed in Reading and all three members are supporters. They played the Purple Turtle Stage outside the stadium after Rob Couhig’s takeover was confirmed in 2025 and lead singer Matt Thomson has stated that playing a full concert at the ground is the band’s “dream”. Reading chants Like most teams do, Reading and their fanbase have a wide variety of chants and songs in their arsenal to use on matchday. If you ever visit the Select Car Leasing Stadium, you will likely hear ‘Blue Army’, ‘Come On You Royals’ and a whole host of other tunes blaring out from the stands. Best views and seating plan The strongest views of the pitch at the Select Car Leasing Stadium are found in the West Stand and the Sir John Madejski Stand. The upper tier of the West Stand, particularly the sections around the halfway line, provides the most impressive view inside the stadium. Due to the excellent vantage point, these areas are typically where Reading allocate the majority of their hospitality seating. For supporters looking for a similar view without purchasing hospitality tickets, the blocks closest to these sections, GU5 and GU8, are among the best alternatives. The Sir John Madejski Stand is a single-tiered section, meaning the view is slightly less elevated compared to the West Stand. The most central areas within this stand are blocks Y22 and Y23, offering a balanced perspective of the pitch. If atmosphere is the priority, the right-hand side of the South Stand is the best place to sit. Known as Club 1871, this area is home to Reading’s most vocal supporters and is where much of the noise inside the stadium is generated. The away section is positioned immediately alongside this area on the left side of the South Stand. Seating plan Entrances In most games, home fans can enter through any of the ground’s turnstiles other than those used for away supporters. While this gives fans a greater selection on matchday, we recommend consulting your ticket information before your arrival and entering through the turnstile located closest to your seat. This keeps queues low and your entry time as little as possible. As for away fans, they will enter the stadium via dedicated turnstiles behind the South Stand, located on Shooters Way. Pubs for away fans near the stadium There is a Fan Zone outside the East Stand where fans can purchase food and drink, with home and away supporters encouraged to mix. The club also stages live music outside the Sir John Madejski Stand ahead of games as part of a partnership with local bar the Purple Turtle. In terms of nearby pubs, there aren’t many in walking distance other than a bar in the Holiday Inn which is across the road. As such, we urge away fans to simply enjoy a few pubs in Reading Town Centre before getting a bus or taxi to the stadium. Some good examples include: The Three Guineas , Reading, Station Approach, Reading RG1 1LY The Hope Tap – JD Wetherspoon , 99-105 Friar St, Reading RG1 1EP Oakford Social Club , Berkshire, 53 Blagrave St, Reading RG1 1PZ Home fans As is the case in most instances, home fans have a far greater selection of pubs and bars to choose from on matchday. Some of our top suggestions include: The Nag’s Head , 5 Russell St, Reading RG1 7XD The Greyfriar , 53 Greyfriars Rd, Reading RG1 1PA Walkabout – Reading , Wiston Terrace, Reading RG1 1DG Food and drink at the Select Car Leasing Stadium As you can at many stadiums in the English football pyramid, supporters will have an array of burgers, sausages, hotdogs, pies and of course, everyone’s go-to, chips, to choose from. Getting to the stadium By train Reading Green Park Station is only around 15 minutes walk away from the Select Car Leasing Stadium, while the main Reading Railway Station is situated just over three miles away. The easiest way to get to the ground from the main station is to catch the F1 ‘Football Special’ bus, which leaves just down from the Railway Station on Station Hill (as you exit the station from the main entrance, turn right and head down the steps, the buses line up on the left-hand side). By air For those travelling from further afield, perhaps overseas, the nearest international airport to the Select Car Leasing Stadium is Heathrow Airport. Once there, you will want to take the RailAir bus (boarding at Stand 9 in Terminal 5), or the Heathrow Central Bus Station (CBS) from stands 6-15a. Both of these services terminate at Reading Railway Station, at which point, you should follow the directions outlined above. By car The easiest way to access the Select Car Leasing Stadium by car is via Junction 11 on the M4. At this point, Reading and the stadium itself are well-signposted and will appear on your left-hand side after a short while. SatNav postcode: RG2 0FL Where is the best place to park for the Reading game? There is some limited parking available at the stadium itself for a cost of £10, but it can be a bit of a lengthy process to get out of the car park at the end of the game. There are also a number of unofficial car parks in the area, which are located at local businesses. Bon Hale a visiting Sheffield United fan informs us: “We parked in at a warehouse car park located on Acre Road at a cost of £5. Passing the Select Car Leasing Stadium on your left, follow the A33 for about half a mile, then turn back on yourself, passing Bennet Road on your left, and then take the next left into Acre Road. “You will see the sign “match parking”, where there is a large warehouse on the left. It is gated with security. It is then only a short walk to the ground from here. We also spotted another matchday car park in Bennet Road but this cost £10.” Park & Ride Alternatively, there is a Park and Ride facility at Mereoak (postcode RG7 1PB) near Junction 11 of the M4, which has buses running to Reading town centre via the Select Car Leasing Stadium. Select Car Leasing Stadium disabled facilities and accessibility Having been opened in 1998, the Madejski Stadium is fairly modern compared to most grounds and has good facilities for disabled supporters as a result. The following facilities and services are available as standard on matchdays: 332 accessible seats (278 for home fans and 54 for away supporters) 13 accessible toilets (11 for home fans and 2 for away supporters) Audio commentary (request in advance needed) Sensory room Accessible catering counters 136 accessible parking spaces However, if you have any specific needs that are not explicitly met by the facilities outlined above, we strongly recommend contacting the club ahead of time to ensure you have the most comfortable matchday experience possible. Select Car Leasing Stadium ticket prices As we have come to expect as football fans, ticket prices at the Select Car Leasing Stadium, and virtually every other ground, depend on your age and where you want to sit. A breakdown of ticket prices for the 2026-27 season is as follows: Advanced Prices Adult – £21-£28 Over 65s – £20-£23 18-24 – £17-£20 14-17 – £7.50-£13.50 Under 13s – £4.50-£9.50 Matchday Prices Adult – £24-£31 Over 65s – £23-£26 18-24 – £20-£23 14-17 – £10.50-£16.50 Under 13s – £7.50-£12.50 Select Car Leasing Stadium capacity The Select Car Leasing Stadium can host 24,161 fans, offering a mix of stands with great views and atmosphere. At the north end, the Eamonn Dolan Stand holds 4,946 supporters, while directly opposite, the slightly smaller South Stand accommodates 4,350. Away fans are situated in the southeast corner of the South Stand, with a typical allocation of just over 2,300. A video screen towers above the visiting supporters, and the remainder of the stand is reserved for home members, including safe-standing areas for those who prefer to watch the game on their feet. Next to the away section is the Sir John Madejski Stand, the second-largest at the ground, with room for 7,286 fans. Facing it is the West Stand, the stadium’s Main Stand and largest section, seating 7,579 across two tiers. Between the upper and lower levels, hospitality suites provide premium views, while the tunnel and dugouts are positioned at pitch level, giving spectators close-up access to all the on-field action. Select Car Leasing Stadium tours Reading FC do in fact provide tours of their Select Car Leasing Stadium, which is fairly unique for a club competing in the third tier of English football. Unfortunately, there isn’t a huge amount of variety, with just one package being offered, nor availability, with tours only available on certain dates through the year in most seasons. However, a tour of the ground will grant supporters access to the following areas: Players’ Lounge Directors’ Lounge Players’ changing room Pitchside Fans will also be afforded the opportunity to see a replica of the Championship trophy up close. Prices for these tours vary depending on which category ticket you need and whether you are a season ticket. General Adult – £12 65+ – £10 18-24 – £10 Under 17s – £6 Under 13s – £4 Season ticket holders Adult – £9 65+ – £7.50 18-24 – £7.50 Under 17s – £4.50 Under 13s – £3 Nearby attractions Whether you arrive in Reading a few hours before kick-off or are planning on making a short trip of your visit to the town, you will need things to do. Thankfully, Reading has plenty to offer in this regard. Reading Museum As you might have guessed, Reading Museum provides visitors with an extensive history of the town as well as housing artefacts from around the world. Among the permanent galleries at the venue are the Sir John Madejski Art Gallery, which is home to an ever-changing variety of works, a Roman Slichester exhibition, ruins of the Reading Abbey and a Riverside Museum too. For those interested in history it is a must-visit and as an extra bonus, admission is free. Beale Wildlife Park Located a little further away is the Beale Wildlife Park, which requires a short 30-minute journey via public transport from Reading town centre to access. If you love animals, this might just be the place for you. The park states that it contains over 160 species of birds, reptiles, mammals and other animals for you to visit. From Arctic Foxes to black and White Ruffed Lemurs – there really is something for everyone. Retro football pictures Having originally opened in 1998, there isn’t much that be classed as ‘retro’ at the Select Car Leasing Stadium. However, it is still a ground with plenty of history and a rich one at that. Where it all began Reading FC plays its first football match at Madejski Stadium. pic.twitter.com/ZuruGF10Er — 2000 Live (@25YearsAgoLive) August 22, 2023 By definition, one of the oldest ever photos of the Madejski Stadium, the above photos show what the ground, surrounding areas and fans looked like during the club’s first-ever game at their new stadium. A reminder of the Premier League Madejski Stadium pitch looking good ahead of Reading v Tottenham at 4pm pic.twitter.com/fX0n6KZC (via @ReadingFC ) #RDGTOT — Premier League (@premierleague) September 16, 2012 While Reading is now a club attempting to recover from irresponsible ownership, the Royals were once a Premier League side. It was just as impressive then as it is now. Concerts at Madjeski Stadium Due to the impressive facilities and modern design of the Madejski Stadium, the ground can be transformed from a football stadium into an excellent host of music concerts. Some of the more notable performances to have taken place at the home of Reading include: Busted – 2004 Elton John – 2005 Bananarama – 2005 Red Hot Chilli Peppers – 2006 JLS & Jessie J – 2013 Ground history Reading initially played their home games at the Reading Recreation Ground. After that, they bounced around a few places, including the Reading Cricket Ground, Coley Park and Caversham Cricket Ground. In 1896, Reading started playing their home games at Elm Park. They spent almost a century there until the Hillsborough Stadium Disaster Inquiry report (Taylor report) required all teams in the top 2 tiers of the Football League to have an all-seater stadium. Due to the Taylor report, Reading had to look for another stadium as they had just gained promotion to the First Division. As a result, the Madejski Stadium was built, and Reading moved in 1998. The Royals have played their home games at the Madejski Stadium ever since. Latest developments Royal Elm Park The latest development at Madejski Stadium actually has very little to do with football, not directly at least. ‘Royal Elm Park’ is a housing development adjacent to the Madejski Stadium that was completed in late 2023/early 2024. The brand-new housing complex cost approximately £500 million to construct and contained a reported 600 homes—one-bedroom, two-bedroom, and three-bedroom units. The complex also includes a wide variety of entertainment facilities that will further cement Madejski Stadium as a hub of the Reading community. Record and average attendance Record attendance At The Madejski Stadium: 24,184 vs Everton (Premier League, ) At Elm Park: 33,042 vs Brentford (FA Cup 5th Round, ) Average attendances 2025-2026: 12,194 (League One) 2024-2025: 12,535 (League One) 2023-2024: 13,115 (League One) 2022-2023: 14,027 (Championship) 2021-2022: 13,193 (Championship) Reading local rival Unlike many clubs across the English football pyramid, Reading do not have a large number of local rivals with whom they share long standing animosity. That has not always been the case, however. The Royals once enjoyed a fierce rivalry with Aldershot Town, although the fixture disappeared following Aldershot’s dissolution in 1992. Reading vs Oxford United rivalry One rivalry that has endured is Reading’s relationship with Oxford United, largely because of the close geographical proximity between the two clubs. While it is not regarded as one of the fiercest derbies in English football, matches between the sides still carry added significance for supporters. The fixture has been played relatively infrequently in recent decades due to the clubs often competing in different divisions. Reading vs Swindon Town Much of the same can be said for Reading’s rivalry with Swindon Town. The fixture is another derby born primarily out of geography and remains an important contest for many Royals supporters, although opinions on the intensity of the rivalry vary across the fanbase. One indication of the lingering feelings between the clubs is that the downvote button on Reading’s main Reddit community is a Swindon Town badge. Born out of relative proximity, the derby is important to some sections of the Royals fanbase and less so to others. For what it is worth, the downvote button on the main Reading Subreddit is a Swindon badge. Hillsborough is one of the oldest stadiums still in use in the English Football League, making it worthwhile for visiting supporters to visit. The away end at Hillsborough is located in the upper tier of the West Stand, otherwise known as the Leppings Lane End. A typical allocation in this area of the stadium is 3,700, but this can be increased to around 8,000 for cup matches. The lower tier and northwest corner also come into use. Some fans naturally have some scepticism about visiting the Hillsborough away end, as this was the end of the stadium where the tragic Hillsborough disaster occurred in 1989. The end was widely regarded as unsafe throughout the 1970s and 1980s, but it was redeveloped after the disaster and is now perfectly safe for supporters. The view from the away end is generally very good, mainly when the action is down at that end of the pitch. However, some supporting pillars are scattered about, which can result in some fans having a restricted view. The facilities inside the stand aren’t tremendous, but fans can buy food and drinks on the concourse before kick-off and at half-time. Some modernisation is perhaps needed in the West Stand, but if you want an old-school English football experience, Hillsborough is as good as it gets. New Hillsborough disaster inquiry ahead 36 years later, the Hillsborough disaster, one of the most horrific and tragic in football history, is still a topic of discussion and controversy. Some of the culprits behind this tragedy are still unknown, but new evidence has come to light recently, which might give the families of the deceased hope that some of the culprits will be charged. A new investigation into the deaths of the 96 football fans was ordered, as an independent report suggested that the police tried to cover up their poor handling of the tragedy. The report itself claims that the police’s incompetence was the reason behind the death of 41 people. Those lives could have been spared if the police’s actions had been adequate, which, alas, hasn’t been the case. The families of the casualties never accepted the official version of the events, campaigning for over 20 years under the slogan ‘Justice for the 96’. Sheffield City Council issue Prohibition Notice In July 2025, ahead of the beginning of the 2025-26 Championship season, Sheffield City Council issued a prohibition notice in relation to Hillsborough’s North Stand. This came after Stadium Advisory Group meetings and club discussions and set out to prevent fans entering the stand until assurances of the stand’s structural integrity were provided by the club, after engineering specialists could no longer confirm the area was safe for supporters. This notice was later lifted after proof of remedial works by the Owls was provided and verified, allowing for spectators to use the North Stand from the start of the Championship camapign and preventing the enforced movement of those with season tickets in the area. The match was resumed around five minutes later, after fans were cleared from the pitch, and ended in a 5-0 defeat for the Owls, with the supporters group in question left to hope that the protest will act as a catalyst for further fan action. Sheffield Wednesday enter Administration On , Sheffield Wednesday and Sheffield 3 Limited, the owner of Hillsborough, entered administration amid rising debts and cash-flow issues, resulting in resulting in late wages on many occasions and an eventual HMRC winding up order. While the stadium is no longer owned by the club directly, it is believed that the administrators will seek to conduct a sale of both the Owls’ parent company and Sheffield 3 Limited as a package, meaning ownership could return to the club under a new party. It is hoped that under new ownership, following the conclusion of the administration and purchase of the club, Hillsborough could receive much-needed funding in many areas, including the above-mentioned North Stand, albeit with other aspects likely needing a more immediate financial resolution. For more attractions near Hillsborough in Sheffield, you can check out the following places, including Sheffield United’s Bramall Lane: Holly Hagg Community Farm The Great Escape Game Sheffield Hillsborough Park and Walled Garden Peak District National Park Sheffield Wednesday ground history Hillsborough first opened its doors in 1899 and has been the home of Sheffield Wednesday ever since. It has become one of the most prominent football grounds in England over the years and has been used as a venue for international matches and 27 FA Cup semi-finals. The darkest day in the ground’s history came in April 1989 when Liverpool fans were crushed inside the Leppings Lane Stand at one end of the stadium. In a tragic turn of events, 96 Liverpool fans were killed, with one other dying several years later as a result of the injuries suffered on the day. The ground managed to survive the disaster, but substantial renovations were undertaken to ensure that a repeat of the incident could never happen again. The stadium was converted into an all-seater facility with the demolition of all terraces, and improved turnstiles were installed, along with additional emergency exits. It wasn’t the only disaster to happen at the stadium, as back in 1914, a match between Sheffield Wednesday and Notts County was suspended after a wall at the Penistone Road end collapsed, injuring 70 supporters. Latest developments at Hillsborough The club had previously announced ambitious plans to increase the capacity of Hillsborough to around 45,000. The proposals were centred round a major redevelopment of the Leppings Lane End, including an additional tier and filling in the corner between the West and South Stands, as Sheffield hoped to become a host city for England’s 2018 World Cup bid. Those plans went on to be shelved, and after years of limited investment in Hillsborough under former owner Dejphon Chansiri, attention has instead turned towards modernising and improving the existing stadium. Sheffield Wednesday entered administration in October 2025 amid major financial problems, but the club began a new era in May 2026 when Arise Capital Partners, led by David Storch, completed a takeover, bringing them out of administration in the process. The change of ownership has already resulted in significant investment at Hillsborough. Storch revealed in August 2026 that around 100 work orders were being carried out across the stadium, with the new owners having invested millions into Hillsborough and the club’s training facilities. Work includes improvements to water and hot-water supplies, replacement lifts, upgraded WiFi and changes to stadium access. The food and drink operation is also being overhauled, with Delaware North providing catering and Molson Coors increasing drinks-serving capacity, while hospitality areas, the club shop and other parts of the stadium are also being refurbished. This follows safety-related work carried out on the North Stand in 2025. Sheffield City Council temporarily issued a Prohibition Notice before allowing the stand to reopen after the required immediate remedial works were completed and verified by structural engineers. A longer-term programme of works was also agreed. For now, there has been no confirmation that the old 45,000-capacity redevelopment proposals will be revived. The immediate priority under the new ownership appears to be repairing and modernising Hillsborough after years of underinvestment, although the scale of the work taking place represents the most significant push to improve the stadium for some time. Together, they form the ‘Steel City’ derby, named as such due to Sheffield’s long history of producing steel for the rest of England. Given that Sheffield is arguably the rightful home of football in the country, after all, the city did play host to football’s first-ever local derby , it is perhaps unsurprising to learn that this rivalry dates back to 1890. Since then, tension have only risen and it is now widely considered to be one of the fiercest derbies in English football. In fact, the two clubs have discussed a potential merger multiple times over the years, only to receive huge amounts of backlash from both fanbases. Sheffield Wednesday are now winless in eight games against their rivals dating back to 2012, with Sheffield United having won each of the last four Steel City Derbies across the 2024-25 and 2025-26 Championship campaigns. It is unclear when Sheffield’s two teams will next square off, after Sheffield Wednesday suffered relegation to League One at the end of 2025-26 while Sheffield United stayed in England’s second tier. They will not meet in 2026-27, therefore, unless they are drawn against one another in a cup competition which last happened in 2000, and with both teams already out of the EFL Cup leaving the FA Cup as the only possible way of meeting this season. Another notable South Yorkshire rivalry for Sheffield Wednesday is with Barnsley, with the clubs separated by around 20 miles. The fixture is often referred to as a South Yorkshire derby and has been contested regularly throughout history. The rivalry became particularly prominent in the 2010s with the clubs spending several seasons together in the 2010s and early 2020s. Perhaps the most memorable and significant recent meeting came in the 2023 League One playoff final at Wembley, when Sheffield Wednesday beat Barnsley 1-0 after extra time to secure their promotion to the Championship. They will reunite in the 2026/27 season following the Owls’ relegation back to League One, with the meeting at Oakwell scheduled for November and the reverse fixture at Hillsborough in the calendar for March 2027. As requested by the hosts I got to the ground early due to the dreaded Covid test checks. They said turnstiles would be open at . I got there at and they weren't and there was nobody in the programme kiosk. I wandered down Leppings Lane past the programme shop mentioned in the guide with its adjacent busy sandwich bar and found a Burger King on the next Junction. Fans from both teams in there but no animosity. Walked back for , got a programme, went through the Covid test point and turnstiles the up the stairs to the concourse on the upper tier and had a very tasty cup of Yorkshire Tea. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the stadium? Stadium oozes history but of course being in the Leppings Lane End (Now officially called the West Stand), is still poignant for those of us old enough to remember watching the events of 1989 as they unfolded. Good view from the upper tier though you will need to find a spot where your view is not impeded by one of the supporting pillars. If your club has sold the away end out (not a problem for the 1300 Argyle fans) some of the seats are directly behind the pillars and I mean within inches so you will see nothing. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The PA is excruciatingly loud to the point of being painful and for the 10 Minutes before Kick Off tries to get the home fans singing which was met with apathy apart from the traditional 'Hi Ho Sheffield Wednesday' just before kick off which the entire crowd joined in with. Maybe it is just my dislike for the original song but to me this is not a patch on the atmosphere generated by their neighbours across Sheffield with the Chip Butty song. Turning to the game itself; I have seen Argyle 25 times this season and this was the worst performance by far. We lost 4-2 and could have been 10-2. Home fans were very noisy for 5 minutes after each goal and them went quiet again Comment on getting away from the ground after the game Walked back to the Tram Stop. Whilst the tram to the ground had a conductor, after the game barriers are erected around the tram stop and you have to show your ticket or buy one from staff at the entry point. This is pointless as the tram stop is just a sign on the pavement and people were simply crossing the road from the opposite pavement and joining the crowds inside the barrier. I managed to get on the first tram that arrived that was packed to a dangerous level and finally made it back to Cathedral tram stop and walked back down the hill to the hotel. Sunday, I reversed my train route back to Plymouth Summary of overall thoughts of the day out Lovely old stadium and good weekend. Shame about Argyle not turning up. Please note that if, like me, you have mobility issues, there are an awful lot of very steep hills in Sheffield. See more 3rd October 2021 Rob Pickett Game Attended Sheffield Wednesday v Oxford United Competition League 1 Date 02/10/2021 Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the ground itself? Living in Sheffield, I have visited Hillsborough a few times, but it had been some years attending as an Oxford fan I had some friends staying overnight and we were all looking forward to the game with a large L1 attendance in e offing. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? My friends parked up at mine and we each made use of a City Wide bus tram ticket for £5.10. This also involved some walking in inclement weather but was a good option. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? We visited The New Barrack Tavern, a quality multi-room old style pub. Several real ales and real ciders were available at reasonable prices. We got there at 1310 which was timely. 10-mins later it was heaving. There was a friendly atmosphere and if you like real ale, then do pay the venue a visit. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the stadium? It is about a 12-min walk to the stadium from the NBT. Some picked up the usual burger and fries from a choice of vans on the way. Hillsborough is an old style but imposing stadium. Once in here are some very good views from the upper tier of Leppings Lane. For those of a certain age, you cannot help but think of those events on that day when you enter the stadium. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. I didn't use the facilities and I barely noticed the stewards. As Oxford had bought a fair few fans, there was a cracking atmosphere in the away end. From an Oxford perspective it was a very good game. We deserved a 1-0 lead at HT. Wednesday came back into the game in the 2nd half and got an equaliser. Both teams pushed forward but Oxford grabbed an excellent winning goal late on. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game Fairly straightforward walk to the tram stop. Be prepared for a very packed tram on your return journey. But it was seamless enough. Wednesday regularly have crowds on 20/K+, so it is bound to be busy. We then got the bus in city centre and proceeded to start the evening. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out From an Oxford perspective a great day out. Wednesday is an atmospheric stadium and worth visiting. Our choice of pre-match venue was top notch. Many L1 fans may not have been to Hillsborough and I would recommend they take the opportunity this season. See more 5th August 2021 Will Game Attended Sheffield Wednesday vs Derby County Competition Championship Date 29/02/2020 Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the ground itself? Its such an old iconic ground with a great away capacity. Plus their are many pubs and bars 2 minutes away from when you first step foot off the train. As well as the ground only being half an hour away from me their are no changes and the train goes straight to the steel city from most places. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? The tram was straight there, and the tram was one of the highlights of the day. Singing all the way to Hillsborough not letting anyone on the tram unless they were a Derby fan. Classic football. Their are loads of tram stops around the city as well so don't worry about missing one. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? The show room. Not really a pub but a cafe with a bar. It sells good beer and soft drinks, it lets anyone in whatever they're wearing if they want to eat, or just drink. Its great calm before the storm. The fans in their were basically all Wednesday/United fans and they all just wanted a bit of football talk and banter. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the stadium? My first thought was how big the ground was for the team. I mean it would be a miracle if they ever filled it up, However the away end was great we were so high up we could see the hole pitch. plus all three of our goals were all scored on our side. Scenes! Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. The game itself was class. A domination led to a 1-3 win for the rams and the limbs were unmatched, half the away support was down the stairs and they took the stewards with them! They were fine with it though as they were very relaxed. the toilets were bog standard and I would advise you get the drinks in before the game as the queues were something else. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game It was quite a long wait for the tram/bus back to the train station but it was suspected anyway so I think you should maybe get away from the ground on 90 minutes. (unless you're pushing for a late draw or win of course) but you don't want to be waiting 30 mins for someway back as we were having things thrown at us. from their though it was very simple back to home. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out Great day out win or lose would always highly recommend to any league 1 fans looking for a new stadium to go to this season. See more 18th September 2020 Jack Tyldsley (Bolton Wanderers) Sheffield Wednesday v Bolton Wanderers Championship League Saturday 10th March 2018, 3pm Jack Tyldsley (Bolton Wanderers fan) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting Hillsborough? I had been to Hillsborough once before in a 2-1 win. With both sides close in the league, this was a big game and one we couldn’t afford to lose. Hillsborough is a big ground and one I was looking forward to revisiting. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? We drove to the game from Bolton in the morning. Our trip was easy and we soon found a car park a few minutes from the ground. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? We arrived and went to McDonalds, and then approached the stadium. The home fans didn’t have much to say to us; both knew it was a big game. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of Hillsborough? On approach I remembered how big it actually was. The away end is quite ugly from the outside but has a good concourse and as we took our seats I was once again shocked at the sheer size of the ground. It is massive, a lot bigger than it looks from outside. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. We had brought 2000 fans to Hillsborough for this one and we were in fine voice up until we conceded controversially in the 70th minute. All looked lost until our big substitute striker Wilbraham popped up with a 93rd minute equaliser sending our fans into raptures. The game ended 1-1 but it felt like a win for us. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: We exited the ground to find held back outside the ground, to allow the Wednesday fans who weren’t best pleased with us to disperse. This was completely ridiculous – barricading 2000 away fans into the same end as the disaster years ago. But once we got away we had a safe journey home. Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: Good day. Good ground. Good result. See more 26th February 2020 Dan Maguire (Doing the 92) Sheffield Wednesday v Charlton Athletic Championship Wednesday 26th February 2020, 7.45pm Dan Maguire (Doing the 92) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting Hillsborough? I was working up in Leeds so this was an opportunity to visit another ground number 68 of the 92 OR 67/91 this season! How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? It was a 4 am start from home to get up to Leeds for work. The trip from Leeds to Sheffield was about an hour in traffic. I was planning to park in the Wednesdayite car park but this was closed off so I ended up parking down Herries Road (S6 1QW) where there were multiple car parks costing £5. From there it was a 5-10 minute walk to the stadium. What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? Before the game, we picked up our tickets and then went into 'The Wednesday Tap' for a beer. A really nice bar, it felt warm and the beer was only £3.60 a pint!. The locals not overly friendly though. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hillsborough Stadium? A very historical ground and looking a bit old now, however. Hillsborough is an impressive stadium and reminds you that this is an ex-top division club. The corner seating is badly designed and lack of legroom would have been a problem if it was a sell-out. Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. A pretty drab game with an injury-time winner. Neither team deserved a win. Food-wise no there were no vegan options but they did black coffee! My mate had a burger which he said was pretty poor. Comment on getting away from the ground after the game: We left around 85 minutes (yes we missed the winning goal!) and got back onto the M1 pretty easily. We had a clear run to the south arriving home at . Summary of overall thoughts of the day out: I'm happy to have made the trip and seen this classic stadium. The travelling all went well and I had no issues parking my car so all in all a good trip. See more 2nd January 2020 Brian Moore (Millwall) Sheffield Wednesday v Millwall EFL Championship Saturday 2nd January 2020, 3pm Brian Moore (Millwall) Why were you looking forward to this game and visiting the Hillborough Ground? An easy train trip from where I live so as a regular away supporter it was nice to have a little later start than normal. Also, the Sheffield Tap bar at the Railway Station is one of my favourite real ale pubs. How easy was your journey/finding the ground/car parking? A quick trip by train then a cab ride to match was £8 which is virtually the same as the Tram fare would have been for the three of us! What you did before the game pub/chippy etc, and were the home fans friendly? The Sheffield Tap is the venue of choice for any real ale fans and there are always plenty of taxis outside the station to get you to the stadium. What you thought on seeing the ground, first impressions of away end then other sides of the Hillsborough Stadium? A big old fashioned stadium, somewhat modernised but not a soulless bowl, thank God! Comment on the game itself, atmosphere, stewards, pies, facilities etc.. 0-0 and a fully justified scoreline Zzzzzzzzz! Pies, what pies?! No food when we arrived at ten to three. Staff apologetic but told what little they had received had sold out quickly. £33 a ticket pah, pathetic. Even worse the PA system was incomprehensible and very low volume. Considering what happened in this stand many years ago, the inability to make clear emergency/evacuation announcements is not acceptable as a safety issue. (I have since written to the club and the stadium manager has advised me that he is taking action to rectify this – so fair play to them for the posit

https://fulhamsupporterstrust.com/news/2.text: Representing your views since 2003 Bluesky Facebook X Email Fulham Supporters' Trust Home About History Structured Dialogue Aims Your Trust Board FAQs Craven Cottage Documents Online safety guidance News Fixture Lists Men - colour coded Activity Book Club Fan Survey 2019 Non Standing Away Seats Future Ticketing Strategy (part 2) Future Ticketing Strategy (part 1) On The Ball Opinion Police Liaison Riverside Stand Johnny Haynes Trophy TOOFIF Book Launch Contact Join Us Home News Awayday Guide: Wycombe Wanderers Awayday Guide: Wycombe Wanderers 7th August 2017 Fulham have been drawn against supporter-owned League Two side Wycombe Wanderers in the first round of the Carabao Cup. There are still tickets available for tomorrow night’s fixture at Adams Park. Tickets for away fans – located in the East Stand – are priced at £15 for adults, £12 for over 60s and £5 for under 16s. These are on general sale and should now be purchased by visiting the Fulham ticket office in Stevenage Road or calling 0203 871 0810 . Those supporters requiring wheelchair or ambulant disabled tickets should call the Wycombe ticket office on 01494 441 118 . GETTING TO ADAMS PARK CLUB COACHES The official Fulham coaches will leave Craven Cottage and Motspur Park at 5pm. Season ticket holders and members can book a space on the coach for £13 for adults and £5 for juniors, whilst general sale places are available for £18 for adults and £10 for juniors. BY CAR On matchdays, there is significant traffic around Adams Park so drivers are advised to leave plenty of time to complete their journey. Adams Park is clearly signposted from the M40. Leave the M40 at Junction 4 and take the A4010 (John Hall Way, signposted Aylesbury). Cross over three small roundabouts into New Road continuing down the hill to two mini roundabouts at the bottom. Turn sharp left at the first into Lane End Road and continue to the next mini roundabout at which turn right into Hillbottom Road. Adams Park is situated at the very end of the road. CAR PARKING A limited number of car parking spaces are available at Adams Park, priced £5. You can also park in some of the industrial units along Hillbottom/Lane End Road for the same price. This might be a better option as the official car park gets very congested and there are usually serious delays in leaving after full time. There is some street parking available, but this is subject to restrictions on matchdays, and traffic wardens are in operation. BY RAIL Supporters can reach High Wycombe station from London Marylebone. The ground is around 2.8 miles from the station and a taxi should cost around £6. Trains leave Marylebone at , , , , and tomrorow night. BY BUS The best way to reach Adams Park from High Wycombe is via the Arriva football special bus service, which is priced at £2 for a single fare or £3 return for adults and £1 for a single (£1.50 return) for juniors and concessionary bus pass holders. For tomorrow night’s fixture, buses will leave at the following times: Wycombe Railway Station: 17.50 and 18.50 Eden Bus Station: 18.00 and 19.00 Handy Cross Park & Ride: 18.10 and 19.10 Adams Park: 18.20 and 19.20 The return journey from the ground will take place ten minutes after the final whistle, but can be very crowded. AWAY PUBS Many Fulham supporters will opt for the large away fans’ marquee that will be open at Adams Park again tomorrow night and there is a mobile catering unit, selling hot food, drinks and pies located nearby. There are not many pubs located near the ground, due to it being on an industrial estate. The exception is The Hourglass in Sands (144 Chapel Lane, High Wycombe HP12 4BY, tel: 01494 511125 ), which is about fifteen minutes walk from the ground, sells real ale and has previously welcomed away fans. Your other best bets are located in Wycombe itself. The Falcon , a popular Wetherspoon’s pub in the town centre, has catered for Fulham fans on a number of previous visits (9 Cornmarket, High Wycombe HP11 2AX, tel: 01494 538610). The nearby O’Neills offers a big screen, with the usual food and drink fare (Paul’s Row, High Wycombe HP11 2HQ, tel: 01494 532499). Closer to the station are The Bootlegger (Crendon Street, High Wycombe, HP13 6NQ) and The Flint Cottage (Amersham Hill, High Wycombe, HP13 6NQ). LIVE COMMENTARY BBC Radio London are providing live commentary of the game from Adams Park at 7pm on their BBC London Sport show. Our Supporter Liaison Officer, Kristine Green, gives fans a rundown of all the key matchday information in preparation for tomorrow’s game. What kit are we in for this game? We’re in black and white for this game What’s the ticket information? There are strictly no tickets available at the turnstile on the day. Tickets can be purchased online by clicking here. Adult – £22.00 Senior 65+ – £15.00 12-17 – £10.00 Under 12 – £5.00 How do I get to the ground? Postcode for the ground is BB5 5BX Leave the M65 at junction 7, heading towards Clitheroe at the roundabout. Turn right at the lights and follow directions for the A678. Follow the road and then turn right towards Accrington on the A680. Carry straight on through the next set of lights at the Greyhound Pub. Take the first left after the Crown Pub onto Livingstone Road. What stand are we in? Around 500 are in the away Coppice Terrace with the rest of the allocation located in away seating. When do turnstiles open? Turnstiles open at 1.30pm Where is the best place to park? Plenty of street parking around the ground with no resident restrictions. Limited parking is available for a donation, 50 metres away from the stadium entrance on Livingstone Road (BB5 5BX) Parking for disabled supporters? Disabled parking is on a first come first basis as marked above with ‘parking for a donation’. Nearby street parking is also available. What is the nearest train station to the stadium and what is the approximate distance and walking time? Accrington Station is on the East Lancashire line and approximately a 15-minute walk from the stadium. Recommended pubs for away fans? Coley’s Bar at the ground is open from 12pm but requires a match ticket, Town fans are welcome to use this after the game too. You can also grab a bite to eat here. Alternatively, you have the Crown and The Grey Horse, all near to the ground. In town you have The Stanley, Bee’s Knees and The Commercial (Spoons) – they’re all about a 20-minute walk from the ground. Food available in the area? Non pub food is limited around the ground. There’s a chippy on Whalley Road which is on the walk to/from the town centre. There you have the usual chain outlets for food. Where is the nearest cash machine to the Stadium? There’s a cash machine on Whalley Road as you head towards town, but this has a charge. Plenty of free to use machines in town – which is a 20-minute walk from the ground. What food and drink is available on the concourse at the stadium? Inside the ground there is also a bar and standard football food. The ground is now cashless. Is there a programme? Accrington Stanley no longer produce a printed programme but have a digital copy. QR codes are available around the ground. What is the process for supporters looking to bring flags into the stadium? Flags are no problem – just make sure that they don’t cover any advertising or walkways. & REDBRIDGE For everyone joining us at The Hive Stadium for tomorrow’s fixture against Dagenham & Redbridge. We will be open from 11am and recommend arriving early to avoid the queues. From 11am all bars will be open for supporters – Legends Bar & Hive Bar for home fans and Bar 66 for away supporters. Our ticket office will be open from 11am tomorrow. The Home ticket office is located next to the main car park and the away ticket office is located around the back of the north stand. We recommend purchasing tickets online to save on waiting times. Tickets are still available to buy HERE! DIRECTIONS: BY CAR: From the North (M1) 1. Exit at Junction 4 of the M1 on to the A41 towards Harrow/Edgware 2. At the roundabout take the 3rd exit onto Spur Road/A410 3. At the next roundabout turn left on to the A5 4. After 300 metres turn right at the traffic lights on to Camrose Avenue 5. Continue straight along Camrose Avenue and The Hive will be on your right just after the width restriction. Match Details Fixture: Chesterfield vs Grimsby Town Venue: SMH Group Stadium Turnstiles Open: 6:30pm Kit Colour We will be wearing our Cream Third Kit for this fixture. Ticket Information Town were issued an allocation of 1,061 tickets, which have now sold out in full. There will be no further allocation available, and no tickets will be available on the day. Away Supporters Grimsby Town supporters will be located in the East Stand (Blocks E1 and E2). This is a side stand, rather than behind the goal as used in previous visits. Entry is via turnstiles E1–E3. Getting To The Ground Postcode: S41 8LF By Car: Leave the M1 at Junction 29 and follow signs for Chesterfield (A617) towards the town centre. Take the 4th exit at the first roundabout towards Sheffield (A61) At the Tesco roundabout, take the 1st exit At the next roundabout, take the 3rd exit (ASDA will be on your left) The stadium will be on your right-hand side Parking: Parking at the stadium is for permit holders only. Supporters are advised to use street parking around the ground, while being mindful of local restrictions. Please note: Sanforth Crescent and Nelson Street (opposite the stadium) are access only and should not be used. Recommended postcodes: S41 9AP S41 9BE S41 9BH Disabled Supporters: Parking for disabled supporters is available subject to availability. To book, please call 01246 269300. Cost: £12.00 By Train: The nearest station is Chesterfield, approximately a 20–30 minute walk from the stadium. Taxis are available outside the station for those who prefer not to walk. Food & Drink There are several options available around the ground: Retail park nearby featuring KFC (Lockoford Road, S41 7EW) North Sea Fish Bar and other takeaway options along Sheffield Road The Hub café, located behind the East Stand Inside the stadium, a range of food and drink is available, including: Pies and hot dogs Hot and cold drinks Alcohol Both cash and card payments are accepted. Cash Machines The nearest free cash machines are located at: ASDA Supermarket (Sheffield Road, S41 8JZ) Essex Garage next door Programme A printed matchday programme will be available around the ground, priced at £3 (cash only). Flags Flags are permitted but must: Carry a fire safety label Be used in line with steward instructions Recommended Pubs For Away Fans The designated away pub is: The Derby Tup (Sheffield Road) – Real ale and food available Other options include: Cricketers Inn (Stand Road) The Beer Parlour (Sheffield Road) Lock Keeper (Brewers Fayre, Tapton Lock Hill) Victoria Club (Sheffield Road) Mariners Respects We’re proud of the outstanding support Grimsby Town receives both home and away, and we want everyone attending to enjoy the match in a welcoming and safe environment. Abusive, indecent, or discriminatory behaviour – including racist, homophobic, sexist, sectarian, xenophobic, or anti-disability actions – will not be tolerated. The Club may issue bans, including indefinite bans, to anyone engaging in such behaviour. We look forward to seeing the Mariners backed loudly and proudly at the SMH Group Stadium. Safe travels to all supporters making the journey.
